nytimes.com.title: King Charles Meets Both Joy and Criticism on Caribbean Tour
nytimes.com.text:
More than 100 residents of the South American nation of Guyana lined up outside an Indigenous cultural site on Friday, eager for a glimpse of King Charles III, the figurehead of a British state that ruled here until independence almost 60 years ago. Some brought their small children.
Standing nearby in the searing sun, about two dozen protesters waved signs demanding that Britain pay reparations and apologize for the millions of enslaved Africans who were trafficked across the Atlantic in the 1700s and 1800s. They chanted loudly: “Not our king!”
As Charles makes a seven-day visit to three of Britain’s former colonies, his country’s history of slavery — and what he and the British government should say or do about it — continues to divide opinion across the once-sprawling empire.
“They bought slaves, sold slaves and made money from slavery and then paid the slave owners millions of dollars and the slaves and their descendants got nothing,” said Elton Campbell, referring to British legislation passed in the 1830s that compensated slave owners for the freeing of slaves after the country outlawed the practice.
Mr. Campbell, a 76-year-old insurance agent in Guyana’s capital, added, “Let the king explain that to the nation and our Black people around the world.”
For the first time on Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham of Britain said the government was open to offering a formal apology for the country’s role in the slave trade, which he described as “brutal and barbaric.”

nytimes.com.title: Do Animals Grieve?
nytimes.com.text:
Do Animals Grieve?
Coyotes are not obvious romantics. Their habit of stalking across the landscape alone has earned them a reputation as solitary creatures — and not particularly popular ones, with a public image that ranges from troublesome nuisance to dangerous predator.
But they are deeply loyal mates. They remain with their partners for life, grooming each other, sharing food and raising pups together. “Basically, until death do us part,” said Sara Freeman, a neuroscientist at Utah State University.
In her airy, third-floor laboratory, Dr. Freeman is trying to understand how coyote couples forge these bonds — and what happens when they are broken.
“This is a widowed brain,” she said, pulling a few foil-wrapped packages from an ultracold freezer one morning in August. Each held a block of brain tissue, collected from a female coyote who had outlived her mate.
A student began shaving the frozen tissue into paper-thin slices, using the tip of a small paintbrush to nudge each translucent cross-section onto a glass slide. Later, the researchers would examine the samples, looking for neurological signs of “what we would call a grief state,” Dr. Freeman said.

nytimes.com.title: Deportees Turn to TikTok to Document Life Starting Over
nytimes.com.text:
When Laymone Khambounleung was deported to Laos last August, his mother’s relatives met him at a holding facility. He did not know what they looked like.
It was one of many unknowns Mr. Khambounleung faced when he was removed from the United States, the only country he had really known, over convictions including burglary and threatening a family member.
Now, he is learning to navigate daily life in a country he left four decades ago as a baby. Mr. Khambounleung, who grew up in Louisiana, can speak Lao, but he cannot read or write in the language. He has befriended other men who, like him, left the country as children and assimilated in the United States.
And like deportees across Latin America, Africa and elsewhere in Asia, he is sharing glimpses of his life on social media, hoping to raise awareness about the challenges and opportunities people face when they are removed to unfamiliar home countries, or third countries to which they have no ties. For some, their online posts also provide an income.
In Mr. Khambounleung’s videos, his reactions to sights in Laos, narrated in his Louisiana accent, have attracted millions of views.
“It’s all new to me too,” Mr. Khambounleung, 41, said in an interview. “I wanted to let the whole world see the Lao culture also, experience it with me while I’m experiencing it.”

nytimes.com.title: Up in the Clouds With the Pope, It’s Still Commercial
nytimes.com.text:
A day before Pope Leo XIV departed for France in September, on the fourth major international trip of his papacy, the crew of the plane he was to use, known colloquially as “Shepherd One,” gathered to learn the inviolable rules of the flight.
No selfies with the pope, said Gennaro Anastasio, the senior cabin manager, as he reeled off a list of dos and don’ts.
If the Holy Father offers his hand, shake it, don’t kiss it. Make no personal requests of the pontiff, such as asking that he pray for family members. Check the bathroom at the front of the plane — the one used by the pope — several times throughout the flight and keep it spotless. Don’t speak directly to the pope, but talk to his personal secretaries.
And mind your language. The men wearing black robes with red sashes and skullcaps should be addressed as “eminenza,” the salutation for cardinals, the highest-ranking clergy except for the pope. The men in purple caps and sashes are bishops and should be greeted as “eccellenza.”
“Don’t mess up,” said Mr. Anastasio, an impish 67-year-old. “If, though, you call a bishop ‘eminenza,’ he’ll say, ‘No I’m not an eminenza,’” he added with a chuckle. “And you can say, ‘You’ll become one!’”

nytimes.com.title: Why Did Snakes Lose Their Legs? And 9 More Animal Mysteries
nytimes.com.text:
Why Did Snakes Lose Their Legs? And 9 More Animal Mysteries
Why did snakes lose their legs?
Scientists know that all snakes descend from a reptile that lived about 160 million years ago. But that ancestor had four legs. What rendered those limbs unnecessary?
Some scientists contend that being limbless gave early snakes an advantage — a leg up, as it were — on land, by helping them thrive in narrow, underground tunnels. Others propose that elongated bodies evolved for swimming in the water.
Fossils highlight the debate. In 2015, researchers examined X-ray models of the inner ear of an animal closely related to the ancestor of modern-day snakes. The anatomy suggested that these ancestors lived underground. But fossils of primitive snakes with developed hind legs have also been found in marine limestone, suggesting that the first snakes may have lived underwater.
“It’s hard to tell what exact conditions drove the evolution of this body plan,” said Tiago Simões, an evolutionary biologist at Princeton.

nytimes.com.title: A Lesson From Germany
nytimes.com.text:
Over the past few weeks, Donald Trump has been negotiating a lot of potential business deals with Vladimir Putin. His administration has discussed lifting sanctions, including on Moscow’s flagship government investment fund; in some cases, that’s already happened.
What’s going on? Some see favoritism toward an autocrat Trump has seemed to admire (and an attempt to lower U.S. fuel prices before midterm elections tomorrow.) The administration argues that it’s all part of a broader effort to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
For me, as a German, it’s all a bit of a déjà vu. When I was Berlin bureau chief a few years ago, I wrote a lot about Germany’s longstanding policy of trying to influence Russian behavior with business and energy deals. Even after Moscow invaded Crimea, Berlin approved another major gas pipeline. The policy was abandoned only after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Today, I write about the lessons of Germany’s failed Russia policy for the Trump administration.
Trump’s Ostpolitik
First, there was the potential Lukoil deal.
Last month, my colleagues reported that the Trump administration wanted a U.S.-led consortium to buy the international assets of one of Russia’s biggest energy companies.
Next, the administration waived some U.S. sanctions to buy Russian diesel and leaned on Europe to resume buying Russian gas. Then we learned that it considered a proposal to buy Russian technology to gain access to and liquefy natural gas in Alaska.

nytimes.com.title: ‘This Hour Has 22 Minutes,’ a Canadian Sketch Show, Beats American Late Night to the Punchline
nytimes.com.text:
Hours after Katie Zacharia was fired as White House press secretary five days into the job, the Canadian satirical series “This Hour Has 22 Minutes” captured the chaos in a sketch posted online — beating American late-night comedy shows to the punchline.
Some 48 hours later, and a week before the rapper Nicki Minaj traveled on Air Force One to rally for President Trump in Michigan, “22 Minutes” imagined the MAGA darling as Ms. Zacharia’s successor.
In both cases, the creative team on the show, Canada’s version of “Saturday Night Live,” did not wait for their weekly broadcast. The polished sketches went straight to the show’s TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, attracting nearly 24 million views.
For the last 34 years, this sketch comedy show has reliably roasted Canadian and American politics, culture and quirks. But “22 Minutes” is having a renaissance buoyed by Mr. Trump — in particular his trade war, tariffs, threats and insults toward Canada. Television audiences are up, and social media viewership is growing rapidly.
“Social media has opened up our show beyond what I thought was capable,” said Stacey McGunnigle, a cast member and writer who has created and portrayed many MAGA women, most memorably Karoline Leavitt, Natalie Harp and, ever so briefly, Ms. Zacharias.

nytimes.com.title: China’s Message to Its Rivals: You Need What We Make
nytimes.com.text:
They are among the biggest machines in the world: steel cylinders, some as long as a football field, armed with rotating discs that can chew through rock to clear the way for roads and railways. Known as tunnel boring machines, they are made by only a handful of companies, mostly in factories in China.
India uses them to dig tunnels, including in the Himalayas, to improve its ability to send troops to defend its contested border with China. But starting next month, Beijing is likely to be able to control whether India gets to buy them.
The machines are part of a broader effort by China to control what leaves Chinese factories and laboratories for foreign lands. In the past month, Beijing has moved to control the exports of dozens of technologies, including drones, artificial intelligence models and agents, and certain processes used to develop advanced medicines and to make solar panels.
The overall push could make it much harder for companies in the United States and elsewhere to set up solar energy equipment factories that would compete against Chinese manufacturers. And it could soon make it more difficult for anyone outside China to gain access to the latest and most powerful Chinese A.I. models.
The planned restrictions show that Beijing is doubling down on its strategy of making Chinese factories indispensable to the world, even as many governments are alarmed by their countries’ dependence on China and are pushing to be less reliant.

cnn.com.title: Fake warnings of nuclear attack posted on hacked Russian and Ukrainian emergency apps
cnn.com.text: Emergency warning apps in Russia and Ukraine were hacked on Sunday, according to authorities in both countries. It’s not clear whether the hacking of the apps is linked. The apps warn the public of missile, drone and other threats. But rather than spread panic, the fake messages appear to have had little impact on war-weary civilians – and instead began to generate some imaginative memes. The messages posted on Ukraine’s public air raid app late on Sunday claimed that the capital Kyiv and other areas were subject to nuclear ⁠and chemical alerts as well as the threat of street combat. Another fake message said Russia’s ⁠hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian air force said ‌on Telegram. “There ⁠is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel!” The app had been recently updated to show the movement of drones in real time. Stepan Tanasiychuk, who leads Ukraine’s Air Raid Alert project, said Monday it was gradually being restored, with new yellow and red alert levels currently available on the map. “The team is taking additional measures to secure the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future, Tanasiychuk said on Instagram. “We realise how much unnecessary worry and inconvenience this has caused.” In a separate event, ⁠the mobile app of Russia’s emergencies ministry – Emercom - was hit by a “massive cyberattack” that resulted in ⁠”the spread of false information to the public,” state news agency TASS quoted ⁠the ‌ministry as saying. One of the fake messages, which appeared on the app in the Moscow region as well as in areas across Russia, claimed that “NUCLEAR WARHEADS ON P1-SUN DELIVERY SYSTEMS have been launched across ALL regions of Russia.” It then added an expletive-laden warning. Efforts to address the vulnerability and restore normal operation are underway, the ministry said. It played down the significance of the incident, saying that alerts are distributed through regional and municipal systems such as sirens and loudspeakers, SMS messages and media broadcasts. “All electronic resources belonging to our government agencies are under constant threat of cyberattacks,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday. “As technologies, including AI, continue to evolve, the threat of cyberattacks is growing,” he said. Few people appear to have fallen for the false messages. Some suggested it had undermined their trust in official warnings. One Russian user said they had deleted the Emercom app “and I won’t be installing anything like that again. How can they leave apps like this vulnerable? It’s complete nonsense, of course, but what if it weren’t?” Among comments on Instagram among Russian users of the app, one said the fake alert “was written in such a way that it’s impossible to believe it’s real.” Another wrote: “It was hard to believe such nonsense. … How did (the Emergencies ministry) even let this happen.. let themselves get hacked.” “You wake up, open Threads and see tons of posts like this,” another commented. “BUT THANKFULLY IT’S FAKE!” Others joked that they had not even received the warning, with one writing: “This information was reserved for the chosen ones, don’t worry, you’re not important enough to be hacked.” One resident of Kyiv responded to the alert about street fighting by posting: “Good thing our mayor is a boxer.” Another social media post made up a long list of additional threats, including: “Cat invasion — Cats are taking over the city. Hide the sausages. Pancake emergency — The city has run out of pancakes. Stay home. Clown attack — Clowns have been spotted in the city. Do not go outside without a mask. Alien invasion — UFOs are approaching Earth. Prepare for contact.”

cnn.com.title: Here’s where Trump’s housing agenda stands before midterms
cnn.com.text: America’s housing market is paralyzed, with buyers pulling back and builders growing more pessimistic ahead of the midterms. Adding to the strain: Mortgage rates have surged back above 7% in recent weeks, hitting a three-year high of 7.4% last month. The average 30-year fixed rate eased slightly to 7.24% last week, according to Freddie Mac. America’s housing woes run deep. Homebuilding hasn’t kept pace with demand since the 2008 financial crash decimated the country’s housing industry. Elevated mortgage rates have also pushed up monthly payments for buyers, all while home prices keep climbing each month to record-high levels. As of the third quarter, the average household must earn $115,600 in income to afford the typical cost of housing – that’s 75% higher than the $66,200 required five years ago, according to Oxford Economics. That has translated to the number of homes trading hands to hover near 30-year lows for the past three years. President Donald Trump won the 2024 election amid growing frustration over the cost of living. Two years later, affordability remains a defining issue heading into the midterm elections, as Americans continue to grapple with high prices for housing, groceries, gasoline and other everyday essentials. But while the White House has taken some steps aimed at housing affordability during Trump’s second term, largely through executive orders, the issue has featured relatively little in the administration’s public messaging over the last two years. Trump, who was a real estate developer for decades, said on the 2024 campaign trail that his plan for tackling the cost of housing would primarily rely on lowering interest rates. He doubled down on that promise this year. “People that own their homes, we’re going to keep them wealthy. We’re going to keep those prices up. We’re not going to destroy the value of their homes,” Trump said at a cabinet meeting at the start of this year. “We’re going to make it easier to buy. We’re going to get interest rates down.” For a brief moment, mortgage rates appeared poised to fall. In January, Trump directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the government-sponsored enterprises that underpin much of the US mortgage market, to buy $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities in an effort to push rates lower. Rates dropped earlier in the year, dipping below 6% in February for the first time since 2022, when the Federal Reserve began its fight against post-pandemic inflation, raising hopes that cheaper borrowing would ease the housing affordability crunch. But the reprieve was short-lived. Mortgage rates climbed once again after the US began its war with Iran, and have remained elevated since. Mortgage rates are tied to the 10-year Treasury yield, which moves with investors’ expectations for inflation, economic growth and the Fed’s interest rate policy. In recent months, the bond market has been hit by renewed inflation fears, an oil-price shock linked to the Iran conflict, rising federal deficits and a surge in AI investment. And early signs point to the bond market turmoil adding to the housing market’s woes. Pending home sales fell to a record low in September, in data going back to 2001, according to the National Association of Realtors. New home construction also dropped to a four-month low, Census Bureau data showed, as elevated borrowing costs continue to weigh on the market. The gloom is spreading to builders, too: Homebuilder sentiment, a measure of how confident the industry feels about the housing market, sank to a 14-year low in September, according to the latest survey from the National Association of Home Builders. Overall, the housing market’s issues are going to take a long time to solve. But some bright spots remain: Rents have stabilized nationally over the last few years, said Yonah Freemark, a principal research associate in the Housing and Communities Division at the Urban Institute. That’s partly due to increased multifamily apartment construction between 2020 and 2024, which helped relieve demand pressures, he added. Trump’s complicated housing agenda Overall, the federal government may not have much power to affect the housing market’s supply, because zoning and permitting decisions are made by local and state governments, said Daryl Fairweather, Redfin’s chief economist. “In places that have been builder-friendly and have allowed supply to meet demand, we have seen prices come down and affordability improve,” Fairweather said, pointing to Austin, Texas, as an example, which has seen home prices fall from their peak in 2022. The city expanded its housing stock by roughly 30% between 2015 and 2024, according to Pew. Last month, Trump signed an executive order that directs federal agencies to ease the burden of mortgage insurance and refinance costs, among other measures. “President Trump has been laser-focused on making housing more affordable,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. “The President will not stop fighting until the American Dream of homeownership is within reach for every American, which is why he continues to sign bold new executive orders and calls on Congress to pass further legislation.” But the White House’s tariff regime has added to the cost of building housing, according to the NAHB – and deportations have slowed home-building projects in many areas that rely on an immigrant construction workforce. Some White House proposals to improve housing affordability never materialized, such as a 50-year mortgage or the ability to make mortgages portable, which would allow homeowners with lower rates to take their existing loan to a new property when they move. Most housing initiatives were also handled by executive order, rather than through legislation. The one exception was the ROAD to Housing Act, which Congress passed with broad bipartisan support this summer. The bill included measures to increase the supply of housing and a provision to limit large investor purchases of single-family homes, which codified into law one of Trump’s executive orders. However, Trump allowed the measure to become law without his signature, rather than signing it or vetoing it. At the time, Trump called the housing bill “a big yawn” and “of minor importance.”

cnn.com.title: Why your party will (or won’t) have a good Election Day
cnn.com.text: Election Day is tomorrow, and while there are high expectations for Democrats, it’s impossible to know for certain what will happen in the race for control of Congress. Many Democrats are worried about the polls overestimating the strength of their candidates again, while President Donald Trump and some in the GOP seem sanguine in the final days. So, what if Republicans overperform or even keep their majorities? And what if Democrats have a historic midterm? Let’s break down how each of those scenarios could happen. Why Republicans could have a good night The polls were wrong A Kansas Senate poll released by The Washington Post on Friday epitomized the nightmare scenario for Democrats: that polls — especially in red states — could systematically underestimate Republicans because they don’t respond to them as much. This “nonresponse bias” led to polls being off in the 2016 and 2020 presidential elections. It hasn’t been seen as much in the midterms in the Trump era, but that doesn’t mean it couldn’t happen. And given Democrats are chasing a lot of red territory, this would likely take a big chunk out of their gains. The Senate map was just so red Consider this: Even if the margins of the 2024 vote uniformly shifted toward Democrats by 10 points in every state, Democrats would still get to only 49 Senate seats. In other words, they could notch one of the biggest popular-vote victories in decades and still not win the Senate because this year’s battlefield is overwhelmingly made up of Trump states. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, which requires them flipping at least two states that Trump won by double digits. (To underscore the difficulty of the playing field for Democrats, they are on offense in only one state where Kamala Harris won in 2024.) The GOP pulled an upset in Maine and/or Michigan The number of GOP Senate seats Democrats need to pick off increases if they lose the ones they’re defending — namely Maine, Michigan or both. Democrats probably should have put those away by now, but haven’t — in part thanks to Democratic Senate nominees who aren’t running as well as the gubernatorial nominees in the same state. The GOP’s gerrymandering was too successful It’s conventional wisdom that the House very likely flips to Democrats. But if Republicans pull the unthinkable and keep their majority — or even just keep Democrats’ gains to a minimum — the GOP’s brazen mid-decade gerrymandering push will likely have played a role. The effort, which Democrats weren’t able to match because they lack as much control in state governments, will have allowed Republicans to win as many as nine additional seats. They surely won’t win all of those, but the creation of those safer GOP seats raised the bar for Democrats. Voters didn’t care much about the Iran war, corruption and other unpopular Trump ideas So much of what Trump has done has been unpopular — often by large margins. But if Republicans do better than expected, a big reason might be that voters didn’t care enough about Trump’s actions for them to matter. Maybe they think his White House ballroom and efforts to glorify and enrich himself are gauche, but that behavior isn’t as important to Trump’s base as culture wars and opposing Democrats. Maybe they don’t like the Iran war, but since it’s not a conventional ground war with many US troop deaths, it’s not as front of mind. Why Democrats could have a good night Trump’s historic unpopularity By many measures, Trump is the most unpopular president in modern history heading into a midterm. He’s 30 points underwater in the CNN Poll of Polls, with 34% approving of his job performance and 64% disapproving. And Trump is so ever-present that it’s nearly impossible for Republicans to distance themselves from him. It’s simply very difficult to win elections — no matter how favorable the Senate map is to Republicans — when people dislike the face of the GOP by a nearly 2-to-1 margin. Trump’s coalition broke down Trump swept the swing states in the 2024 election in large part by making big gains with young people (especially men), Latinos and infrequent voters. But the polls suggest all three groups have turned sharply against him. And it’s not just that; his tariffs and the Iran war appear to have damaged Trump’s standing with his most reliable and consistent demographic: White voters without college degrees. The GOP hoped Trump was building a lasting new coalition. But it hasn’t turned out when he hasn’t been on the ballot, and now it might desert the GOP. Trump’s neglect of affordability Trump’s cardinal political sin might have been his utter neglect of what almost always polls as voters’ chief concern: affordability. He was elected in large part because of high inflation under former President Joe Biden and his own promises to fix it quickly. But Trump not only launched policies that exacerbated economic problems — a recent New York Federal Reserve study found the overall cost of consumer goods would have fallen without his tariffs — he also called affordability a “hoax” and falsely claimed he had fixed the problem. Polls showed Americans never bought that, though. Around three-quarters said he and his administration hadn’t focused enough on affordability. And more Americans blame Trump for economic problems than ever blamed Biden. Broken promises Related to the two preceding items is that Trump simply didn’t do the things he promised. He said he wasn’t going to start wars, but he did. He said he was going to fix inflation, and it’s now worse. A recent AP-NORC poll found that 54% of Americans said Trump didn’t try to keep his promises. And even among those who said he did try, more said he had failed to actually keep them (28%) than said he kept them (17%). That’s 8 in 10 Americans who said he’s failed to keep his promises. Podcaster Joe Rogan, who backed Trump in 2024, has been big on this. It’s one thing to break promises when the economy is good (as Trump did in his first term); it’s another to break them on voters’ central issue. The GOP mobilized non-White voters — in the wrong way Perhaps no demographic has swung against Trump by as much as Latino voters. That’s in part thanks to his economic policies, but also a mass-deportation effort that is widely seen as overzealous. There is also some evidence that the Supreme Court further weakening the Voting Rights Act and Republicans gutting heavily Black congressional districts could be mobilizing Black voters. That demographic, especially, could play a major role in Senate races that Democrats are targeting such as in Florida, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina, as well as those they’re defending like in Michigan. Corruption Corruption has emerged as a major concern for Americans — sometimes even polling above prices. But more significantly, there is growing evidence that voters’ concerns about corruption are more of a problem for Republicans than Democrats, perhaps because of a spate of headlines about Trump’s self-enrichment and members of his administration apparently leveraging their positions for financial gain. CNN and New York Times/Siena polls have shown Democrats leading Republicans on the issue by 7 and 11 points, respectively. And a CBS News poll showed 52% of Americans said corruption would increase if Republicans win the midterms versus just 37% who said the same if Democrats won.

cnn.com.title: The high-tech efforts to restore ‘climate hero’ mangroves
cnn.com.text: Gangly, densely rooted, and waxy-leaved, mangrove trees may look strange but don’t let their appearance fool you; these plants are nothing short of magical. There are more than 50 “true” mangrove species of trees and shrubs known to grow in the intertidal zone of shorelines in tropical and subtropical climates. Their unique look is thanks to a variety of adaptations in their roots and leaves that make them able to survive conditions including the high salinity of seawater, low-oxygen mud, and constantly changing tides. “Mangroves are beneficial in so many ways,” Dr. Amna Almansoori, a marine scientist at the Environment Agency­ Abu Dhabi (EAD) told CNN. “I really love mangroves!” Almansoori isn’t alone in her affinity for these plants. Mangroves support wildlife that lives in and around them — including at least 340 threatened species globally — acting as a habitat for everything from manatees to monkeys. They even act as a source of food as their leaves shed into the sediment around them, breaking down to form nutrient-rich organic matter to feed a variety of wildlife. The tidal trees protect coastal communities from the impacts of storms and floods, by acting as buffers that slow the swell of waves and reducing the height of a storm surge before water reaches land. Their roots stabilize the sediment in the soil around them, building ground and counteracting coastal erosion. Mangroves are also one of the most effective carbon sinks, able to absorb and store more than four times as much carbon dioxide as the average terrestrial forest. According to the Mangrove Alliance, the trees are responsible for storing 21 billion tons of carbon dioxide globally, something they can do for thousands of years. “From a climate perspective,” Almansoori said. “I would say that mangroves are heroes.” Sowing seeds of hope Mangroves first became a priority in Abu Dhabi in the late 1960s, shortly before the era of its oil boom, which brought a period of rapid urbanization for the emirate. Coastal development resulted in a loss of mangrove cover across the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The late Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan initiated parallel restoration and plantation programs, making Abu Dhabi a pioneer of mangrove conservation. The United Nations Environment Program estimated a 35% decline in global mangroves from 1980 to 2000, before the rate of loss fell by 44% between 2000 and 2020, according to the Mangrove Alliance. In contrast, Abu Dhabi saw its mangrove cover increase by 92% between 1987 and 2022. These days, “You see a thriving forest. From 3,000 hectares, now we have 17,600 hectares,” Almansoori said. The Abu Dhabi Mangrove Initiative (ADMI) describes its work as “science-based restoration,” using data, scientific mapping and monitoring to inform its conservation. It is working toward the UAE’s goal of planting 100 million mangrove trees by 2030; in 2023 alone, the ADMI distributed over 6 million mangrove seeds across Abu Dhabi using specially adapted drones. While planting by hand involves sending large groups of people to sensitive natural areas and risking disruption to the ecosystem, the initiative’s custom-built drones reduce this impact. The drones can travel long distances and access more remote areas that ADMI research deems is most opportune for planting. Each drone can carry approximately 6,000 seeds, scattering them into tidal mud to germinate and bring new mangroves to life. Turning the tide While they might act as a force against climate change, mangroves too are at risk from the effects of a warming world. As protection efforts have strengthened, mangrove numbers have seen small gains over the past decade, according to Global Mangrove Watch. But some countries have continued to see a net decline since the start of the decade including Myanmar, Indonesia and Nigeria. For these nations, the loss of mangroves threatens the supply of food, shelter, and the lives of those living near the shore. In Abu Dhabi, mangroves are still classified as endangered despite the overall increase in coverage, due to the threats posed by climate change — one of the most significant being rising sea levels. “A lot of water can suffocate them, but less water won’t help them grow,” Almansoori explained. If the seas rise faster than the height of the sediment mangroves grow on, the plants may be submerged. For the ADMI, protecting and restoring existing mangroves is a priority. A recently launched mangrove hydrological restoration project hopes to study the optimal water flow for mangrove health and hydrological conditions needed for long-term recovery of degraded mangroves. To Almansoori, it’s vital that increasing mangrove coverage is done with their long-term health and conservation in mind. “We do want areas to increase in terms of coverage, but we would like to see them increase in a healthy manner,” she said. “So that we can see them thrive [not just] for biodiversity, but also for mankind and for climate change.”

cnn.com.title: How officials are preparing for Election Day disruptions — including from Trump
cnn.com.text: Election officials have spent months preparing to run the 2026 vote — and bracing for what could disrupt it. They’re training workers, tightening security and readying legal challenges for threats that could stretch well beyond Election Day. “Lately we have to take into account really horrible, worst-case scenarios, whether that is outside actors or foreign actors,” Maricopa County Supervisor Thomas Galvin said. “But the most important thing is that we have to be prepared.” Planning for trouble is part of running elections. But this year’s preparations by state and local officials come amid a ramped-up campaign by President Donald Trump and his allies to undermine confidence in voting integrity and assert greater federal control over elections. “Sadly, a new hazard on the list this time that’s never been on the list before is the possibility that our own federal government would try to interfere somehow, directly or indirectly,” Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, a Democrat, told CNN. What Trump could do Officials have spent months considering what that might look like: a last-minute executive order, ballot seizures, federal agents at the polls or efforts to undermine trust in the results. Trump and his allies continue to allege widespread noncitizen voting and election fraud, including in midterm voting already underway. They have threatened to prosecute election officials who fail to secure the vote or allow noncitizens to cast ballots and have filed lawsuits to restrict the counting of disputed ballots in California and the certification of results in Alaska. “The more this stuff comes up, and the fact that it is based on so much disinformation or half-truths, it’s incredibly frustrating,” said Matt Crane, the Executive Director of the Colorado County Clerks Association and a Republican. “We’re going to keep working our asses off to make sure the election runs well on Tuesday and that people can have confidence in the process.” Some election leaders have prepared for the administration to potentially take even more drastic steps on or after Election Day, like disrupting polling places, confiscating ballots or election equipment, challenging the results or going after election administrators. So far, however, Trump’s attempts to interfere have mostly played out in the courts and with letters demanding that election officials set aside certain ballots so that those who cast them could be investigated — requests administrators have been rebuffing. Early in-person voting has been underway in states across the country — in some states, for weeks — and there have been no reports of major disruptions involving the federal government. But officials are prepared in case that changes. Last week, Trump attacked Minnesota’s elections, as he has other states’, writing on Truth Social that a Republican candidate could lose only “if they cheat by playing games with the Ballots as they come in.” “The Federal Government will be watching closely,” Trump wrote. For Minnesota leaders, it only validated their concerns and preparations, which included two trips to closed-door conferences this year where they met with officials from other states to game out doomsday scenarios — and how they’d respond. “We are sort of shadow boxing here,” Simon said. “We don’t know when or if the blow will land, and hopefully it never will. But we would be foolish not to be thinking through worst case scenario.” Others fear the biggest threat of federal disruption could come after the midterms, fueled by challenges to the results and allegations of fraud. “What’s the administration going to say to try to put a cloud over everything?” Crane said. “And then as all that rhetoric ratchets up over here, the concern is always that violence against election officials and our facilities increases as that disinformation increases too.” Fearing disruptions at the polls State and local leaders have been drilling poll workers and coordinating with local police on how to respond if ICE officers or other federal agents show up at voting sites. Wisconsin’s Elections Commission advised poll leaders to alert municipal clerks, inspect badges or warrants, document encounters and keep agents outside when possible. Cherokee County, Georgia, led by a Republican election director, added similar training for its poll workers after its Trump-aligned State Election Board asked the administration to investigate Georgia’s election systems. Arlington County, Virginia, sued to keep armed federal officers away from its polling places. In Arizona, the voting-rights group LUCHA has trained election observers to watch for immigration agents. Minnesota officials have spent months reassuring voters that polling places are safe and officials are ready if ICE shows up, following a major immigration enforcement surge in Minneapolis earlier this year. Some local leaders have rehearsed an even more disruptive scenario: federal agents arriving to seize ballots or voting equipment. Boulder County, Colorado conducted trainings for election officials on what federal warrants look like and encouraged them to strategize with the county attorney’s office on how to respond. Others in the state focused on airtight chain-of-custody records so they can pinpoint what’s been taken if ballots are seized. “This is new territory, I think, for just about everybody,” Boulder County Clerk Molly Fitzpatrick told CNN. “So, we’ve provided guidance around making sure that you always follow the law.” For Fulton County, Georgia, that concern follows the FBI search  of an election hub in January, when agents took hundreds of boxes of ballots and records from the 2020 election. County Board Chairman Robb Pitts says he still doesn’t know where the records are and is fighting to recover them. He fears another intervention on Election Day. “Worst possible scenario: Election Day, before the votes are counted, they come in, confiscate the ballots, take them off. What do we do now?” Pitts told CNN. “People say that’s impossible. Well, what I’ve learned with this administration: the impossible is always possible. We’re prepared, though.” The Justice Department plans to send more than 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states has opened another front. They’re federal lawyers — not law enforcement — with narrowly defined powers, but election leaders fear a DOJ reshaped under Trump could push past those limits. Minnesota and Wyoming are among several states barring DOJ monitors from direct access to polling places. Wyoming’s Republican leaders accused two monitors of overstepping during the August primary by seeking to question voters and workers and inspect voting machines. Colorado offered access with conditions, including an escort from the secretary of state’s office. DOJ declined and will keep its monitors outside. Meanwhile, Minnesota is sending state observers to keep tabs on their federal counterparts — effectively monitoring the monitors. The administration says its monitors, a longstanding presence in US elections, won’t disrupt voting. Their role is to observe and document potential problems for post-election investigations and challenges. “What’s concerning is that they are looking for something. Something no other election monitor has ever been able to find,” Ingham County, Michigan Clerk Barb Byrum told CNN. Byrum has served in her post since 2013 and has never seen DOJ monitors in her county until this year. She said she was suspicious of their presence during the August primary – because the DOJ’s justification included incorrect claims about long lines and improper balloting in her county – but things went smoothly. “They didn’t see anything out of the ordinary,” she added. “So why are they coming back? Well, they’re coming back, I think, to cast more doubt on the integrity of our elections.” Lawsuits ready to go States have pre-drafted potential legal challenges before any confrontation occurs. Others have preemptively hired outside attorneys. They’re prepared to rush to court and get immediate relief or an injection if federal interference becomes a reality. Nevada Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar described preparing “Mad Libs” legal filings, leaving names and jurisdictions blank so lawyers can move quickly, especially if agents come to the polls or attempt to confiscate machines or ballots. “We made sure to have pre-drafted legal finds and a lot of legal research completed and ready to go to be able to respond in moments if something is actually occurring,” Aguilar said. “And the top two major issues was one, federal agents had polling locations, and two, the feds coming in and taking the machines and the ballots.” Nevada is already under federal scrutiny. The Department of Homeland Security says it identified thousands of possible noncitizens registered to vote there — figures state leaders dispute. Nevada officials have received seven grand jury subpoenas in recent months, though they declined to discuss details, citing legal constraints. Aguilar says he has been told he is under DOJ investigation. His staff is juggling those demands with the work of running an election. “It’s mostly having to reassure them that we will work to protect them,” he said. DOJ issued subpoenas to California election officials and sued the state last month, alleging that roughly 20,000 possible noncitizens are on its voter rolls and may be voting in the midterms. The administration wants those ballots separated and withheld from the count until citizenship can be verified. Crane, the Republican head of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the local officials he works with have those subpoenas “in the back of their minds” as they try to carry out the election. “There’s more pressure now because you know one little mistake can be amplified into a national disinformation campaign,” Crane told CNN. ‘They want us talking about it’ Election officials are walking a delicate line heading into Election Day: preparing for the worst without making voters fear the polls. Arizona Secretary of State Adrian Fontes pushed back on concerns about federal action, saying he thinks fear is part of the administration’s strategy — and its threats run up against legal limits. “The threats themselves are the voter intimidation. The idea that voters are worried means that the administration is getting what they want,” Fontes told CNN. “I don’t mean to be blithe about it, but the reality is that until something happens, it’s just an empty threat.” Other election leaders share his concern that the administration’s promises to scrutinize the midterms could keep voters home. They stress that they have no evidence of planned Election Day disruptions that would prevent people from casting ballots. Their preparations, they say, are a precaution — not a reason to stay away. Still, Fontes has spent months making sure local officials understand states’ authority over elections and that local law enforcement is prepared to enforce the boundaries of federal oversight. His message: Anyone who interferes with voters will face consequences, whether an activist or a federal agent. “If they’re breaking the law, we’re going to prosecute them,” he said. “It’s just that simple.” Safety concerns for poll workers Election officials are also preparing in case private citizens, activists or partisan observers disrupt disrupting polling places and ballot-counting sites. Online, activists are already pushing recycled claims of rigged elections and alleged problems with ballots and voting machines. Minnesota charged two right-wing influencers, including James O’Keefe, with felony counts of unlawful voting and identity theft for a stunt they recorded at several polling places during the August primary. Officials fear those narratives could become ammunition to challenge results or undermine public trust in the outcome. Election offices have spent years strengthening their defenses against threats with added cameras, bullet-resistant glass and tighter access controls. In recent weeks, Georgia election workers have handled mail wearing gloves and masks after suspicious letters reached election offices and lawmakers nationwide. In Irwin County, Georgia, poll workers are getting another piece of equipment for Election Day: panic buttons.

cnn.com.title: The top 11 Senate seats most likely to flip, the day before the midterms
cnn.com.text: On the eve of the election, Democrats appear within striking distance of winning the Senate majority, but many seats in play are in toss-up territory in deep-red states that could still break in either party’s direction. Democrats have expanded the map in ways few predicted at the start of the year, and the national environment has seemed to favor the party for many months. President Donald Trump’s approval rating sits at 34%, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls average, and voter frustration on the economy, the Iran war and corruption appears to be driving Democratic energy across the country. And for the second time this year, CNN is expanding its list to reflect that. This list has expanded to 11 seats to add South Carolina, a red state that has grown competitive in late polling. Texas and Kansas – two other seats few envisioned being on the battleground map in January – have moved up in their positions. Democrats will need to flip four Republican-held seats while holding onto all their own to win the Senate majority this year. And Republicans are spending heavily to defend their Senate majority, fueled by President Donald Trump’s political network as well as tech titan Elon Musk. Over the final month of the midterms, Republicans are outspending Democrats on advertising in the 11 races on this list: $560 million to $521 million, according to AdImpact data. Excluding Georgia and North Carolina – where Republicans have all but waved the white flag – the gap is significantly larger, about $550 million to $469 million. Our ranking of the seats most likely to flip in November is based on CNN reporting, including conversations with strategists involved in Senate races, as well as our analysis of candidate fundraising, polling and the partisan environment in the states.  The final ranking is not a prediction of who will win individual races or which party will secure control of the US Senate, but they offer a snapshot of where the contests stand as the midterm campaign season ends. 1. North Carolina North Carolina is the Senate seat most likely to flip on Tuesday, with Democrats appearing on track to win their first Senate race in the state since 2008. Democrat Roy Cooper, the state’s former governor, was leading GOP Senate nominee Michael Whatley by 14 points among likely voters in a final poll from High Point University/YouGov. No one is expecting a Democratic margin of victory to be that large in a state Trump won three times. But aware of the issues here, Republicans have pulled back on spending in the final stretch. Democrats spent $10.4 million over the last two weeks compared to $2.5 million from the GOP. 2. Ohio The CNN Poll of Polls average shows former Sen. Sherrod Brown leading GOP Sen. Jon Husted by 5 points, 50% to 45%. Brown, who lost his bid for a fourth Senate term in 2024, moved early to define Husted, who was appointed to the seat vacated by Vice President JD Vance. Democrats have hit Husted hard on data centers, the Epstein files, and corruption. Their most-run ad in the final two weeks reminded voters of Husted’s connection to an energy scandal in the state. The top Republican ad during that same period focused on Brown’s stances on taxes and immigration. Ohio’s Senate race has seen the second most spending this cycle, and Republicans outspent Democrats by about $141 million to $102 million in October, according to AdImpact data. Ohio has trended rightward in the Trump era, and the president traveled to the state three times in the final month to help get Husted across the finish line. But his most widely circulated comments from these rallies focused more on complimenting Husted’s body than issues impacting voters. Ohio’s race for governor attracted heightened attention in the closing stretch as GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy ran a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent. Acton has led Ramaswamy in recent polls, further suggesting the landscape might be ripe for Democratic wins on Tuesday. 3. Texas Texas hasn’t elected a Democrat statewide in 32 years and a CNN Poll of Polls shows no clear leader in the race between James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton. But a perfect storm of conditions may converge to make the Democratic dream of turning Texas blue a reality, even as the red nature of the state and the onslaught of GOP spending could lead to Democratic heartbreak once again. A CNN Poll of Polls average shows no clear leader in the contest, but a pair of polls released in the last few days – including one from the New York Times/Siena and another from CNN – show Talarico performing ahead of Paxton, outside the margin of error. The CNN poll conducted by SSRS last month found the Democrat was benefiting from deeply negative impressions of Paxton and significant support among the Black, Latino and Asian voters in the state who turned toward Trump in 2024. Fueled by strong fundraising, Talarico dominated the airwaves for the summer months after Paxton’s defeat of GOP Sen. John Cornyn, who warned of a “massacre” for Republican candidates in Texas if the state’s embattled attorney general was the nominee. The GOP cavalry eventually came in for Paxton with more than $278 million in ad spending since the primary, according to AdImpact data. Musk – the largest disclosed donor in US politics – singlehandedly accounted for $168 million of the GOP spending on the race, which received more of his funds than any other contest. Much of the GOP attacks on Talarico have hinged on cultural issues, including criticizing his past statements on gender and religion. Texas leads all states in early voting with 7.7 million ballots cast, according to data from the Texas secretary of state. Early voting data has shown high turnout in Democratic counties. Latino voters, a voting bloc showing signs this year of shifting away from Trump, have made up a higher share of the early vote than the last election. Texas GOP Sen. Ted Cruz has sounded the alarm about the early voting surge, saying Friday on his podcast, “We could lose every single statewide race.” This is still Texas, a bastion of American conservatism. Trump won the state by double digits in 2024, and Republicans are depending on their base turning out in droves on Election Day despite some uneasiness around Paxton’s candidacy. Republicans are also watching how the option of a libertarian candidate might factor into voter decisions on Election Day. 4. Maine At the start of the cycle, Maine was viewed as one of Democrats’ top pickup opportunities. This Senate race was among the most volatile contests this cycle due to the sexual misconduct allegations around Graham Platner and his eventual exit from the race. One day out, a CNN Poll of Polls average shows Democrat Troy Jackson leading GOP Sen. Susan Collins by 4 points – 50% to 46%. Collins is the only GOP incumbent running in a state Kamala Harris won in 2024. And polling also has shown the race is a referendum on Collins, who is running for a sixth term. A CNN poll conducted by SSRS found about three-quarters of likely voters behind each candidate in Maine said their choice is motivated by Collins more than Jackson. The outstanding question is whether Collins can outrun her state’s negative views of the GOP and Trump. The senator continues to stress her independent approach, though Democrats argue she sides with Trump most of the time, including in their top ad in the final two weeks. GOP groups have flooded the state with ads reminding voters what Collins has achieved for the state. The top Republican ad in the closing weeks leveled political and personal attacks against Jackson, calling him “a crook and a creep.” 5. Alaska Alaska moves down two spots as a late-breaking development regarding the two Dan Sullivans could be a wild card. Republicans have long worried about the inclusion of a second Dan Sullivan, a former schoolteacher, on the four-way ranked-choice ballot in November, but The New York Times reporting alleging Democrats recruited a Senate candidate with the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan injected new uncertainty in the race. A NYT/Siena poll released Sunday showed no clear leader in the contest between Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola and Sen. Sullivan – 48% to 46% – suggesting a tightening in the race may have occurred. In August, Peltola came in 8 points ahead of the incumbent Sullivan in the state’s all-party primary in August. Alaska is notoriously difficult to poll. Peltola out-raised Sullivan in the first two weeks of October and had more cash on hand entering the final stretch. But the GOP slightly outpaced Democrats in ad buys in the state for the last two weeks. Peltola has denied any involvement in the alleged efforts to stack the ballot, even as Trump has suggested she drop out of the race and state and federal criminal investigations are underway. Legal experts are broadly skeptical that the alleged ballot-stacking rises to the level of a crime. Alaska’s vote count could take longer than other states due to ranked choice voting and the state allows for mailed ballots postmarked before or on Election Day to be returned to the elections office within 10-15 days. In a close election, there could be a scenario where the Alaska results won’t be known for weeks. 6. Kansas Kansas moves up two spots as GOP Sen. Roger Marshall appears on shaky ground against Democrat Adam Hamilton, who is hoping to be the first Kansas Democrat elected to the US Senate since 1994. A NYT/Siena poll released Sunday showed Hamilton leading Rogers 49% to 44%, while a recent CNN poll conducted by SSRS found no clear leader in the contest. The CNN survey found a majority of likely voters said they would prefer Republicans to control the Senate but 53% view Marshall unfavorably. Voters across the Midwest, including many farmers and ranchers, are feeling the squeeze of high diesel prices and Trump’s tariffs. A New York Times report about hundreds of former Marshall patients being sued for unpaid bills, with some even being arrested, has emerged as a flashpoint in the race. Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor, has tried to stitch together a broad coalition in a state Trump won by 16 points. The president traveled to the state on Sunday to rally his base voters, and Republicans are hoping the red-leaning landscape could ultimately prove insurmountable for Democrats. But Democrats have made big moves to put the state in play in the final stretch. Democratic groups outspent Republicans by about $45.7 million to $31.5 million in October, and entering the final weeks, Hamilton had $2.9 million in the bank compared to Marshall’s $810,000. 7. Iowa Iowa keeps its spot in the race to replace GOP Sen. Joni Ernst. CNN’s Poll of Polls average shows no clear leader in the contest between Democrat Josh Turek and GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson who sit at 46% and 45%, respectively. Trump won Iowa by 13 points in 2024, and the state has not elected a Democratic senator since 2008. Hinson also has proven to be one of the most politically adept Republicans running this cycle. Though she has campaigned alongside the president, Hinson has worked to distance herself from the president on the Iran war, tariffs, and beef imports. But the GOP congresswoman still faces voter angst over the rising cost of diesel, fertilizer and other goods utilized in the agriculturally reliant state. And like Kansas, Democrats outspent Republicans in October, here by nearly $20 million. A top Democratic ad during that period ties the GOP congresswoman to high gas prices, tariffs and the war with Iran while Republicans have run with an ad dinging Turek on immigration. An expected strong performance by Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor, could also benefit Turek in the end. 8. Michigan Michigan shifts down two spots, as new signs suggest Democrat Abdul El-Sayed may have an upper hand over GOP former Rep. Mike Rogers – even as a stunning cross-party endorsement came into play in the closing days. Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens on Sunday decided to abandon El-Sayed and back Rogers, a remarkable break from her party. The simmering tension between El-Sayed and Stevens exploded into public view in the final days of the campaign after a bruising primary – and a recent new argument – that hinged largely on differing views on US aid to Israel. The Stevens endorsement, coming less than 48 hours before Election Day, highlights El-Sayed’s challenge in winning over parts of the Democratic coalition that favored Stevens in the primary, notably Black and Jewish voters. But it also resulted in state and national Democrats – some of them no fans of El-Sayed – issuing strong statements Sunday in his favor. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, whom CNN has reported unofficially backed Stevens in the primary, accused her of a “despicable betrayal.” CNN’s Poll of Polls average shows El-Sayed leading Rogers in Michigan – 50 to 45%. That includes a NYT/Siena poll, which found El-Sayed with an 11-point advantage. A CNN poll conducted by SSRS last month revealed signs the progressive was consolidating support among Democrats, including earning the support of 95% of Democratic likely voters. Some 1.5 million early votes had already been cast in the race as of Sunday, approaching half the number that were cast in Michigan during the entirety of the 2022 midterms. Ultimately, this race could boil down to how Michiganders feel about the economy amid high gas prices and Trump’s trade war with Canada. One of the top Democratic ads for the final two weeks focused on healthcare as they attempted to link Rogers to high costs fueled by pharmaceutical companies. The president has worked hard to turn out base voters in support of Rogers, who lost a Senate race in 2024 despite Trump appearing at the top of the ticket. But Rogers is also grappling with the unpopularity of Trump’s second term. The president’s approval rating with likely voters sits at 33%, according to CNN’s new poll. 9. New Hampshire Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas seems to be on more solid footing over GOP former Sen. John Sununu than during the summer months. A University of New Hampshire Survey Center poll found Pappas up 12 points over Sununu among likely voters in the state. The survey also found Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte statistically tied with her Democratic opponent Cinde Warmington. Some Republicans are still holding out hope that a strong showing by Ayotte could benefit Sununu. But negative views of Trump may dent Sununu despite his attempts to distance himself from the president. 10. South Carolina South Carolina is moving onto this list for the first time. A New York Times/Siena poll released last week showed a tied race between appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews, a physician. Graham is running for a full term after her brother, Lindsey, unexpectedly died in July. She had shaky moments in her campaign, notably saying “national security is not my thing” when asked about Taiwan in a debate. She has not won over key parts of the Republican base. GOP Rep. Ralph Norman, who was on stage during Graham’s debate flub and lost to her in a close primary runoff, revealed to CNN his entire family was not voting for his former opponent and argued she’s not a true conservative. Trump has visited the state twice in the last month as he looked to rally GOP voters to turn out. Andrews has significantly out-raised Graham in the campaign. And outside spending has poured into the state, each side set to spend about $17 million over the final two weeks in a frantic scramble to reach voters. The fundamentals of the state are still in Graham’s favor. Trump won the state by 18 points in 2024. But the close nature of the race is giving some Republicans anxiety heading into election night. 11. Georgia Republicans started the cycle with Georgia as a top offensive opportunity, but one day before the election, a GOP win in the Senate race may be off the table. Sen. Jon Ossoff has run a strong campaign and outpolled GOP Rep. Mike Collins, whom Trump endorsed in the GOP runoff, throughout the contest. Ossoff has also dramatically out-raised and outspent Collins. The conversation around Ossoff has centered less around if he will be reelected than on whether he’ll decide to pursue higher office in 2028. He has repeatedly rejected talk of a White House run. Though he’s expected to win on Tuesday, Ossoff’s political clout will still be tested. The Georgia Democrat has worked hard to lift gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms in her race against GOP nominee Rick Jackson, so we’ll be watching to see whether Ossoff’s can help carry her in this competitive contest. (A Bottoms win would put her in a position to fill a Senate vacancy, which matters greatly to Democrats who want Ossoff to run for president.) Other states on the bubble There are a number of states we were watching throughout this contest that never fully materialized as actual chess pieces on the battleground board. That includes two races featuring GOP incumbents – Nebraska and Mississippi – and another for a seat held by a retiring Democratic senator in Minnesota. Maybe they would’ve come online in a more serious way with more money and time, but at this point, flips in these three states would be a big surprise on Tuesday.

cnn.com.title: Brazil’s left reinvented the right’s online playbook. It helped Lula win
cnn.com.text: For three weeks in October, Veridiana Cunha became a so-called “soldier” for a digital army fighting to reelect Brazil’s leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Every few minutes, the 48-year-old would interrupt her day job in São Paulo as a copy editor and check WhatsApp for new instructions. She even reactivated an Instagram account she hadn’t used since 2022 and learned how to post on X for the first time for the cause. “I’d edit a text, then go to the army. Edit another text, then go to the army,” she told CNN of a WhatsApp channel, led by Congressman André Janones, that became a virtual campaign headquarters during the final weeks of Brazil’s presidential campaign. Cunha was one of millions of Brazilians who joined the channel called “Lula’s Army.” Their mission: to reverse Lula’s first-round defeat on October 4 to the right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, scion of former President Jair Bolsonaro. And they succeeded. Lula won the election on October 25, which analysts partly attribute to the eleventh-hour strategy of harnessing a digital playbook long associated with Brazil’s right of using WhatsApp to amplify political messaging and mobilize voters. From coordinated social media campaigns to reclaiming national symbols, the online strategy mobilized many to vote for Lula, in an effort that experts say offers a striking example of how the Brazilian left learned to fight the right on its turf. Millions of “soldiers,” one command WhatsApp is a powerful force in Brazilian politics. Jair Bolsonaro’s successful presidential campaign in 2018 was supported by extensive networks of private groups that spread videos, political messages and disinformation. But ahead of the October 4, first-round vote, Lula’s campaign had struggled to compete with the right’s digital operation. While Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign had long made social media a central part of its strategy, Lula’s team underestimated its importance, according to Lucas Fernandes, a political analyst at BMJ Consultores Associados. “The right understood this and applied it on several fronts, not just to Flávio’s candidacy, while the left failed to make that transition,” Fernandes said, highlighting social media as one of the key factors for Flávio’s victory in the first round. That changed after Lula’s defeat when Janones, 42, emerged as a central figure in this new playbook. The congressman for the state of Minas Gerais created the WhatsApp channel in April. After Lula’s first-round loss to Bolsonaro, Janones transformed it into a virtual command center, issuing coordinated instructions to supporters who were suddenly confronting the possibility of losing the presidency. Viktor Chagas, a professor at Fluminense Federal University who researches political communication, described Janones as a politician who “fights the far right with the same resources it uses,” resorting to emotionally charged messages, aggressive language and, at times, content of dubious origin. It was a strategy he deployed on the channel, which saw it swell from 50,000 followers before the first-round vote to nearly 11 million in three weeks as Janones rallied supporters to help Lula stage a historic comeback. From anti-system figure to digital general of Lula Within Congress, Janones is known for his combative style, which he dubbed “cultural Janonism,” adopting tactics associated with Bolsonarism, according to Chagas. This included provocative language, emotionally charged posts, and attacks on his adversaries. It also turned Janones into a polarizing figure, who last year was suspended by Congress for three months for offensive statements against another combative lawmaker, the right-wing politician Nikolas Ferreira. Through videos, audio messages and social media posts, Janones instructed his followers to promote hashtags, comment on livestreams, share videos, like posts, publish photos making the “L” hand gesture in support of Lula, and recruit new members. He called for a panelaço — a traditional Brazilian form of protest in which people bang pots and pans — during Flávio Bolsonaro’s highly anticipated interview on TV Globo, as a way to boycott the broadcast. Janones also urged supporters to avoid commenting on opponents’ posts, warning that engaging with their content could inadvertently boost its visibility through social media algorithms. The pace was so intense that Janones went so far as to condemn resting unless the “soldier” could find a replacement for the “missions.” On October 17, he wrote on the channel: “If there is a substitute soldier, the change is authorized. Pass him the cell phone. Rest and come back in ten minutes.” Chagas described the strategy as a form of “gamification,” which fostered a sense of collective purpose. According to the academic, that structure gave progressive digital activism a level of coordination that had been absent even during Lula’s successful campaign in 2022. Bolsonaro’s strategy focused on disseminating content from a few major influencers, while “Lula’s Army” had a centralized command that instructed its members to create and disseminate their own content as well as official lines. Janones not only told them what to share but taught them how to do it, experts noted. Leonardo Magalhães Firmino, chief executive of research firm IPSE Global, compared the method to training thousands of small social media managers. But the rise in online activity also raised concerns about misinformation. In one widely circulated image by the left, Brazilian soccer legend Ronaldo appears to be wearing a national team jersey bearing Lula’s ballot number, 13, and making the “L” gesture. The image was manipulated by artificial intelligence and posted by a Colombian artist, according to Brazilian fact-checking outlet Agência Lupa. Ronaldo’s representatives said it had been used without his authorization. While Janones’ tactics tend to pursue democratic ends, Chagas argues that they could also degrade public debate by reducing complex political discussions to a constant confrontation. CNN reached out to Janones, who has previously denied spreading disinformation, for comment. On the channel, Janones called himself “general,” assigned daily “missions” to Lula’s supporters, and urged them to take the campaign beyond their own social media. The tactics frustrated Bolsonaro’s supporters. On October 11, a supreme court judge ordered the suspension of the WhatsApp group following a complaint by Bolsonaro’s campaign for alleged disinformation. The decision was later overturned. Did the “army” change the outcome of the election? Lula’s victory was decided by factors beyond the digital battle: electoral participation, the redistribution of votes from eliminated candidates, and geographical changes in support for candidates. But Janones’ online mobilization was fundamental to Lula’s victory, says Firmino. “I have no doubt. Without that, I don’t think the comeback would have happened,” he told CNN. “He organized the militancy, he gave them a method. I think that’s the main point.” According to Firmino, the right underestimated Janones’ strategy, saying that he only spoke with Lula supporters. But that was the point: the goal was to speak directly with the “soldiers” who were already converted, not the undecided. The “soldiers” were the ones who would take the message beyond the channel and to their family, friends, undecided voters, and those thinking about abstaining, he said. ‘I managed to change a vote’ For Cunha, the missions meant much more than a political cause. Her mother, a longtime Lula supporter, became seriously ill in August and she spent weeks by her side in the Brazilian state of Minas Gerais, so she did not vote in the first round. Back in São Paulo for work, she needed a distraction and a purpose, which she found in digital mobilization. “The Army saved Brazil, it saved Lula and it saved me a little too,” she said. Participating in the campaign allowed her to feel closer to her mother and continue fighting for a cause they both shared. But one of her greatest satisfactions came on election day, when a friend, who was thinking of abstaining, finally went to the polls and voted for Lula. “I managed to change a vote,” Cunha said. No one can determine how many stories like hers translated into additional votes on a national scale. But for Cunha, the victory had an unexpected consequence: After three weeks spent almost entirely campaigning, getting back to normal proved harder than she imagined. “I think we’re living through a kind of post-traumatic stress from the Army, like we’ve really gone to war,” she said. “We’re exhausted, but we want more missions. We feel like we can conquer the world.”

cnn.com.title: The huge stakes of an unusually momentous midterm election
cnn.com.text: Midterm elections are always a verdict on a sitting president. But the 2026 edition could become something rarer and more significant — a catalyst that points the way to a new political era. Tuesday’s election is critical for Trump’s presidency and legacy. It could either sustain the MAGA movement’s decadelong grip on national life or initiate its decline. It could result in redemption for Democrats two years after their crushing defeat in the last presidential election. And in both parties, it will demarcate the opening chapters of the 2028 presidential race. The midterms are the first chance for voters to place some constitutional restraints on a freewheeling president who has the most aggressive view of executive power in modern times. If Democrats win back the House of Representatives or the Senate on Tuesday, Trump will face a seismic tide of investigations: into his conduct; his Cabinet; alleged government corruption; his legacy construction spree; turmoil at the Pentagon; and his own fortune, which has swelled since he returned to the White House. More broadly, the election is also a referendum on nearly two divisive years in which Trump has sought to dismantle swaths of the federal government and used the power of his office to target political enemies. Abroad, he’s replaced traditional global leadership with America First nationalism while starting a new Middle East war; fraternizing with Russian and Chinese dictators; and carrying out extrajudicial killings of alleged traffickers in the Pacific and Caribbean. But Democrats also have a lot at stake as they tried to repair a brand tarnished by high inflation and lax border security under President Joe Biden’s administration and the chaos of his aborted reelection bid. For voters to trust them again, they must prove they’re more than just anti-Trump; they must deliver results at a frantic political moment and despite a president who will put up ferocious resistance. Failure would invite voters’ wrath in 2028. Election Day could also turn into a crucible for US democracy itself. Trump has already challenged the conduct of elections in Alaska and California and drawn comparisons to his effort to overturn the 2020 election by signaling last week that he’d accept the results of the midterms only if he deems them fair. But most importantly, the elections are a chance for politicians to listen to the people whom they often seem to forget they serve. Millions of Americans are desperate for relief from the costs of food, housing and healthcare and feel rising anxiety about the possible impact of AI on their job security. Trump’s strange campaign Trump is the most unorthodox president of modern times. But his decision to make the election about his performance amid a deeply unpopular war and boiling public dissatisfaction with his decisions was iconoclastic even for him. His erratic final pitch, delivered on a journey through wobbling GOP districts in red states, touched on almost everything but the economic issue voters care about most. He boasted about the new ballroom he’s building at the White House; bizarrely lauded the backside of Ohio Sen. John Husted; and lashed out with some of the most explicit anti-Muslim and bigoted rhetoric of any US election campaign. On Sunday, the president shrugged off polls showing Democrats heavily favored to recapture the House and threatening multiple Republican senators in states he won by wide margins, instead promising a triumph for the GOP on Tuesday night. “A vote for any Democrat anywhere in the country is a vote to put a deranged group of extremists into power and it could really hurt us, and we are not going to let anything hurt us, because we have the greatest country right now,” Trump said in Iowa. House Speaker Mike Johnson, at Trump’s side, vowed, “We are going to win and shock the world on Tuesday night. I believe it.” But if voters react badly to Trump’s depiction of a new economic “golden age” and evident indifference to their struggles, he will be consigned to a lonely political plight — shocking even for a man once subject to multiple criminal cases. His self-themed campaign would make it an unusually personal blow, especially if his handpicked Senate candidates lose in states like Texas and Georgia. The idea that Trumpism has permanently changed politics would be called into question, and the GOP would be plunged into soul-searching over its future direction. And next year, the isolation would become more acute under the relentless pressure of Democratic investigations after the end of a rubber-stamp Republican Congress. A Democratic victory would turn into a fateful test A good night for Democrats would count as a political earthquake only two years after Trump staged one of history’s greatest comebacks by beating Democratic nominee Kamala Harris to win a nonconsecutive second term. Yet even if the party were to win both chambers, Trump will still enjoy considerable clout, including with expansive constitutional authority to conduct foreign policy. The president’s history of spurning checks and balances means he’d fight any attempt by Democrats in Congress to rein in his powers, with showdowns likely over the war, budgets and policy-making. But if Democrats rack up the net gain of four seats needed to win the Senate, they will acquire the ability to block Trump’s campaign to complete his conservative transformation of the judiciary and potentially to fill any new Supreme Court vacancy. And any potential Democratic majorities could also challenge Trump on his conduct of the war with Iran — which he is waging without congressional authorization — and funding for military operations if he has failed to end the conflict by the time new lawmakers are seated on January 3. “Right now, (it) is about stabilizing the country itself and providing some check against not just an out-of-control presidency and a corrupt presidency but everyone’s costs,” Democratic Sen. Brian Schatz told CNN’s Kasie Hunt last month. “Diesel, gasoline agricultural products, consumer products … everything is up, and I think people want to see us do not everything but a few things that will take the pain out of what they’re experiencing.” But while the loss of Congress could turn Trump into a lame duck, he’s unlikely to act like one. The history of his first term suggests pitched legal battles over congressional subpoenas and attempts by Democratic investigators to penetrate deep into the administration and trawl for evidence in his family finances. The president’s veto power, and the requirement for 60 votes to pass major legislation in the Senate, means Trump will be able to temper Democratic hopes for sweeping change. Lessons for 2028 are already being drawn The midterm results will also shape the 2028 presidential race likely to explode into life as soon as the votes are counted. A huge GOP defeat could raise doubts about whether Trumpism will outlast Trump’s political career.
