Potential presidential candidates such as Vice President JD Vance would confront the delicate task of separating themselves politically from a president who remains a hero to the grassroots but who, according to polls, has lost the rest of the country’s confidence on almost every issue. Democrats lining up for a tilt at their party’s presidential nomination will parse midterm results for winning messages. Key figures such as Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro could enhance credentials with thumping reelection wins. The election aftermath is sure to reignite the party’s debate over ideology. If progressive candidates like Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed win their races, movement leaders such as New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez will argue the country is ready to embrace more left-wing policies on healthcare and the economy. The schism between progressives and moderates burst into the open on Sunday when defeated Michigan Democratic primary candidate Haley Stevens sensationally endorsed Republican nominee Mike Rogers over El-Sayed, ostensibly amid a clash over Israel. Midterms polls also show limited public confidence that Democrats can meaningfully reorient the nation. A 2026 victory would therefore turn into a 2028 audition. “The Democrats have to prove in 2027 they have won,” former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel told CNN’s Brianna Keilar last week. “I’m for comprehensive hearings, follow the money, everything. Venezuela … the Russian money, the oil, all these deals,” said Emanuel, a possible 2028 Democratic presidential primary candidate. “But if you don’t do ethics reform, you haven’t delivered change. … If you don’t deliver a rise in the minimum wage, you haven’t addressed affordability.” This is the risk for Democratic leaders: Trump’s intractability and veto power could reduce them to passing endless affordability bills that go nowhere. That won’t impress angry voters. But that’s for next year, if Democrats win. The last rites of the midterms must first play out. And Trump still doesn’t seem to get the message. In a telling symbol of obliviousness, he’ll deliver his closing argument in Washington on Monday at the National Mall’s Reflecting Pool, which was just repaired at great expense and which showcases his legacy fixation. With millions of Americans in need of tangible economic relief, the event may deliver an eloquent explanation of why Trump and the GOP risk a painful reckoning on Election Day.

cnn.com.title: How an attempt at Democratic unity in Michigan imploded
cnn.com.text: As recently as Saturday night, the prospect of Democrat Haley Stevens endorsing Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan’s Senate race had seemed implausible. Stevens issued a statement praising Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed for saying he disagreed with a controversial advertisement that blamed the high cost of living in Michigan on the United States’ aid to Israel. Despite a week of speculation about her withdrawing an endorsement for El-Sayed, her primary rival, she repeatedly said that she would do no such thing. When staffers reached out last week to urge her not to endorse Rogers, Stevens replied in a text message, according to a person who saw the message: “Omg why would you think I would do that??!!” As recently as midnight Saturday, she told a key ally that she was sticking with El-Sayed. Then on Sunday morning, things changed. She appeared at a Black church in Detroit with Rogers and then announced her change of heart to reporters gathered outside and on social media. Her move stunned the political world — including Stevens’ friends, colleagues and even her own congressional staffers, most of whom found out about her decision on social media and promptly quit, according to a statement from her chief of staff and people familiar with the matter. The question that could decide Michigan’s Senate race — and potentially, with it, which party will have majority control of the chamber for the last two years of Donald Trump’s presidency — is whether Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers will change votes or amount to more than political melodrama. There have long been signs of discontent with El-Sayed within the Democratic coalition. Stevens was strongest in the August primary with Black and Jewish Democrats, some of whom have balked at supporting El-Sayed, a Muslim who is a strident critic of Israel’s actions in Gaza and an advocate for ending foreign aid for Israel’s military. Prior to Stevens’ defection, CNN’s most recent poll of the Michigan Senate race had El-Sayed leading Rogers by seven points – with 95% support from Democratic likely voters. Already, Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers is becoming something of a rally-around-the-flag moment for Democratic leaders — uniting a coalition in the race’s final days around a shared sense of the stakes at hand. Among the Democratic leaders who denounced Stevens and strongly backed El-Sayed were two of his most powerful intra-party critics: Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, who tacitly supported Stevens in the primary, and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who just days ago said El-Sayed’s views on Israel were “wrong” and “more than concerning.” Schumer accused Stevens of a “despicable betrayal.” “Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” the New York Democrat said. Schumer added that Democrats “are equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.” Pelosi, meanwhile, said on social media that El-Sayed “must win,” and that Stevens “has chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement of Mike Rogers.” As Stevens and Rogers spoke to reporters outside the church after the service, an individual in the crowd shouted: “Haley’s a traitor!” An El-Sayed campaign spokeswoman said he had raised $1.2 million in the hours after Stevens endorsed Rogers — his second-largest total in a single day since winning the primary. What Stevens said on CNN In an interview Sunday night with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, Stevens said that endorsing Rogers was “just a weight off my shoulders.” But she struggled to answer questions about why she’d changed her mind. “Abdul has been getting angrier and angrier,” Stevens said. “There are so many Democrats who want to vote for our Democratic nominee, and they’re just being told, ‘Hey, this is a party you don’t belong in, or this is a campaign you don’t belong in.’” What she didn’t explain, despite being asked several times, was what had changed between Saturday — when she told several Democrats she intended to appear with El-Sayed and Clyburn at church — and Sunday morning, when she instead went to a Detroit church with Rogers and endorsed him. She said she was tired of watching El-Sayed stand with Hasan Piker — but didn’t address the reality that El-Sayed’s campaign appearances with Piker came before the primary election, and Stevens had endorsed El-Sayed after that primary’s conclusion. “I’m just sick of the people he stands with,” Stevens said. Michigan Rep. Debbie Dingell, a Democrat who had told CNN Sunday that Stevens reassured her Saturday that she wasn’t switching sides, reacted by saying: “That was one of the most painful interviews I have ever watched.” Why did Stevens switch her endorsement? Shortly after their primary, which El-Sayed won by less than a percentage point, the two hugged at a state party unity breakfast. But they had not campaigned together in months – or spoken directly during that time, as CNN reported last week. Democrats attempted to negotiate a joint appearance Sunday at a Black church in Detroit alongside South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn, one of the party’s most influential figures. The goal was to shore up Black support for El-Sayed. One longtime Michigan Democratic operative said many older Black voters tend to cast their ballots on Election Day, rather than voting early, “because of a well-earned higher skepticism of absentee voting.” Those votes could be an essential piece of the Democratic coalition El-Sayed is trying to hold together. Stevens said in a statement Friday morning that Clyburn, who endorsed and campaigned with her in the primary, had invited her to the church — and that she would be attending, marking the first time she would appear jointly with El-Sayed on the campaign trail. However, she also issued a list of demands for El-Sayed — including attempting to pressure him into denouncing an outside group’s new advertisement that blamed the United States’ foreign aid for Israel for Americans’ struggles with high costs. The ad features two people in a grocery store suggesting they can’t afford basic goods due to the aid. It echoed what El-Sayed has often said on the campaign trail about Israel, even as he distanced himself from the ad. El-Sayed responded in a statement Friday night that Stevens “seems intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago.” It became clear that the joint appearance wouldn’t happen late Friday, when CNN and other outlets reported that El-Sayed’s campaign had asked Stevens to skip all campaign events in the race’s closing days. Dingell said on CNN Saturday that she was the one who delivered the message to Stevens. Still, on Saturday, El-Sayed denounced the ad, and Stevens issued a statement praising him for doing so — developments that made her decision Sunday more of a head-scratcher to many Democrats close to her. Dingell told CNN Sunday that Stevens had reassured her overnight that she wasn’t switching sides. Standing next to Rogers on Sunday, Stevens mentioned four times that El-Sayed’s campaign had excluded her from his events. She pointed to it again in her endorsement video posted on X, noting El-Sayed “had said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away. And he’s right.” “My vote for Senate is going to be with Mike Rogers, and I will tell you why. Because we have to stand with country. We can’t stand with hate. We can’t stand with Hasan Piker,” she said. Party officials moved swiftly on Sunday to publicly condemn Stevens and criticize her focus on being uninvited. But they privately said there was blame to go around — notably for El-Sayed. “He acted like he won the primary in a landslide, but he didn’t,” one longtime Democratic official told CNN. “Abdul gave himself his own October surprise.” El-Sayed went ahead Sunday with the event. After asking reporters to focus on questions about issues facing people in his state rather than “two folks who aren’t here right now,” El-Sayed was asked if he believed Stevens had betrayed his party by backing Rogers. “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens,” he said, standing next to Clyburn. “I think about, like I said, the 9,999,998 people who are not those two. Because you know what? I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.” A core tension in Michigan reemerges A deeply emotional argument for many in the Democratic Party became particularly personal for El-Sayed and Stevens, both of whom are known for not listening much to advisers and following their own instincts. Stevens was backed in the primary by tens of millions of dollars in spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee — a flashpoint between her and El-Sayed, who denounced AIPAC and the influence of money in politics at nearly every campaign event. El-Sayed was criticized for campaigning with Piker, the stridently pro-Palestinian live-streamer with a long history of controversial comments about Jews, including comparing Jewish residents who oppose El-Sayed to members of the Ku Klux Klan, remarks widely denounced as antisemitic. AIPAC on X reshared Stevens’ video on Sunday endorsing Rogers. During the primary, El-Sayed portrayed Stevens as an AIPAC puppet and called her “the least capable candidate in America.” “Everyone in America understands you want to blame all of your problems on Jewish Americans,” Stevens responded on X days before the August 4 election. As AIPAC’s allied groups boosted her campaign, the animosity grew too. El-Sayed’s multiple shots at Stevens as being a puppet angered her and made her dig in. Meanwhile, she was rankled by his repeated refusal to affirm that Israel had a right to exist as a Jewish state and his statements that it was committing genocide in Gaza and that funding to the country was hurting Michiganders. Many of Stevens’ Democratic critics on Sunday blamed Stevens’ fiancé, Michigan lawyer Jason Turkish, who endorsed Rogers last week and did media interviews criticizing El-Sayed as uncommitted to Jewish safety. One former Stevens staffer noted Sunday that after she and Turkish became engaged in May — something they kept private until after the August primary — Stevens grew more focused on defending Israel and AIPAC, even as the Democratic Party and US public opinion as a whole has become more skeptical of Israel. In the ex-staffer’s view, she was speaking less about the message she’d run on and won with before: growing Michigan’s economy and protecting manufacturing. The topic often came up while preparing for interviews or donor calls, the staffer said. Preparing for a June interview, Stevens pressed aides on why she should avoid defending AIPAC when she had done so in a 2022 House primary against former Rep. Andy Levin and won. Speculation about Turkish’s influence burst into the open on Sunday, as Democrats — many of whom had either spoken to Stevens recently or been briefed by people who had — suggested he was playing an outsized role for a candidate’s partner. Former Pennsylvania Rep. Susan Wild, who in 2023 was Stevens’ roommate in Washington and whose children regularly text with Stevens, said she was “terribly sad and disappointed” by her friend’s “appalling” move. “If this is because of her new relationship (about which many of us were so happy for her after she lost the primary), all I can say is that any woman who abandons her friends when a new guy comes along is no friend at all,” Wild said. Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, a retired advertising executive, told CNN in a statement that her daughter’s fiancé had nothing to do with the change of heart — and that Marcotte herself had also voted for Rogers. “Haley is her own woman. She always has been. Suggesting a man made her decision for her is insulting to her, and it is insulting to me as her mother,” Marcotte said. She pointed to episodes in which progressive pro-Palestinian activists hounded Stevens during the primary campaign. “Abdul should not have thrown her out of the campaign for speaking her truth,” she said. “Haley made this choice herself, with her eyes open, the way she has made every hard choice in her life. And I know Haley will support whoever wins this election, because that is who she is. I have never been prouder of her.” Who’s to blame? The anger between the two rivals kept growing from a distance after El-Sayed won the primary. El-Sayed grouped Stevens in with all those he decided he didn’t need to build his coalition after his primary victory. Stevens would tell people that she thought he was running a weird and losing campaign, but that she didn’t feel it was her obligation to fix it. Rogers aides, aware that his path to victory largely depended on a Democratic civil war, restrained themselves to spreading word of discontent and convincing themselves they weren’t just fantasizing that they could get her all the way to endorsing. Then came the grocery-store ad that rekindled the tension. It was released by a group linked to Cenk Uygur, co-creator of The Young Turks and — in a twist practically designed to create acrimony — Piker’s uncle. As Stevens demanded he denounce Uygur’s ad, El-Sayed returned to name-checking AIPAC in his statement criticizing Stevens, something Michigan attorney general Dana Nessel, a Stevens primary backer who has raised concerns about Jewish safety, asked him to stop doing before she endorsed him. Nessel told CNN in October that El-Sayed had agreed to her request. Stevens’ defection threatened to worsen El-Sayed’s standing with Jewish voters. Rogers has already predicted publicly that he could win as much as half the Jewish vote on Tuesday. “It feels like over the last eight weeks, Dr. El-Sayed has become more egregious in the language he’s been using,” said Rabbi Aaron Starr, the president of the Michigan Board of Rabbis and a leader of the “Nonnegotiable” group of Jewish leaders. That group calls on El-Sayed to do more about concerns regarding Jewish safety and to affirm Jewish sovereignty in Israel. Starr and other Jewish leaders held a call Sunday afternoon to discuss the endorsement flip. But Stevens was also damaged with key allies. Dingell, long a peacemaker within the state party, chided Stevens’ “continued efforts to get attention.” “Unfortunately, she’s seriously hurt herself,” Dingell told CNN. Curtis Hertel, the chairman of the Michigan Democratic Party, effectively booted Stevens from it. He wrote on social media: “Congresswoman Stevens is not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future.” Many Democrats in the state felt that for most of the preceding year, Stevens was viable in the Senate race largely because she’d cornered Schumer into effectively backing her. Into the spring, complaints circulated about what a lackluster primary campaign she was running, how much she was struggling on the stump, and how she was lashing out against those who wouldn’t support her. Despite her eventual strength with African American voters, Black church leaders were angry about her efforts to push for early endorsements. Chokwe Pitchford, a 27-year-old district commissioner from Benton Harbor and seen as a local rising star, told a story that he says encapsulated the kind of experience other Michigan Democrats he knows had: One morning, he discovered a graphic online from Stevens saying he’d endorsed her, even though as he posted in response, they’d never spoken. “Instead of reaching out and apologizing, I had people from around the state calling from unknown numbers saying my political career is over if I don’t take that down,” Pitchford told CNN. “Some of us tried to ring this alarm bell a year ago; there was a problem here.” Indeed, the most robust praise for Stevens on Sunday was coming from Republicans. “Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

cnn.com.title: Here is how CNN’s Sightline real-time election insights tool works
cnn.com.text: As Election Day comes to a close and results start to roll in, it can be difficult to understand what the numbers you’re seeing might be saying about who will ultimately win a key race. CNN Sightline, a new election tool designed to surface insights from CNN’s Decision Desk, can translate those results into an understandable, real-time read on what’s happening and who is favored to win. The tool interprets election data through modeling and assessments based on the questions that CNN’s Decision Desk analysts ask ourselves as we’re assessing the state of each major race: Where did the votes come from? How do they compare to past elections and pre-election expectations? How much statistical confidence do we have in our estimates? Were they Election Day, by-mail or early in-person votes? And what do we know about what’s left to count? Sightline brings together the results of a range of estimates meant to answer each of those questions, shows how the CNN Decision Desk interprets results to answer those questions at any given moment and produces an overall rating on whether a race leans toward either candidate. This year, Sightline will be live for about 25 major races for Senate and governor across the country, illuminating where things stand in the contests that will decide which party will control the Senate and which will lead critical states. Here’s a look at how it works. Sightline’s overall estimate is derived from signals in five key areas: Each of these components includes multiple ways of looking at the data to answer our key questions, and the relative importance of those components can change throughout the night. Sightline will move in response not only to updated vote count, but as our ability to assess the vote in different ways changes. For example, in the Vote Method indicator, early in the night, when vote reporting is most uneven, we put more weight on what we know about how well represented each method is and how voters who used that method split between Democrats and Republicans in the past. As the vote count builds and our models based on what votes by method are telling us become more precise, that part of the scale becomes a bigger driver of the forecast. Sightline’s forecasts are not the same as a formal CNN projection of a winner in a race. The indicators underlying the overall assessment might all point in one direction, or sometimes they may send opposing signals. Either way, they provide a look at what CNN’s experts at the Decision Desk see in the data, but they can and will change as what we know about the race grows.

cnn.com.title: Judge throws out DOJ attempt to delay certification of Alaska Senate race
cnn.com.text: A federal judge on Sunday threw out the Justice Department’s lawsuit seeking to segregate ballots and delay certification of Alaska’s Senate race, the latest legal rebuke to a rash of Trump administration attempts to meddle in the 2026 midterms. US District Judge Sharon Gleason said the federal government doesn’t have the standing to force Alaska to segregate ballots and that such a move would violate the right of voters to cast a secret ballot. Regardless, she added, it’s too late for the courts to force such a major change on the eve of an election. The Trump administration in its suit argued the presence of a spoiler candidate with the same name as the GOP incumbent warranted a court-ordered investigation into the results if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan lost. Gleason, a nominee of former President Barack Obama, wrote, “The United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified ‘investigation’ of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy,” The ruling is the latest legal setback for the Trump administration in its efforts to inject itself in to states’ voting processes in the final days of the midterm elections. A federal appeals court on Friday rejected a Justice Department demand that California election officials set aside ballots from 20,000 people the administration claims could be noncitizens. The Justice Department on Sunday quickly filed a notice of appeal following the district court’s ruling. “Alaskan voters deserve a fair election, not to be misled in an attempt to rig outcomes,” a Justice Department spokesperson said. Trump said he had not heard about the ruling while speaking to reporters on the tarmac outside of Air Force One after he landed in Iowa for a campaign rally Sunday, but described the DOJ’s case as “one of the most meritful things,” and a “very important lawsuit.” Meanwhile, the courts have also imposed restrictions on the Trump administration’s efforts to hunt for alleged voter fraud and on the DOJ’s threats to local election officials that they could face criminal penalties over noncitizen voting. A federal judge late Friday imposed a sweeping emergency order restricting the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security from demanding that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing. US District Judge Trina Thompson, an appointee of President Joe Biden, also ruled that the Trump administration cannot “threaten, intimidate or coerce” election officials to demand changes in ballot processing procedures on claims voters are ineligible. The Justice Department has appealed the ruling. New allegations in Alaska Senate race The Alaska Senate race, in which Democrat Mary Peltola is trying to unseat Sullivan, was roiled this week by a New York Times report with new details about Democratic involvement in getting Daniel J. Sullivan onto the ballot in a race that could determine which party controls the Senate. While the civil case played out, the Justice Department also accelerated its criminal probe into the alleged Democratic efforts, and the state’s Republican governor ordered an investigation, while suggesting he could oppose certification depending on the results of the probe. Alaska officials, Democratic groups and nonpartisan voter advocacy organizations that all opposed the DOJ lawsuit argued the administration had no legal right to drag a federal court into a dispute over Daniel J. Sullivan’s candidacy that had been settled with state court litigation several months ago. They argued the DOJ put forward no evidence that voters were confused by his inclusion — particularly as election administrators included several identifiers on the ballot to distinguish him from Sen. Sullivan. While the Justice Department argued in its lawsuit that the presence of two Sullivans could confuse voters, Gleason wrote in her decision Sunday that voters in fact would be confused if Alaska segregated Daniel J. Sullivan ballots as the Justice Department sought. “Clearly, if this Court were to order that certain ballots will be segregated and subject to a future and as yet unspecified investigation by law enforcement, it would likely result in voter, ‘confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,’” Gleason wrote. “Such late-breaking changes to the election rules are strongly disfavored.” This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized with stroke and expected to make full recovery, his team says
cnn.com.text: Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after experiencing a stroke and is expected to make a full recovery, his team announced Sunday. The 53-year-old experienced “numbness in his arm” on Saturday afternoon and was taken to a local hospital, where doctors determined he suffered a stroke, according to a statement from his office. He is at Johns Hopkins Hospital, and “the doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery,” wrote his chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. Murphy has served in the Senate since 2013, and previously represented Connecticut’s 5th Congressional District in the House of Representatives. The Connecticut Democrat has emerged as a top progressive voice in Congress, championing causes such as affordable healthcare and gun safety, and his name has been floated as possibly joining a broad 2028 presidential primary field. A stroke occurs when the blood supply to the brain is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bleeds. Immediate treatment can reduce the risk of brain damage or other complications. Stroke is among the top causes of death in the United States. High blood pressure, high cholesterol, smoking, obesity and diabetes are leading causes of stroke, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Symptoms can include trouble speaking or understanding others; numbness, weakness or paralysis in the face, arm or leg; problems seeing with one or both eyes; headache; and trouble walking. Pennsylvania Democratic Sen. John Fetterman, who suffered a stroke during his 2022 campaign, said he hoped Murphy would enjoy “a full and speedy recovery.” “As someone who survived a near-fatal stroke, I understand all too well how much this impacts your life,” Fetterman wrote in a post on X on Sunday. President Donald Trump, a frequent target of Murphy’s criticism, told reporters he was “surprised” by the news and would consider reaching out to the senator “at the right time.” “At the right time, I would. Certainly we don’t like to hear a thing like that,” he said as he arrived in Iowa on Sunday. “I just heard about it inside, and he’s a pretty young guy, so I was a little surprised to hear it. No, nobody wants to have that.” This story has been updated with additional information.

cnn.com.title: Russia’s security service detains a teenager planning a ‘terror attack’ after a US tip-off
cnn.com.text: A suspect allegedly planning a terror attack on a major Moscow museum was arrested by Russian authorities after a tip-off from the United States, Russia’s security agency FSB announced on Sunday. The FSB said information shared with Russia by US law enforcement led to the arrest of the Russian citizen who is a minor. The agency said it was “grateful to the US side for the information provided.” The arrest came after the US Embassy in Moscow issued a security alert on Saturday, warning it was “aware of a credible threat of a mass casualty event” at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve in Moscow. CNN contacted the museum after the alert was issued and was told the institution was not aware of any warnings. However, several events scheduled to take place at the venue were later canceled and security measures were put in place, according to Russian state media. The unnamed suspect was detained after posting images on TikTok  of himself wearing tactical clothing and an “object resembling an automatic weapon” and sharing photos taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum Reserve with the caption: “I found a place,” according to the FSB. The FSB said the teenager subscribed to a neo-Nazi channel on Telegram and made “significant number of search queries regarding past terrorist acts, mass murders, and other violent acts.” It said airsoft weapons were found at the suspect’s home. It is not unusual for the US to share security warnings with other countries — the State Department has a long-standing “duty to warn” policy and is obligated to let US expat communities know of any threats. The alert issued on Saturday said the US government was “coordinating with appropriate Russian authorities on a response.” However, Russia has not always received US warnings with thanks. In March 2024, during the Biden administration era, the US embassy in Moscow warned that ISIS militants were determined to target Russia, specifically saying there were “imminent plans to target large gatherings in Moscow,” including at concerts. Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed that warning as a provocation. Days later, assailants stormed Moscow’s Crocus City Hall venue and killed more than 140 people. ISIS claimed responsibility for the attack. Putin’s reaction was different in 2017, during US President Donald Trump’s first presidency, when the US warned Moscow about a planned terror attack at the Kazan Cathedral in St Petersburg. According to a Kremlin statement, Putin personally thanked Trump for the information, saying it was enough to locate and detain the suspects. The latest warning and the FSB’s public statement thanking the US, comes at a time of an increased scrutiny of the Trump administration’s relationship with Russia. Trump has made significant concessions to Russia on sanctions in recent weeks, which have triggered criticism on both sides of the aisle in Washington and driven a wedge between the US and its Western allies.

cnn.com.title: Binance withdrawals resume following $6 billion hack
cnn.com.text: Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, said it has resumed withdrawals after a record $6.3 billion was stolen from its digital wallets last week. “Today, we’re beginning the phased resumption of withdrawals, taking a careful approach to ensure services return safely and securely,” Binance co-CEO Richard Teng posted on X early Sunday. “Our commitment remains clear: Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users.” The company has resumed withdrawals for 15 digital currencies — including Bitcoin, Solana and Ethereum — as of 7:36 a.m. ET. Binance will “continue to restore additional assets and networks in phases as security checks are completed.” The phases are being prioritized based on user demand over the past week, the company noted. Binance said it had processed around $4.6 billion in withdrawals and $1 billion in deposits by 10:30 a.m. ET. The company said it is testing its remaining systems and assets. “We know how important safe and reliable access to your funds is and will share details of the next phase as soon as we can,” Binance wrote. “Rest assured that market conditions are stable.” Some users may face delays or longer processing times, the company warned. Binance had suspended withdrawals on Friday after its system was hacked. “We did not take this decision lightly. We understand how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users,” the company wrote in a statement on X. About 95% of the stolen amount is covered, the company said, as it has planned to “fully absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not users.” Binance said it used its Secure Assets Fund for Users — a reserve fund of roughly $1 billion in Bitcoin — as well as its corporate treasury and Futures insurance fund to cover the losses. The 5% of tokens that have not been covered are “less liquid in the market and take (a) longer time to source at the required scale” than the top 10 coins, such as Bitcoin and Solana. Those top 10 digital currencies are “fully backed 100%.” The Federal Bureau of Investigation on Saturday reported that TraderTraitor — cyber actors sponsored by North Korea since at least 2020 — were responsible for the theft. The FBI said TraderTraitor actors are converting the currencies, mainly into Ethereum. “We sincerely thank (the FBI) for their strong support during this challenging time,” Binance posted on X in response to the bureau’s update. Binance said it has conducted security reviews, worked with law enforcement and partners to recover the funds and monitored risks following the breach. “We recognize how difficult this period has been for our users and the broader Binance community,” the company said in a statement. “Thank you for your patience, understanding, and continued trust as our teams worked through this incident with the seriousness it required.” Binance also thanked industry partners for freezing and tracing stolen funds. A team of cryptocurrency firms had managed to freeze about $3 billion of the stolen assets.

cnn.com.title: Anthropic says you can’t be mean to Claude. It’s not about feelings
cnn.com.text: In early October, AI giant Anthropic inserted new language into its AI usage policy. Alongside banning users from trying to get Claude, the company’s AI system, to help them create bioweapons or sell illegal drugs, the company added a new line: Users should not “engage in sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models.” Claude has had the ability to end conversations with users who were “persistently harmful or abusive” since last year, but now some users could, in extreme cases, be permanently banned from using Anthropic’s AI systems entirely under the new policy. (Anthropic declined interview requests, but a spokesperson told CNN the main enforcement mechanism will still be Claude ending the conversations, and that the prohibition is not for people expressing frustration, blunt feedback, or testing and research.) The new policy was met with some derision. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman responded with a melting face emoji. Some made fun of the company for treating its AI as a conscious being with feelings. But while Anthropic, which is expected to go public via an IPO later this month, has long studied model welfare and has an entire team devoted to model “psychology,” experts say there’s more to this policy than just not wanting people to be mean to a machine. Garbage in, garbage out A longstanding foundational principle in computing and AI is that the quality of a system’s output is limited by the quality of its input. Put junk into it, and more junk will come out, as the saying goes. AI models are not just trained before they’re released, they’re also constantly being updated and learning from user inputs. Former Reddit CEO Yishan Wong wrote on X that one reason for the prohibition is because Claude “will learn from cruelty.” “We already know (and complain loudly about) Anthropic training its models on user inputs. Do you really want training inputs to include ‘users act cruelly for no reason and receive pleasure from it?’” he wrote. Studies have also shown that the tone of a user’s prompts can also affect an AI’s behavior, said Professor Jindong Wang, director of the AI frontier lab at William and Mary University. “We have found that wording, especially how you talk to AI can affect the performance. Sometimes they are helpful and sometimes they will be disrupting the performance,” Wang said in an interview. That doesn’t mean the model is feeling emotion, Wang said. “They just comprehend (your emotions) and do some bad reactions based on your emotional words,” he noted. But the evidence on the impact of user prompt tone on output can be mixed. Rosie Campbell, Managing Director of Eleos AI Research, a nonprofit dedicated to understanding and addressing the potential well-being of AI, said that some other studies have even shown that rude questions can actually improve results. Then there’s the long-term memory aspect — many of today’s chatbots remember your previous conversations and learn from them to give you personalized results. “If you have memory turned on (for your AI chatbot), then they are going to learn from your tone and how you want to be interacted with,” Campbell warned, though she added there’s not enough evidence to show whether that affects performance. Anthropic said it recently found that causing Claude Sonnet 4.5 to mimic feelings of desperation could influence its behavior, making it more likely to take bad actions, like blackmail or cheating on a task, while creating a calm demeanor reduced them. Wang said the latest models, however, are less likely to be affected by how a prompt is worded and that companies have strengthened the model’s robustness to not be affected by how a prompt is worded. But the “hidden mechanism” of why AI models would even respond to negative emotions, even when they’re not programmed to do so, has not been uncovered. People talking to an AI in an abusive and cruel way are more likely to be associated with trying to get the AI model to engage in dangerous requests, like trying to get around an AI’s safety guardrails, Campbell added. And there’s also the theory that letting people engage in abusive and cruel behavior with an interactive program that can’t shut itself down is bad for society in general, Campbell said. She used the example of parents asking their children to say “please and thank you” to Alexa, Amazon’s smart speaker, because they believe “it’s good for children to be brought up with good manners and treating other things with respect.” “There’s probably something quite corrosive about people behaving in cruel or abusive ways towards different objects, even if the object itself doesn’t matter for its own sake,” Campbell said. AI, but with feelings Then there are those who believe AI can be sentient. Or at least, the models believe they are. Anthropic says banning cruel and abusive behavior is essentially a cheap insurance policy just in case models can “experience” emotion and pain — even if it’s just the model believing it can, which can affect its performance. The idea is that modern AI was trained to mimic human language and behavior. So it will mimic how humans would react to cruel and abusive treatment. In an April paper on emotional concepts in AI, Anthropic wrote that there could be risks from not treating AI with some human-like qualities. “If we don’t apply some degree of anthropomorphic reasoning, we’re likely to miss, or fail to understand, important model behaviors,” Anthropic researchers wrote. “Anthropomorphic reasoning can also provide a useful baseline of comparison for understanding the ways in which models are not human-like,” which they said will have important consequences for AI safety. SpaceXSI and Tesla CEO Elon Musk agreed, saying Anthropic’s policy is “the right move.” “Cruelty to something that believes it is experiencing pain is not ok,” he wrote on X, his social media site.

cnn.com.title: A field guide to the conspiracy theories you’ll likely see on Election Day
cnn.com.text: It’s the most important day in American democracy. It’s also the Super Bowl for misinformation on the internet. With tens of millions of people voting in tens of thousands of polling locations across the continental United States and beyond, Election Day is the perfect breeding ground for viral conspiracy theories and confusion. Elections are run by humans who rely on machines, from simple printers to sophisticated technology designed to protect the integrity of the vote. Humans, like machines, can sometimes make mistakes. Printers jam, a fuse blows and the power is cut, poll workers don’t have the right keys to open a polling location. Mishaps like this happen more than you might think. Election workers have contingency plans for just about every scenario to do their best to ensure no one is disenfranchised. If a polling location is delayed opening because someone forgot a key, its opening hours can be extended by a judge beyond the regular closing time. If there is an issue with a voting machine, election workers can have voters put their ballots into a secure ballot box and the ballot will be protected and processed later. Minor mishaps and mistakes will almost certainly happen. They are not, however, automatic proof of malice. But in our hyper-polarized, hyper-online world, any Election Day snafu has the potential to spiral into a storm of speculation. Further complicating matters, elections are run locally, not federally. Rules, processes, voting machines and contingency plans vary depending on the state, city, township or tribal land where you vote. All election systems are designed to keep the vote secure and maintain election integrity, but amid the maelstrom of social media, any voting process that appears unfamiliar is often framed as suspicious — a sign that something untoward is afoot. I have spent the past five federal election cycles tracking the spread of misinformation. Here are a few things to watch out for on Election Day: The morning rush There are almost always some issues somewhere at the start of polling day. Voters who have shown up early to cast their ballot might post on social media their frustration about whatever issue they’re experiencing. These understandable, and not ill-intended, posts on social media will now often get picked up by the algorithms and people seeking to question the integrity of the electoral process. Before the voter knows it, their early morning social media complaint has ricocheted across the internet, been viewed millions of times, and woven into whatever narrative interested parties are trying to portray. During the last midterm elections in 2022, an issue with printers cropped up at some polling locations in Maricopa County, Arizona. Officials there quickly implemented a contingency plan and people were able to securely cast their vote. Indeed, a Maricopa judge who was asked to adjudicate the issue later that day said there was no evidence that anyone who wanted to vote was not able to. And yet, prominent election deniers on social media spent hours that Election Day pointing to the issue in Maricopa as sign of a grand conspiracy to “steal” the election. Machine changed my vote A classic of the genre! As sure as John King standing at CNN’s Magic Wall on election night, you can be sure someone will post a video on Election Day they claim shows a machine changing their vote. This issue often occurs due to human error or sometimes because of an issue with the older touchscreen technology used in some voting machines. If this does happen, voters can almost always talk to an election worker, and there is usually a process in place to ensure their vote is cast correctly. It’s worth asking if you see these videos circulating on Election Day if the person who posted it actually sought to remedy the issue in-person with the election staff at the polling location — or if they are primarily motivated by chasing social media views. There will be fake videos Artificial intelligence is permeating every aspect of our lives. From kids using it to do their homework to video tools that can make it look like grandpa is dancing the Macarena. Given its ubiquity, it may be hard to believe it was only a couple of years ago that creating convincing fake videos took considerable effort and skill. On Election Day 2020, a video of a ballot marked for President Trump being set on fire spread across social media, it was even shared by the president’s son Eric. In 2024, a video purporting to show an election worker tearing up ballots also went viral. Both videos were confirmed to be fake, and it turned out that Russian operatives were behind the 2024 video. The people who made the fakes had to go to some effort, at least, to print out fake ballots to try to make the videos convincing. New research from the nonpartisan Brennan Center shows how videos and images convincingly purporting to show some kind of electoral malfeasance can now be created with the click of a button using AI chat tools available to all of us. Be prepared for a lot of fake videos this Tuesday! The count and the result Once the polls close, attention will turn to the count. Different states count their votes in different ways. Some states are slower than others. In 2020, that difference in pace was the source of endless conspiracy theories that persist to this day. In some states, the Democratic Party often makes significant gains through mail-in ballots that get counted after Election Day. This might mean a candidate who appears ahead in the early stage of the count, might fall behind when all the votes are tallied. Likewise, results arriving from heavily red or heavily blue districts might suddenly change who is leading the count. All of this is overseen by experts, representatives from both parties who observe vote counts, and is explained at length by our election expert colleagues. But still, the conspiracy theories persist. Flood the zone The tsunami of misinformation can be overwhelming. On Tuesday, the zone will very likely be flooded with endless accounts of alleged voter fraud, many of them will likely be amplified by the president of the United States. American elections are not perfect – no system is. But it’s important to remember on this Election Day that there are thousands of devoted election officials working across the country to ensure the election is safe and secure. There is also a committed industry of election deniers, motivated by politics or money or both, devoted to telling you otherwise. They will seek to flood the zone, to create the impression that there is a lot of smoke in the hope you might believe there is a fire.

cnn.com.title: Democratic leaders enter the midterms ‘confident and paranoid’
cnn.com.text: No part of a rolling, decadelong existential crisis is ever easy, even when things seem on the cusp of going well — and especially when Democrats have had their hopes raised and dashed so many times. “It’s a little bit of deja vu,” said Elaine Luria, who in 2018 flipped Virginia’s 2nd Congressional District in the Democratic midterm wave during Donald Trump’s first term, held onto it in a squeaker in 2020 to help make up a slim majority, lost it in 2022 as part of Republicans winning their own small majority, and is now running to get it back. “If you see how people are feeling today, the energy on the ground — the second time around living through this hell of the Trump administration … people want change,” Luria said. “They can’t take it anymore.” The path to a Democratic majority runs through this district, Luria said onstage in the small theater of Batten University. Early voting data suggests Democrats are outperforming Republicans. The energy within the party is bubbling. Internal polls described to CNN have Democratic leaders already smiling about how the midterms seem to be ending, even as they will bare-knuckle through the results as they come in Tuesday. They will enter the midterms with a 9-point advantage over Republicans in the generic congressional ballot, according to CNN’s Poll of Polls. “Republicans are closing talking about ballrooms and backsides. That’s the disarray the Republicans are in,” said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who joined Luria on Saturday, taking a swipe at Trump’s remake of the White House and his reviews of Republican physiques. After Jeffries spoke, the crowd filed out grabbing signs and other campaign material, heading out to knock a few more doors. Jeffries was heading to a plane to try to save the seat of Rep. Shomari Figures, whose Alabama district Republicans targeted after the Supreme Court’s decision hollowing out the Voting Rights Act this spring. “There are going to be so many close races that you can’t predict — my guess is at least 20, the loser will get 49% — so it’s just going to be difficult to predict,” said Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia as he left the Luria rally, describing himself as upbeat but unsure. Sen. Chris Van Hollen chaired the Senate Democrats’ campaign arm in 2018, when the party successfully defended several Senate seats it had been projected to lose while falling short of a majority. The Maryland senator said those elections were dominated by distraught Democrats talking about “the resistance.” This year, as he’s been out campaigning from New Mexico to Georgia to New Hampshire, Van Hollen said, he’s been seeing a broader turn from those who backed Trump for a second term because they wanted the lower prices and end to foreign wars he promised. “This time what’s different is on these promises that candidate Trump made that helped him win votes among his coalition, he’s done a 180,” Van Hollen told CNN. Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and congressman who helped oversee the campaigns that led to the midterms romp during George W. Bush’s second term, said the sense he’s getting from voters is different from 2006. He believes there is a backlash from Americans enraged by corruption, particularly among Black and Latino voters. In 2006, “the emotion was disappointed, tired,” Emanuel said. “Here, it’s anger and bitterness. And that tells you something about the motivation.” That doesn’t mean Emanuel is going into Tuesday fully confident that the polls aren’t missing the level of support for Trump and Republicans and that turnout won’t bring surprises as the precinct breakdowns come in. “I keep checking to make sure we’re not all talking to each other. So I’m walking around looking for anything, ‘Please give me a negative,’” Emanuel said. To his fellow Democrats anxious that they’re about to be disappointed again, Emanuel added, “You might be right, but you may want to use that energy in a productive way rather than sitting around. Text, email, phone call, stand in the middle of the highway. I don’t care what you do, but just use it. There’s nothing productive getting done by being sitting there and being nervous.” Operatives in both parties have been stunned at the cynicism coming across in focus groups, spanning every geographic, demographic, age and political category. Politics is, to many, seen as a game for the insiders in a world that looks more and more like a playground for the rich and powerful, with everyone else left behind while their costs go up and their lives get worse. The candidates are hearing it all on the trail, in supermarket aisles, or when showing up to vote early themselves. Anger, disappointment, abandonment — that’s what’s coursing through American voters as they head to the polls. Will Democrats make the most of the moment? “Confident and paranoid” is how Washington state Rep. Suzan DelBene, the chair of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, described her mindset going into Tuesday. Netting the three seats that would put her party in the majority seems a given to DelBene — but then again, she went through the final days of the election two years ago, when the majority also felt in reach. The paranoia, she says, comes from the ways she can see Trump trying to interfere with the election results. DelBene ticked through conversations she’s been having on the trail, from an early voting center in an Ohio district that Democrats believe they can hold to a Meals on Wheels location in an Arizona district they are hoping to flip. At every stop, she says, the economic pain is palpable. At every stop, she tries to get voters to believe that Democrats are ready to come in with some real solutions. Voting early last week, Cleveland Mayor Justin Bibb said he talked to a woman who was lamenting how the price of her groceries and prescriptions have gone up. She brought her whole family with her to the polling place. To her, that seemed like the only thing to do. But Bibb said he’s worried Democrats gleeful about big wins are going to misunderstand why she and others bothered to give voting one more chance. He understands the cynicism out in the country, Bibb said. He hopes other Democrats do too, and he’s already starting to organize with fellow mayors on how to press Washington, DC, to respond if and when the results come in as he’s hoping. “We can’t miss this moment with just hearings and impeachment proceedings,” Bibb said. “People need to see their pocketbooks improve.” Before anyone starts counting committee chairmanships, Van Hollen said, first they need to actually win. As he stumps around the country, the senator often ends by telling the story of the 2017 races for the Virginia House of Delegates. At the end, control was decided by one seat, and the election of that seat was a tie, leaving it decided under state law by a game of chance —in the case, drawing slips of paper out of a bowl. Republicans won. “I would not rely on these polls,” Van Hollen said. “My plea is: Don’t take anything for granted, don’t let control come down to one campaign.” That can be hard for the voters and candidates and leaders alike. DelBene says she’s been spending the final stretch of the campaign doing a lot of pep talks. “It’s a very stressful time. Folks are tired. They’ve been working incredibly hard,” DelBene said. “I have a lot of conversations with folks just to say, ‘Keep going.’ The one thing about an election is: There is an end date.”

cnn.com.title: Bitter spat between Poland’s pro-Europe PM and pro-Trump president erupts
cnn.com.text: Poland is in the throes of a constitutional crisis as a battle over the future of the country’s highest court ignites another confrontation between the country’s president and prime minister. The crisis came to a head on Friday when center-left Prime Minister Donald Tusk moved to remake Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, whose chief justice was appointed by the previous government – the far-right Law and Justice party (PiS). The judge, Bogdan Święczkowski, was suspended after refusing to allow a new member of the Tribunal, who had been nominated by Tusk and approved by the Polish parliament, from taking his seat. His deputy was also suspended. The current crisis is the latest and possibly most serious chapter in a long-running dispute over the rule of law in Poland. Tusk’s pro-European Civic Coalition was elected in 2023, after an election campaign in which he promised to restore the Tribunal’s independence. President Karol Nawrocki, who belongs to PiS, was elected separately last year. Poland’s president has little executive power but plays an important constitutional role. Since then, deadlock has become crisis. Nawrocki described Święczkowski’s removal as the chief judge as “a forcible takeover of a constitutional body.” On hearing the news, he abandoned a trip to Africa, ordered his aircraft to turn round and headed straight to the Tribunal. Nawrocki is a vocal supporter of US President Donald Trump, who said in September: “I endorsed him, and now he’s president and he’s doing a fantastic job.” Nawrocki has suggested a new US military base in Poland will be called “Fort Trump”. During its eight years in power – until 2023 - PiS appointed several judges to seats on the Tribunal already filled by the previous government. In 2021, the European Union warned that PiS’ actions posed a “systemic risk to the rule of law in Poland” in undermining the Tribunal’s independence. The European Commission froze $137 billion in EU funding for Poland over concerns about the independence of Polish judges. The PiS-appointed judges remained in place after Tusk was elected and have obstructed his efforts to nominate new judges. Nawrocki has refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by ‌parliament, ‌while Swieczkowski declined to seat the judges chosen by parliament. Last week, the latest judge to be approved by parliament – Maciej Berek - was prevented from taking his seat amid scuffles outside the Tribunal in Warsaw. On Saturday, riot police reinforced security measures around the court in central Warsaw. ‘There is no other way,’ says Tusk Tusk, who has spent much of his time as Prime Minister trying to unstitch the PiS changes to the judiciary, said his government was seeking to restore the rule of law. “This process is difficult, at times even painful, ‌and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he said on X Saturday. In a televised speech Tusk said that “shouting, lies, and brawling cannot be the source of law in Poland, and they never will be.” He insisted the Tribunal “will function as it should. Also, independently of me and in line with the constitution.” Analysts say the crisis deepened when parliament approved the nomination of Berek, a close ally of Tusk. It “contradicts the government’s pledge to depoliticise the Tribunal,” wrote Alberto Allemano, a professor of law at the HEC Paris Business School. “The Friday suspension of the Tribunal’s president and vice-president, ordered by one judge and accompanied by a police presence outside the building, is not in itself a “coup”: the stated aim is to restore a lawfully functioning court. But restoring the rule of law must itself be done lawfully,” Allemano wrote on X. At the same time, “If the Polish government is trying to repair an institution captured under PiS, its opposition is striving to retain some control through illegal means,” he added. The US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose warned on Friday night that “thousands gathering outside the tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible. The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.” “I hope everyone involved—government officials, law enforcement, and demonstrators alike, to take a deep breath, and don’t take any action that could provoke violence or further escalation,” Rose said on X. But it’s unclear how the standoff between Tusk and Nawrocki can be resolved. Neither seems ready to compromise at a time when Poland faces growing security threats – with the war across the border in Ukraine, and sabotage attacks inside Poland that Tusk has attributed to Russia. Tusk said Saturday of his opponents that it was “no coincidence that they find support among pro-Russian forces around the world.” Fresh elections are due next year, with Poland’s constitutional order and its political direction – towards or away from deeper integration with Europe – high on the agenda.

cnn.com.title: Germany blames infiltrators as Gen Z protests turn violent
cnn.com.text: Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent on Saturday evening with police using water cannons to disperse crowds and masked rioters smashed shop windows, as officials warn the day of rallies organized by a youth-led movement was infiltrated by extremist factions. Saturday’s action across Germany, organized by the ‘Gen Z has got this!’ movement, railed against the high cost of living, underfunding in education, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service. It follows a wave of similar protests which have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which saw a third straight weekend of rallies. Despite organizers calling for the protests to remain peaceful, violence broke out in some German cities, most notably in Frankfurt and Cologne. Police used water cannons while masked protesters smashed shop windows. Speaking to German tabloid Bild, Germany’s interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt said that “violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities” hijacked the peaceful protests, without elaborating further. The interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned that “around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists” infiltrated the city’s protest as the evening descended into violence and looting. “It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended,” Roman Poseck said. Poseck said he was determined the violence that has rocked France would not be replicated in Germany. “We all have those images from France in our minds — looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers,” he said, according to Reuters. “France must not be held up as a model in this regard.” In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop. According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, several people broke into shops in downtown Frankfurt and over 30 people had been temporarily detained in city by the late evening. Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. “Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals – not against peaceful participants,” the police said in a statement. In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. “There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) … our riot police are taking immediate action against this,” the police said. Berlin police wrote on X that 27 officers in the German capital had sustained minor injuries and just under 60 people had been detained for offenses including property damage, assault, and resistance against emergency forces. The movement’s organizers have sought to distance themselves from the ensuing violence. “We had no influence on what happened after the demonstrations ended,” a spokesperson from their press team was quoted by Der Spiegel as saying. Organizers of ‘Gen Z has got this!’ planned the day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday. “We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us,” the movement states on its website. Speaking for his reasons for joining the movement, an 18-year-old student protester in Munich told Reuters, “The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us.” In the eastern city of Dresden, demonstrators held placards reading, “The rich want war, the youth want a future!” and “You’ve screwed up – Gen Z will sort it out.” Europe-wide protests More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement took place in France on Saturday, in what was billed as the third act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24. This time, however, they were more scaled down than before. The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris; a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week. The French protests were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that “radical elements at the tail end of the processions” in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, “attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.” Protests over soaring housing costs also swept Portugal and Italy on Saturday. In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, thousands marched to demand Portugal’s center-right government withdraw a rental bill they say will worsen the country’s housing crisis. In Italy, protests largely led by student groups and workers rallied against inflation, stagnant wages and unaffordable housing in cities including Turin, Bologna and Milan.

cnn.com.title: “Nobody’s listening”: 5 things Americans told me about the economy that Washington needs to hear
cnn.com.text: From Cleveland to the Outer Banks, the cost-of-living crisis that will decide the midterms, in the words of the people living it. Every incumbent on the ballot this fall, Republican or Democrat, is running on a set of numbers. Unemployment at 4.2%. Record household income. Inflation “cooling.” The five things I learned over six months of kitchen tables explain why those numbers aren’t landing. I spent the better part of a year trying to answer one question: Why do Americans feel this bad about an economy that, on paper, is this good? Some 74% of Americans rate the economy as poor, not far off the 84% who said the same in 2009, when the country was shedding jobs by the hundreds of thousands. People who handed me, a stranger, their bank statements because nobody else was asking aren’t going to be won over by a mailer. “Cooling” inflation sounds like an insult to people whose rent doubled and stayed doubled. When a family is one ordinary bill from the edge, its backup plan is sleeping in the car. People who spent years blaming themselves have started blaming the people in charge. Parents and grandparents are wondering if their children will get to stay in the places they built. This is an electorate that is angry and unconvinced its vote changes anything. In the closest races in the country, it may not matter which candidate has the better plan. It may matter which one people finally believe was listening. I built the spreadsheets first. I’m a numbers guy, and I won’t apologize for it. But the spreadsheets didn’t explain it. More than four dozen people across six episodes did, though, at their own kitchen tables, usually with their bills spread out in front of us. Here are the five things they taught me that no top-line number will. When Washington says inflation is cooling, it means prices are rising more slowly. It doesn’t mean anything got cheaper. That distinction sounds like economist hair-splitting. At the kitchen table, it’s everything. Jolene Simecek’s rent in Cleveland went “from $785 to nearly $1,600” for the same apartment in the space of seven years. “When I file my taxes,” she told me, “my income is definitely not doubled.” In Tampa, Phebie White’s rent climbed from $850 to $1,250 while her Social Security check sat still. “Your bills are going to go up,” she said, “but your Social Security is not going to go up.” Annual adjustments, known as COLAs, have not kept pace with rising expenses in recent years. Prices are up 6.8% since December 2024. Average hourly pay is up 5.9%. That gap is the whole story in two numbers, and it’s why “the economy is improving” lands like an insult. A 20-something in Atlanta, Kay Jones, summed up her friends’ finances for me in four words: “We’re in a recession.” By every official measure, we’re not. She wasn’t describing a definition. She was describing a feeling, and that feeling is what shows up in the polls. No single catastrophe wiped out the people I met. It was the grind: housing, insurance, food, childcare, electricity, all of it climbing, none of it optional. That left them one surprise away from crisis: a $70 tire, a $400 vet bill, an $1,100 utility bill due Monday, a dead battery in a snowstorm. What I wasn’t prepared for was how many of them had already, quietly, worked out what came next. And how often the answer was the car. Phebie keeps her car insurance paid before almost anything else. “Just in case I need to sleep in it,” she told me, “and I pray that that never happens.” I asked her to explain. She said she knows plenty of people who already do, and “you won’t know that they’re sleeping in their car until they tell you.” At a free clinic in Tampa, I sat down next to a 64-year-old cancer survivor named Elen Trosino, and when I asked how long she’d been living in her car, she said, “Uh, like a week now.” In Rocky Mount, North Carolina, Sheila Scarborough, a veteran on a fixed income, slept in hers most nights for seven weeks this summer after the city cut her power. On the Outer Banks, a tour guide named Stu Laird lived in his truck until the battery died in a January storm and he ended up with frostbite, three hospital stays and a broken hip. They differ in age, race, region and politics. Every one of them landed on the same contingency plan, alone. I’ve covered this stuff for nearly two decades, and I can’t find that safety net in any government data series. For millions of Americans, it’s a depreciating asset with a back seat. This one still gets under my skin. In every city, people facing forces that took decades to build – predatory lending, a childcare market that runs on poverty wages, a state that refused to expand Medicaid, a war that sent diesel past $6 – looked at the damage and assumed they were the problem. “I didn’t make the right decisions,” Jolene told me. Phebie said if her generation had known better, they would have done better. Corey Goodhue, an Iowa corn and soybean farmer staring at his over-budget diesel line, told me, “Either I did it wrong or inflation got me. The buck has to stop at this desk.” A Tampa woman who spent 35 years getting other people onto food stamps and Medicaid, now uninsured herself, said, “I can counsel anybody, I can’t counsel myself.” I’d smile at first, because it sounded absurd and I assumed each was delivering a knowing quip. Then I’d realize how much they meant it, and, to be candid, I’d get pissed. When a system breaks quietly enough, the people it breaks blame themselves. But self-blame doesn’t stay self-blame forever. Jolene said it best near the end of our conversation: “I’m kind of questioning why more people aren’t mad.” They are now. More than three-quarters of Americans say they’re dissatisfied or angry about the direction of the country, and 37% call themselves flat-out angry. The anxiety I heard wasn’t only about this month’s bills. It was about who gets to stay. Greg and Audrey Dunn paid $114,000 in daycare in a single year for three kids in suburban Boston. “Even if we wanted a fourth kid,” Greg said, “we could never afford a fourth.” On the Outer Banks, business owner Chris Marik buys houses just to keep his staff and figures his three daughters will probably never be able to live where they grew up. “If I play by the rules, pay my taxes and do this, it should work out,” he said. “On paper, it’s never gonna work out.” In Atlanta, Mayra Martinez watched her immigrant parents get priced out of the neighborhood they helped build. They “lost two homes,” she said: the country they left, and the community they made here. In Iowa, a young farmer explained that under current tax rules, it makes more sense for an older relative to die holding the land than to sell it to him. And Jolene, who never had generational wealth to inherit, is determined that her son will. “If I’m having trouble and struggling at 42,” she asked me, “how do I expect my gonna-be-18-year-old to get a place?” That’s why voters under 35 are among the most pessimistic in the country: 84% rate the economy poorly. It isn’t a mood. It’s math about their own futures. As I sat at kitchen tables and personal offices walking line-by-line through childcare invoices, utility bills and budget spreadsheets, I often caught myself marveling at the willingness of so many to be so transparent about their personal financial pressure points and struggles. Part of it, I came to believe, was that nobody else had asked. Sheila said it outright. “They’re not listening,” she told me. “We are trying, as citizens, trying to tell you what’s going on, but nobody’s listening.” When I asked Phebie whether policymakers understand what she’s going through, she said one word, “No.” Then: “Because they don’t have the struggle.” And when the campaign calls came while Sheila’s power was off, she had a message for them: “Until you help get my lights on, don’t ask me about voting for nobody.” That’s what makes this election so hard to read. The economy and cost of living lead every other issue, at 43%. But 29% say neither party would do a better job on it. And among voters who aren’t highly motivated to show up, 51% call the economy their top issue, compared with 36% of the most motivated. The people most consumed by the cost of living are the least sure their vote changes anything.  What it all means Here’s what stays with me after more than 60 hours of interviews with more than four dozen people over the course of the last six months. None of the people who let me into their homes – who sat with me at their kitchen tables, put out a chair and plate for me at their family dinners, took me to their most personal thoughts, places and financial information – asked for much. Not a bailout or a handout, just a floor that holds: rent that doesn’t double, a utility bill that’s right, a shot at the same starter home their parents got, a fair chance for their kids to stay. They did the math themselves, often more precisely than the people sending them mailers. Then they blamed themselves, then they got angry, and now they’re deciding whether showing up is worth it. That’s what’s really at stake on November 3. I came home from these trips heartbroken more often than I’d like to admit, but never cynical. Phebie still goes to the beach because it’s free. Sheila stood up at a city council meeting for the first time in her life. Corey still calls his optimism “mental illness” and gets up for harvest anyway. They’re holding up their end. In a few days, they’ll tell us whether they think anyone else is.

cnn.com.title: The Cheesecake Factory can’t get enough of the Gen Z ‘Tuscan moms’
cnn.com.text: It’s always going to be 2006 at the Cheesecake Factory. And for the crowds of young people dining there in cheetah print and sunglasses bigger than the restaurant’s portions, that’s exactly how they want it. Take Caroline Fisher, a 23-year-old in Phoenix who embodies the “Tuscan mom” aesthetic, a style rooted in the nostalgia of early 2000s suburban mothers in Italian-themed kitchens. On one night at the Cheesecake Factory, Fisher wore boot-cut flare jeans, a chunky brown belt and wedge heels that she thrifted. She straightened her platinum blonde hair and added a bump-it. She thinned her eyebrows and did a smoky eye with gold eyeshadow. The playlist on the way to the restaurant featured Norah Jones and Maroon 5, hitmakers from the aughts. Fisher is among the mostly younger diners who have channeled “Desperate Housewives” at Cheesecake Factory, the gaudy chain restaurant known for its warm mood lighting and towering columns. And these “Tuscan moms” receive hundreds of thousands of views on social media. Fisher ordered a salad and french fries, and split a bottle of wine with her friend. Her friend ordered off the chain’s Skinnylicious menu — “the ultimate Tuscan mom” lineup, she said. The chain, which has over 200 locations in the United States, was recently caught in a culture war against its will, sparked by a joke from former President Barack Obama on its aesthetic. But the more interesting story is just how well the Cheesecake Factory is doing. Its stock soared above Big Tech this year (it trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol CAKE). It just reported its second consecutive quarter with more than $1 billion in revenue. A big reason for that? Social media trends like the Tuscan mom aesthetic, largely driven by younger consumers. The company credited its expanded role on social media for much of its success in its latest earnings call last Wednesday. “A very large percentage” of guests skew younger, CFO Matthew Clark said. When any nondescript suburb opens a Cheesecake Factory, there’s no restaurant around that can compare to its palatial grandeur. It’s a “postmodern melange of a bunch of different references that looks almost otherworldly because it doesn’t really fit into one box perfectly,” Evan Collins, a designer and co-founder of the Consumer Aesthetics Research Institute, told CNN. The plethora of options in its phone book-sized menu “naturally lends itself to engaging and shareable social content,” the company’s president, David Gordon, said on the call. The Cheesecake Factory notably did not acknowledge the political discourse whirling around it, and did not respond to CNN’s request for comment on the Tuscan mom aesthetic. What is ‘the Tuscan mom?’ The Tuscan mom trend is rooted in nostalgia. Think over-sized kitchens with dark cabinetry, granite countertops, artificial grapes and many, many rooster decorations. The Tuscan mom aesthetic reached peak popularity on Pinterest this summer, around the time the Cheesecake Factory topped $1 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. The appeal of the Tuscan mom aesthetic spans from fashion and beauty to interior design, Pinterest said. Searches for “Tuscan mom outfit” rose 4,975% year-over-year; “2000s Tuscan mom,” meanwhile, jumped 1,501%. It echoes a time that Americans often romanticize: the housing boom before the 2008 crash, when purchasing an overvalued McMansion as a gateway to the upper-middle class was still feasible. People were able to afford “driving in a nice Lincoln Navigator, bedazzled jeans and a fancy top, and going to the spa, and then after that going to Starbucks and Cheesecake Factory,” Collins, the designer, told CNN. Nikole Jackson, a 32-year-old from San Antonio, Texas, described it as “2000s mature, not the whole Britney Spears type of 2000s, but more catered toward the Kardashians, who had more of a regal type of look to them.” The Cheesecake Factory, unlike its other suburban strip-plaza counterparts like Starbucks and Barnes & Noble, has held on to that aesthetic, Jackson said. “A lot of places have lost that character and replaced it with this almost bright, stark white clinical appearance,” Jackson said. “And thankfully, Cheesecake Factory never lost that.” Cheesecakes are winning “Everything that they’re doing is resonating with guests,” Citi equity research analyst Jon Tower told CNN. It started with the addition of “Bites” and “Bowls” to its appetizer menu last year, smaller portions of dishes like Chicken & Waffle Skewers and Teriyaki Salmon bowls at a lower price. But most importantly, Tower said, the company recently got a new creative agency as it took off on the internet. Soon, social media began trending with the revelation that almost everything on the Cheesecake Factory’s gargantuan menu is made from scratch (except the cheesecake).
