For many inflation-fatigued consumers, the fresh food, huge portions and fancy atmosphere are worth the price. “When I get my herb-crested chicken parm, there’s three chicken pieces on that plate,” Jackson said. “And of course, they give you a bunch of bread.” Food influencers began vlogging from the cushioned red booths in the past year. One viral “order hack” — the cajun salmon platter with cajun shrimp and extra Parmesan cream sauce — actually led to higher sales of the longtime menu staple, according to the earnings call. While social media trends come and go as quickly as the free bread at the Cheesecake Factory, Tower said the company has no shortage of content to work with. “They’ve got 250-plus menu items to play with,” he said. Paying no attention to a ‘controversy’ Obama’s recent remarks on the Cheesecake Factory stirred up conversations again on the restaurant’s aesthetic. He joked that President Donald Trump has “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” It quickly imploded, starting with accusations from right-leaning media of Obama-era elitism and ending with a former GOP congressman “clinging to my guns and religion at the Greensboro Cheesecake Factory tonight.” But followers of the Tuscan mom lifestyle had little to say about the comment, if they were even keeping up with the controversy. “Listen, the White House may look how it looks, but I think that the Cheesecake Factory does not deserve the slander because I love it,” Fisher said.

cnn.com.title: The last-minute surprises and sideshows of the 2026 campaign
cnn.com.text: The 2026 midterm elections mostly revolve around deeply serious business. There’s a war going on. Polls show Americans are worried about the economy and affordability, like they’ve rarely ever been. And the results will determine whether and how much Democrats can provide a check on President Donald Trump’s attempted consolidation of power. But as is often the case, the final stages of the campaign have been chock full of things that have nothing to do with all of that — with some of those sideshows potentially more consequential than others. The latest example came Sunday morning, when Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens, who lost the Senate primary, said she’s endorsing Republican nominee Mike Rogers. It was an astounding move after days of a deepening rift between her and Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, but it remains to be seen how that could affect the race so late in the game. And there’s a lot more of that intraparty feuding in other states, but first, let’s recap some of the other sideshows in the midterm campaign. Alaska spoiler candidate One of the most substantial late developments was last week’s New York Times report on Democratic Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign’s role in recruiting the other Dan Sullivan to apparently try to confuse Alaska voters intending to vote for Sen. Dan Sullivan. Peltola maintains that she “knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot” and that she is “not interested in tricking voters.” She also labeled the story “another distraction” and “another diversion” from real issues like affordability. “Every day it’s some new, you know, ‘Look over here’ moment,” Peltola said. Unfortunately for Peltola, it appears that her own campaign gave people good reason to look over there. While Democrats will point to other political dirty tricks in both the distant and recent past, it’s rare that such a trick is tied so directly to a candidate’s campaign. But what’s perhaps most remarkable about all of it is how silly the gambit appears to have been in the first place. There is very little chance that that other Dan Sullivan will actually make the difference in the race. An incendiary gubernatorial ad The Ohio governor’s race was already known as somewhat nasty, but then GOP nominee Vivek Ramaswamy decided to up the ante when he featured Democrat Amy Acton’s mother criticizing her in an ad. This despite Acton having said she has had no contact with her mother since she was 12-years-old, around the time the man her mother married was indicted for allegedly sexually abusing Acton. The ad seemed desperate, at best. And despite initially defending his decision to run it, Ramaswamy’s campaign has discontinued it after reportedly spending only a fraction of what was initially announced. The Cheesecake Factory Meanwhile, Republicans have strained to make a culture-war issue of a quip from former President Barack Obama that Trump has “got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory.” It’s their new attempted “cling to guns and religion.” Republicans have suggested this amounts to Obama talking down to people who enjoy the chain restaurant. Never mind that the Cheesecake Factory’s decor is intentionally over-the-top (or the whole Saddam Hussein aspect). And never mind the Trump is out there talking about how his supporters probably can’t afford to eat at Mar-a-Lago. Trump’s ‘ass’ commentary Trump also continues to mention candidates’ physiques, mostly repeating references to the quality of GOP Ohio Sen. Jon Husted’s “ass.” This is, of course, after Trump repeatedly insulted Texas Senate candidate Ken Paxton’s appearance for unknown reasons. When Vice President JD Vance got a serious question about affordability during a Fox News town hall on Thursday night, he quipped that he was surprised more people weren’t asking him about Husted’s derriere — before proceeding to answer the question. Islamophobic attacks On an uglier level, the GOP’s Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed took a downright bizarre turn last week. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. espoused a bunch of untrue claims about the lack of achievements by the world’s 500 million Arabs. Intraparty drama The Michigan Senate race is now the biggest example. After Stevens’ fiancé — Jewish Democrat Jason Turkish — publicly backed Republican Rogers, Stevens assured voters that she still backed El-Sayed and planned to attend a unity event with him. But things deteriorated quickly from there. On Friday, Stevens urged El-Sayed to more forcefully condemn an outside group’s ad that criticizes US aid to Israel. El-Sayed said he did not agree with the content of the ad, but his campaign told Stevens to stay away from its campaign events, according to a person familiar. And then on Sunday, Stevens — who was set to appear at church with Rogers — tweeted her endorsement of the Republican nominee. When this was just about the person Stevens’ fiancé was voting for, it probably didn’t much matter to your average voter, even as it pointed to potential problems that El-Sayed seems to have with Jewish Democrats. Stevens’ endorsement, however, may catch the eye of more voters. But whether that has Stevens’ intended effect — or simply backfires on her and unifies Democrats — is still a question. Michigan is hardly the only example of intraparty — and intrafamily — squabbling. In the South Carolina Senate race, GOP Rep. Ralph Norman can’t seem to let go of his loss to appointed GOP Sen. Darline Graham, repeatedly saying that voters “deserve better” and feeding into Graham’s major liability: her lack of experience. In the New Hampshire Senate race, we’ve had some Sununu-on-Sununu rhetorical violence. Amid some questions about whether voters know that it’s former GOP Sen. John E. Sununu running rather than his brother, the popular recent former Gov. Chris Sununu, Chris Sununu joked that if voters thought it was him, Republicans would be “up by 30 points.” John E. Sununu didn’t seem to appreciate that idea, responding: “I love my brother, but he’s totally wrong.” It’s unlikely that most or any of these things will actually make a difference in the end. Many people have already voted, and the vast majority of Americans are likely set in their opinions. But people tend to get quite squirrely and desperate toward the end of campaigns. And 2026 is surely no exception. This headline and story have been updated with additional developments.

cnn.com.title: Obamacare continues to shrink as enrollment opens for 2027
cnn.com.text: Holly Hendricks, who is battling an autoimmune disease that leaves her with open wounds down to the muscle, did everything she could to maintain her Affordable Care Act coverage after the enhanced premium subsidies lapsed at the start of this year. But after a few months, the 49-year-old couldn’t handle paying the monthly premiums, which had more than tripled to nearly $1,100. Hendricks, who also has lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, became uninsured for the first time in April. While she scrapes together enough money to afford her 12 daily medications, Hendricks can no longer see her four specialists, get blood work, receive infusions or have a wound care nurse tend to her condition. In September, she developed sepsis and ended up in the hospital for a month, which she expects could saddle her with more than $500,000 in medical bills. “Being uninsured is catastrophic to my health, but when you have to choose between rent, utilities, food and insurance – the more basic needs have to come first,” said Hendricks, a Sarasota, Florida, resident who works full-time as a caretaker for a veteran. Faced with soaring premium payments after the beefed-up subsidies expired, millions of Obamacare enrollees left the market at the start of the year. Only 19.2 million people were enrolled as of February, down 2.6 million from the same period a year earlier, according to the latest federal data. But there are multiple signs that enrollment has continued to fall since then, in part because policyholders like Hendricks couldn’t keep up with the higher monthly premiums amid rising costs for gas, groceries and other necessities. “People who tried to make it work at the beginning of the year might not be able to make it work for a whole year,” said Cynthia Cox, director of the Program on the ACA at KFF, a nonpartisan health policy research group. Some folks are hoping to resume their coverage in January if they can find a less expensive Obamacare plan. Open enrollment begins Sunday in most states, but premiums are expected to jump once again. The ongoing enrollment decline comes as healthcare has been a key affordability issue in the midterm elections. Many Democratic candidates are highlighting that their Republican rivals allowed the enhanced premium subsidies to lapse, as well as voted to slash federal Medicaid funding by roughly $1 trillion as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. Republican-held congressional districts suffered disproportionately greater drops in enrollment between 2025 and 2026, KFF found. These districts account for 55% of enrollees but 67% of the declines. They tend to have higher shares of lower-income residents, who would have a tougher time affording any premium increases, Cox said. Terminating coverage Eighteen states that run their own Affordable Care Act exchanges reported that enrollment declines accelerated during the year due to more people dropping out and fewer signing up via special enrollment periods in 2026. Disenrollments were up nearly 34% as of May, compared to the same period a year prior, according to a State Marketplace Network report. The number of people buying coverage on the individual market, which is largely comprised of the Obamacare exchanges, also fell – by more than 4.6 million as of June, compared to the same month a year earlier – according to KFF estimates. Some states have seen steep declines. Mississippi, for instance, ended 2025 with 338,000 residents enrolled in Obamacare plans. By February, that figure had tumbled to fewer than 192,000 people and fell further to around 125,000 residents in September, Mike Chaney, the state’s insurance commissioner, told CNN. (Enrollment has since edged up to 135,000 people in late October.) Massachusetts saw its first decline in enrollment during the course of the year outside of the Covid-19 pandemic period, said Audrey Morse Gasteier, executive director of the state’s Affordable Care Act exchange. About 8,000 fewer people were on the exchange in September than in February. The loss stems in part from more enrollees dropping their coverage mid-year than they typically do, she said. Even New Mexico, which provides generous state-funded subsidies, saw continued disenrollments and fewer people signing up for coverage mid-year. It had been the only state where enrollment increased as of February, but that bump had largely disappeared by the fall, said Brent Earnest, interim CEO of BeWell, the state’s health insurance marketplace. Kara Windeler is among those who desperately tried to keep her Obamacare coverage, which helped the Clearwater, Florida, resident treat her rheumatoid arthritis, long Covid, severe allergies and other conditions. Her premium jumped to $450 a month, from about $225 last year. Unable to keep working as a skincare specialist because of her health, Windeler had been selling cherished collectibles, borrowing money from family and draining the proceeds of the 2024 sale of her house to pay her premiums. But the funds ran out so she will be uninsured as of November 1. To prepare, Windeler filled 90-day prescriptions for her medications, saw her doctors and received a steroid injection in late October. She plans to ration the medicines so they last longer. Windeler, an independent voter who turned 50 on Saturday, hopes that the Democrats will act to lower healthcare costs if they win control of Congress. “There has to be something done so that people don’t die,” she said. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which oversees the Affordable Care Act exchanges, has attributed the enrollment declines to its anti-fraud efforts. It argues it is rooting out so-called phantom enrollees, who don’t exist, and people who were signed up without their knowledge by unscrupulous brokers seeking commissions. In September, the White House fraud task force announced it was removing 760,000 enrollees from Obamacare coverage. Premiums set to rise again Premiums for Obamacare’s benchmark silver-tier plans will rise 13%, on average, in 2027, according to a KFF calculation of CMS and state exchange data. It’s the second consecutive year of double-digit premium increases and the 4th largest hike since the Affordable Care Act exchanges launched in 2014, Cox said. Still, that’s far less than the 58% average jump in the monthly payments enrollees saw this year, which was exacerbated by the expiration of the enhanced premium subsidies. The lapsed assistance was more generous and helped more people than regular Obamacare subsidies, which were part of the 2010 law and continue to exist. Most enrollees still qualify for these regular subsidies, which will help shield them from the standard annual premium increase for next year. In Idaho, premiums for silver-tier plans will be flat or lower than this year in many parts of the state once subsidies are factored in, said Pat Kelly, executive director of Idaho’s Obamacare exchange. While it’s too early to tell how many people will sign up, Kelly is encouraged by the fact that more people are reaching out to the call center and looking at the exchange’s website since enrollment opened on October 15. Many enrollees nationwide, however, will have fewer plans to choose from since several large insurers have opted to pull out of some or all of the states where they provide coverage. Roughly 1,200 counties will have only one or two insurers on their exchanges, up from about 800, said Katherine Hempstead, senior policy officer at the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation. That means enrollees could have to switch plans – so they need to check that their doctors and drugs are covered by the new policy. Plus, those signing up for coverage could have less access to help since the Trump administration has placed a moratorium on new broker and agent participation in the exchanges as part of its fraud-fighting campaign. At the same time, it has slashed funding for navigators, who also provide enrollment assistance, by 90%. Along with restrictions to immigrants’ eligibility for Obamacare subsidies stemming from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, this means  Affordable Care Act coverage is expected to shrink again next year. Younger, healthier people will likely be the ones to leave first, which could lead to higher premiums for those who remain. Still, some Americans continue to rely on the Affordable Care Act. Julie Kay Roberts has been waiting months for open enrollment to begin so she can look for a more affordable Obamacare plan. The consultant from Southlake, Texas, had to drop her coverage in June after being unable to keep up with monthly premiums that had soared from about $490 to $1,240. Roberts is resigned to having to pay more out of pocket for care to have a plan with lower monthly premiums – even though she considers it more of a backstop in case of a catastrophe such as cancer or an accident. She’s hoping to find a plan that costs no more than $600 a month. “I definitely will be finding an insurance option of some sort,” she said. “I just I don’t like to go without.”

cnn.com.title: How to follow along with CNN’s election coverage
cnn.com.text: Millions of voters will cast their ballots Tuesday in an election that will decide the balance of power in Congress and set the tone for President Donald Trump’s remaining two years in the White House. Democrats and Republicans are battling in tight contests across the country, while the governor’s office in some states is up for grabs. To help you make sense of these crucial races, CNN is offering on-the-ground reporting, in-depth analysis and interactive experiences across all platforms. Here’s how you can access CNN’s coverage. Tune into CNN’s Election Night in America special coverage CNN will also bring you all the key updates and context on air and streaming on CNN’s All Access throughout the day, with election coverage beginning at 12 a.m. ET on Tuesday. Election Night in America special coverage will begin at 4 p.m. ET, and Anderson Cooper and Jake Tapper will co-anchor from Washington, DC, with expert analysis from Dana Bash, Kaitlan Collins, Erin Burnett and others. Stream exclusive content on All Access CNN’s streaming platform, All Access, will offer 12 hours of live and unedited content on Election Day starting at 7 a.m. ET that will give subscribers a behind-the-scenes look at what our reporters are doing on the ground. In the evening, subscribers will have access to campaign headquarters. Our correspondents will bring you a live look at how the candidates and their supporters are awaiting results and their reaction when the race is called. CNN’s John Berman and Harry Enten will also host Office Hours starting at 7 p.m. ET to answer questions at the top of subscribers’ minds as the night unfolds. Subscribers will have the option to quickly get up to speed with regular video catch-ups throughout the night. But if you’re looking to dive deep into the key races, you can watch all episodes of CNN Explains, The Enten Scale, All Over The Map and more on All Access’ content library. Zoom in on the races with CNN’s digital Magic Wall As John King stands in front of the Magic Wall on election night and breaks down the races, you can navigate along with CNN’s digital offering. You’ll have the Magic Wall at your fingertips on the CNN app and CNN.com, where you can follow races across the country with an interactive map that allows you to zoom in as far as the county level. On the app, subscribers will have access to historical data that will allow them to compare results to past election cycles. You can also turn on real-time notifications for key races. Meanwhile, on the website, you can track when polls close and follow the results of ballot measures and local races. Voter polls will also be available to give insight into how Americans of different demographics are voting. Sightline As results start to roll in, it can be difficult to understand what those numbers might be saying about who will ultimately win a key race. CNN Sightline, a new election tool designed to surface insights from CNN’s Decision Desk, can translate those results into an understandable, real-time read on what’s happening and who is favored to win. The tool interprets election data through modeling and assessments based on the questions that CNN’s Decision Desk analysts consider as they’re assessing the state of each major race: Where did the votes come from? How do they compare with past elections and pre-election expectations? How much statistical confidence do we have in our estimates? Were they Election Day, by-mail or early in-person votes? And what do we know about what’s left to count? Sightline brings together the results of a range of estimates meant to answer each of those questions, shows how the CNN Decision Desk interprets those questions at any given moment, and produces an overall rating on whether a race leans toward either candidate. Get live updates from across the country CNN is offering around-the-clock, live updates to get you up to speed on what’s going on across the country as our correspondents share real-time reporting from the ground. The live updates will feature photos and videos as our reporters talk to voters outside polling sites and with candidates as they make their final pitches. CNN will also get you up to speed on any voting issues, legal challenges and reactions from top lawmakers. Regular catch-up posts will be available so you can quickly scan the top stories. You will immediately know when polls close, when CNN makes a projection on a key race and when candidates make their victory or concession speeches. And as results begin to trickle in, our journalists will provide live commentary and in-depth analysis, using their expertise to give you key context on the night’s biggest moments.

bbc.com.title: Ryanair says it may freeze workers' pay and raise airfares
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn (£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its chief executive, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into "temporary pay freezes". Unite, the union which represents Ryanair staff, has been contacted for comment.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to €2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to higher fuel costs jumping by 15%.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be €2bn higher in the short-term.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" – in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices – the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up freezing pay as "maturing labour agreements" – multi-year wage deals with unions – come to to an end and the policy could be implemented from April next year.
It also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

bbc.com.title: Supermarket freezers in Belgium and Sweden hit by suspected cyber-attack
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Dozens of supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting its refrigerators and freezers.
Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets and 15 Carrefour stores were affected in Belgium, while several ICA and Coop shops in Sweden were hit. Thirteen SuperValu shops have also been impacted in Ireland.
Thousands of euros worth of food has had to be thrown away, according to local media reports, with one ICA store in Sweden saying temperatures for its freezers had been set to 50 C (122F).
It is not clear who is behind the attack, which follows a similar incident last month that affected hundreds of French supermarkets.
Delhaize, one of Belgium's biggest supermarket chains, told Belgian media a "computer incident" had occurred overnight at 40 shops.
Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said it was "currently analysing" the incident at 15 of its Belgian stores.
Meanwhile, a spokesperson for ICA in Sweden confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network".
"ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said.
One of the IVA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees."
The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers.
Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden are also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC.

bbc.com.title: Nine killed as small jet crashes on Florida street
bbc.com.text:
- Published
A business jet crashed in a neighbourhood in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board, the US transport secretary has said.
The crash happened near Cresthaven, some nine miles (14 km) from Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump's resort in the wealthy enclave of Palm Beach County, around 12:50 EST (17:50 GMT).
Images show a large crater in the middle of a multi-lane road, with fire and debris from the Learjet 60 aircraft scattered across it, but nobody on the ground was hurt.
The aircraft had departed from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio recorded moments before the crash, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
The person can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
The crew member declared an emergency, yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last remark from the cockpit was "we're out of time".
Unverified footage posted on social media shows what appears to be a dash-camera recording of the moment of the crash. It shows vehicles driving on a residential suburban street, when suddenly an aircraft nosedives into the ground almost vertically, and explodes into a large fireball.
"When you see that video, it's a jarring thing," Florida Governor Ron DeSantis told reporters at a news conference after the crash. "It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."
It is not yet clear who was aboard the jet when it crashed. DeSantis said "as of now, we don't have any reports of anyone who was on the ground...who was killed or injured".
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the crash as a "horrific tragedy", and said the FAA was sending a team to the scene to help an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board.
"Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Duffy added.
Palm Beach County Fire Rescue has declared a "mass casualty incident".
The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office said the crash happened on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants.
At a news conference, DeSantis and local officials said that 600 local residents were being evacuated from a nearby trailer-park community.
The impact of the crash caused considerable damage to local infrastructure, including its water lines, they said, and it would be at least 30 days before the road re-opened.
Thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash, and it was heavily raining as the news conference was held.
Trump had been at Mar-a-Lago on Sunday morning, and departed from an airport nearby on Air Force One about an hour before the crash.

bbc.com.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after 20 years
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
The first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson, Chris Magezi, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.
Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), which was established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
Last week, Gen Muhoozi said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
The withdrawal is being carried out in phases and is expected to be completed in August 2027.
However, Uganda is not ending its entire military involvement in Somalia. Its troops deployed under a separate bilateral security arrangement will remain in the country.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency led al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, for more than two decades.
Uganda forces first deployed to the country in 2007 and played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.
Ugandan troops continued its military involvement under successive Africa Union, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.
It was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin to in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

bbc.com.title: Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".
In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.
She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.
"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.
Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

bbc.com.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets.
Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added.
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with the fallout of the attack.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.
Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.
"The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added.
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them.
The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets.
Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
"Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.

bbc.com.title: Iran killed her teenage daughter - now she is facing up to the regime
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Warning: Distressing content and strong language
Samira says she never used to be political.
"I worked in sales in Iran. I sold cosmetics," she tells BBC Panorama.
But that all changed the day her only child was shot dead in front of her by Iranian security forces. Sixteen-year-old Sevda was taking part in protests against Iran's repressive regime that engulfed the country earlier this year - before the US and Israel launched widespread air strikes which killed the country's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Samira's grief became fury as Iran's authorities then hindered, rather than helped, her search for her daughter's body, she says.
"I realised that finding Sevda wasn't the end, but just the beginning of all the harassment they put me through."
Samira made a dramatic escape from Iran on foot, navigating dangerous mountainous terrain.
She now lives abroad in hiding, describing herself as a "one-woman army fighting the regime". In a search for accountability and justice after her daughter's death, she is intent on naming the members of the security forces and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the protests.
"They'll bring me to the brink of death before they kill me, but finding me won't be easy… Return to normal life? There is no going back," she says.
Samira is among several Iranians the BBC has spoken to since the start of the year. Some, still inside the country, told Panorama they wanted to speak out despite the risks, saying they had found it difficult to hold on to hope once the mass protests had been brutally crushed.
The Iranian embassy in London told Panorama that peaceful and legitimate protests had been hijacked by foreign powers, including the US, which promoted violence, provided weapons and equipment, and compromised public security.
Panorama - Iran: The People’s Story
The story of Iranians who have lived through the most turbulent and traumatic of years, with widespread street protests, a brutal crackdown by the authorities and a war launched against Iran by the US and Israel.
Or watch on BBC One at 20:00 on Monday 2 November 2026.
Sevda was killed on 9 January as she and Samira took part in huge demonstrations on the outskirts of the capital Tehran which had begun the previous month. They had been sparked by economic discontent, before escalating into calls for an end to the country's Islamic Republic.
Though Samira denies she was especially political then, she says her daughter was. Sevda's idols were two other young women - Mahsa Amini, whose death in custody after an alleged violation against the mandatory headscarf triggered mass protests, and Nika Shakarami, who was killed during a subsequent uprising against Iran's strict Islamic dress code for women.
"She kept them alive in her thoughts and always wanted to continue their path [of resistance]," Samira says.
The day before Sevda was killed, the numbers protesting had been particularly high. Samira says she and Sevda had responded to a call by Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran's last shah (king), for demonstrations.
"The security forces had lost control," she says.
The swell in numbers had spooked Iran's government, and the following day a shoot-to-kill order was announced, Samira says. But she had thought it just an empty threat.
"They lied so much in Iran… We couldn't imagine a massacre of that scale."
And they were reassured, she says, by US President Trump's promise that he had their backs.
He had told US media on 8 January: "I have let [the Iranian authorities] know that if they start killing people, which they tend to do during their riots… we're going to hit them very hard."
But nevertheless the crowds appeared smaller on the 9th, Samira says.
Sevda seemed to know the risks, she says. Her daughter took off her earrings and gave them to her grandmother. She also shared her phone passcode with Samira.
The mother and daughter gathered with the rest of the protesters. Sevda then stood on a dustbin and began leading a chant.
"It seemed there were more forces than people," Samira says of the area where they were. "I don't know how, within one day, they gathered so many… Basijis and IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] forces."
The IRGC defends the country's Islamic establishment, and the paramilitary Basij Resistance Force are volunteers for the IRGC.
"A sniper fired from the roof of a building on our right. The bullet must have come from the rooftop. The bullet went through her heart. I couldn't even scream. I just stared at Sevda - her body lying lifeless. Blood was gushing out her mouth and nose. I couldn't believe it, I couldn't believe she was dying. Her eyes were still looking at me."
Samira says she managed to get Sevda to hospital and she was told they were operating on her, but then the door opened and she saw Sevda had been zipped into a body bag.
Sevda's body was taken away. Samira says it took her days to find her daughter again. Like many others, she found herself at one of Tehran's largest morgues.
"Teenagers - young boys and girls. So many had been killed," she cries.
"I died with every bag I unzipped. I'd never seen so many bodies. But I wouldn't give up."
She finally found her daughter. "Three bodies were piled on top of Sevda. That's how we found her."
Iranian authorities acknowledge that more than 3,000 people were killed in the protests, but claim some were members of the security forces. One human rights group, Hrana, however, estimates the number of dead stands at more than 7,000, most of them protesters.
Finding Sevda's body was just the beginning of Samira's battle with the authorities, she says.
To be allowed to take away the body for burial, she says she was forced to say that "terrorists" rather than the security forces had been responsible for Sevda's death.
"They did this to cover up what they'd done on 8 and 9 January, to hide how many people they had killed. They silenced families by telling them to say their loved ones were killed by Israeli or American terrorists."
Nevertheless she was barred from visiting the grave after the funeral, or organising a tombstone, she says.
And Samira says the harassment continued. A few days before the ceremony to mark 40 days since Sevda died - highly significant in Iranian culture - she says she was summoned by a local branch of the Ministry of Intelligence.
"They told me: 'You should give us an interview and say that Sevda was a Basiji and she was killed by the protesters. Then we will announce her [as] a martyr - you will then receive perks, a house, or anything that you want.'"
She is sure this offer was prompted by fear, because she had shared Sevda's death with an Iranian media organisation based in London, once the internet had been reconnected in the country.
"It scared them that I was in touch with external networks or those outside Iran."
To avoid giving the interview, Samira fled Iran as soon as the 40th day anniversary was over.
"I didn't want to trade with my child's blood."
She says people smugglers helped her to escape. She crossed rivers and mountains to get to safety.
A video she made of herself fleeing makes clear her fury.
"This crap government, these bastards, they've harassed me so much," she tells the camera as she marches along a mountain path bordered by a deep ravine.
Samira says after she continued to give interviews to foreign media from abroad, she was charged in absentia with a string of offences, including "moharebeh" - waging war against God - which can carry the death penalty.
To mark what would have been Sevda's 17th birthday, her relatives and friends held a vigil - with Samira watching from exile on a livestream.
"Then suddenly, the feed cut out," she says.
She discovered that the event had been raided, she says, and some of her family and friends arrested by the IRGC.
She says her family was warned by the authorities that, if they continued to gather at Sevda's grave, her body would be exhumed and moved elsewhere.
Now, Samira shares the names, online, of Iranian security force members and officials she believes were responsible for firing fatal shots during the 8 and 9 January protests she and Sevda joined.
"I want justice to be served for every single person whose name I expose, because they have killed so many young people. My goal is for them to be identified so they can be put on trial," she says.
When one of the men Samira named online was later found dead, a regime supporter offered a $5,000 (£3,732) reward for information about her whereabouts, presuming she was responsible. Iranian state media has since reported the arrest of nine people in connection with the death.
Despite the risks, Samira says she refuses to be silenced.
"Every day and every second without Sevda is very difficult for me. It's like a mother who has lost her heart, who has lost her being, has lost her life…
"But the fact that Sevda is not breathing has made it possible for me to stand on my feet… to think about honouring her life and her path... all those bodies I saw, all those body bags I opened looking for Sevda, they all made me fight the Islamic Republic until my last breath."

bbc.com.title: How a Democrat in Michigan rocked the party days before the US midterms
bbc.com.text:
How a Democrat in Michigan rocked the party days before the US midterms
Haley Stevens, a sitting Democratic congresswoman, stood alongside the Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
It was a surprise appearance that saw Stevens endorse the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, instead of her fellow Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed.
BBC's Nada Tawfik was in Detroit, Michigan where the party spat unfolded.

bbc.com.title: Trump makes final campaign push in final weekend before election
bbc.com.text:
- Published
In the last weekend before the pivotal midterm elections, US President Donald Trump has made a final pitch to voters in hopes of keeping Republicans in control of Congress.
Trump held rallies in Florida, Iowa and Kansas - states he won in past elections - in a sign of Republicans' defensive stance ahead of Tuesday's vote.
Facing voter frustration over rising prices, Trump sought to tamp down such concerns and shift focus on attacking Democrats, saying they would "bankrupt" families if elected.
Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance at winning at least partial control of Congress, which would act as a check on Trump's power and could upend the last two years of his presidency.
Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.
Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.
In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.
Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".
Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.
At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.
In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said this weekend that he was "very confident" his party was on course to win control of the House of Representatives, as senior Democrats including former President Barack Obama made final appeals to voters.
A forecasting tool from Harvard University that analyses and compiles multiple polls and historical data suggests that Democrats have a 96% chance of taking the House and a 76% chance of taking the Senate.
A national poll from NBC News posted this weekend suggests that registered voters prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, leading Republicans 52% to 45%.
But along with the last-push campaign stops, this weekend featured a dramatic turn in the Senate race in Michigan - a tightly contested seat currently held by Democrats.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
The move led to widespread condemnation from fellow Democrats and praise from Republicans, including Trump who called her "very brave".
In Alaska, home to another crucial Senate race, a judge on Sunday dismissed an attempt by the Trump administration to delay certifying election results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses due to two candidates appearing on the ballot with the same name.
In the lead up to the election, Trump and his administration have repeatedly cast doubt on both the credibility and security of the vote, despite evidence showing voter fraud is rare. The justice department has launched investigations or demanded votes be set aside in multiple US states.
The stakes are high for Trump, as midterm election results are seen as a measure of how satisfied Americans are with a president's performance.
In most midterm elections, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress to the opposing party - meaning Trump's Republican party has the most to lose.
Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, don't want to relinquish their party's majority in Congress, as losing any seats would hinder their ability to pass laws and shape policies.
Democrats, however, are keen to gain control from Republicans. Holding a majority would enable them to challenge Trump's agenda, give them investigative powers over his administration, and could also help them showcase their vision for America ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
For lawmakers, it's all about gaining or maintaining power and control, but it's Americans who will feel the impacts of their policies.
Who gets elected at the city, state, and federal level affects many aspects of voters' everyday lives, including the cost of gas, rising inflation and grocery prices, healthcare and abortion access, income and property taxes, and immigration.

bbc.com.title: China state broadcaster pulls La Liga matches following Mbappé joke
bbc.com.text:
- Published
China's state broadcaster CCTV did not air a Real Madrid match on Sunday, despite the club's star striker Kylian Mbappé's apology for his "ill-judged" remarks on the late Chinese leader Mao Zedong.
Mbappé drew huge backlash after saying the meme "that makes [him] laugh the most" was the one in which his face is superimposed on a "Chinese dictator" resembling Mao.
China Media Group, CCTV's parent organisation, said last Tuesday it would suspend broadcasts of Spanish football La Liga matches following the furore, which also led to Mbappé being dropped by several Chinese brands.
China's foreign ministry had said it took Mbappé's apology "seriously". Real Madrid and La Liga have also apologised.
China Media Group had earlier demanded apologies from the three parties, calling them "an absolute prerequisite" for moving past the incident.
It has acknowledged the apologies, but has not commented on how long the broadcast blackout will last.
Mbappé, who reportedly made his remark about the meme on French talk show The Bridge, apologised later on Tuesday.
"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he had said.
The joke did not go down well in China, where Mao is revered by the Communist Party, despite his having overseen one of the bloodiest chapters in the country's past.
Mao, who led the Chinese Communist Party to victory in the civil war and founded the People's Republic of China, died in 1976.
During his rule he oversaw the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution, which led to a famine that killed tens of millions and unleashed violent purges across Chinese society.
This is not the first time Beijing has suspended sports broadcasts over political sensitivities.
It pulled NBA games for a year from October 2019 after Daryl Morey, the general manager of Houston Rockets, tweeted in support of Hong Kong protesters during widespread pro-democracy protests in the city.
Morey backtracked on his comment after fierce criticism from Chinese fans, sponsors and commercial partners.
"I have had a lot of opportunity since that tweet to hear and consider other perspectives," Morey later wrote.
"I have always appreciated the significant support our Chinese fans and sponsors...I would hope that those who are upset will know that offending or misunderstanding them was not my intention."
Real Madrid beat Racing Santander 3-0 in Sunday's match, with goals from Mbappé, Jude Bellingham and Yan Diomande.

bbc.com.title: Democrats have high hopes for midterms - but are the polls right?
bbc.com.text:
- Published
The Democratic Party has high expectations as it heads into these pivotal US midterm elections.
A historically unpopular Republican president, an American public unhappy with the rising costs of food and bills, and months of favourable polls point to a good night for them on Tuesday.
Democratic candidates lead in well over the 218 seats needed to flip control of the lower chamber of Congress, the House of Representatives, the polls suggest. And they are tied or narrowly ahead in the key Senate races.
A recent New York Times poll had the Senate race in South Carolina, a state Donald Trump won by 18 percentage points in 2024, as a tie. Recent CNN surveys put the Democrats ahead in Texas, Kansas and Maine.
But are the polls accurate?
Recent US political history is littered with examples where public opinion polls, even ones just days before an election, were off the mark. Trump outperformed predictions on his way to White House victories in 2016 and 2024. His narrow defeat in 2020 came after most surveys indicated a more comfortable win for Democrat Joe Biden.
Earlier this year, polls suggested Democrat Abdul El-Sayed was poised for a double-digit win in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary. Instead it was 1%. In Wisconsin's Democratic primary for governor, the candidate that had a polling lead that approached 20 points lost by a fraction of a percent.
According to Clifford Young, president of Ipsos Public Affairs, which conducts political and market research surveys, polling has become difficult in recent years because it's harder to reach Americans as they abandon their land lines and screen their calls. And many of those who pollsters do contact have become less willing to participate.
"Conservatives, especially those on the far right, are much more anti-establishment by nature," Young says. "And they don't participate in anything. They hate the system. That's the challenge."
If Republican voters are being undercounted in a systematic way, and polling companies don't take that into consideration when constructing their voting models, it could skew their data towards the Democrats.
That's one of the reasons why it has become trickier for pollsters to predict what the electorate will look like.
One explanation for why Trump overperformed in previous presidential elections is that his supporters – many of whom were not regular voters – flocked to the polls in higher-than-expected numbers.
That unpredictability is one of the main contributing factors to those notable recent polling misses, even if the margins in most reputable polls were only off by a few percentage points.
In a close race, those few points can make the difference between victory and defeat for a candidate. And this year, many of the key Senate races are within those narrow margins.
In recent years, midterm general election polls have proven to be more accurate, in part because Trump - and his unique ability to draw disaffected Americans to the polls - was not on the ballot.
In 2022, they suggested Democrats would defy conventional expectations and avoid an electoral wipe-out despite Biden's low approval numbers.
While the party lost control of the House of Representatives, the margins were slim and Democrats maintained control of the US Senate.
While this year's primary results did provide bigger surprises, Young says that nominating contests have historically been volatile, with voters more likely to make up their minds at the last minute. It shouldn't be seen as an indication that the current crop of general election polls are off the mark.
It's common for the party of the president to have a bad night in the midterms.
One of the most notable examples in recent years came in 2010 when Republicans flipped more than 60 House seats and made gains in the Senate.
It came off the back of an economy struggling to recover from the financial crash and conservative fears over President Barack Obama's healthcare reforms. A defeat had been predicted by the polls but not quite on that scale.
The roles are reversed this time, with the Democrats in opposition and the economy on the minds of voters. But there are a number of reasons why Democrats may not have as good a night as history might suggest or as some might expect, given Trump's low approval rating.
Firstly, much of the territory in play in this election Trump conquered with ease in the presidential election just two years ago. It's like a home game for Republicans.
Then there have been changes to House election boundaries over the years that have meant fewer seats switch between parties.
Thirdly, there are fewer swing voters due to the deeper polarisation of the country. Some experts describe the electorate as calcified.
There's also the cash advantage Republicans have enjoyed which has given them hundreds of millions of dollars to spend on attack ads in the final weeks.
Polling models try to capture shifting fundamentals. And a well-designed poll is built to anticipate issues that may make it less than reliable.
Individual polls do have a built-in margin of error – a statistical level of uncertainty based on the sampling size compared to the population as a whole. Taken as an aggregate, polling averages and not individual surveys can provide a more accurate prediction.
At the moment, even the kind of polling lean we saw in recent presidential elections would suggest Democrats are likely to have a good night on 3 November. And polling inaccuracies can go both ways. In last year's state and special elections, Democrats outperformed most surveys as it was their voters who turned out in unexpectedly larger numbers.
The sight of Trump holding rallies in the final days of the campaign in states he won comfortably in 2024 will have lifted Democrats' hopes that Republican internal polling has conservative candidates in trouble.
There's always the chance that voters change their minds right up until election day, however.
Sometimes there are late shifts that can alter the dynamics of a race. Sometimes undecided voters, which still account for a key segment of the electorate in many of these races, all break the same way.
In polling, there will always be some level of uncertainty – and managing that is the art that goes along with the science.
"I think we're doing a better job," says Young. "But part of the problem we always have is not just with the pollsters. Part of it is that we're dealing with humans. Humans are not easy."
Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here. Those outside the UK can sign up here.

bbc.com.title: France launches attempted murder investigation after petrol bomb thrown at police
bbc.com.text:
- Published
Prosecutors in France have launched an attempted murder investigation after petrol bombs were thrown at police during unrest, French media reported.
An image of a police officer with his leg on fire during a clash with protesters in Paris on Saturday has prompted outrage and follows weeks of street protests in France that have also seen demonstrators injured.
The officer, who suffered burns to his ankle and minor injures to his hand, told French newspaper Le Figaro it was a "particularly sophisticated" incendiary device.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said throwing a molotov cocktail at a police line was "what I call a murder attempt", adding officers were working to find the perpetrators.
Hundreds of thousands of people demonstrated across France in largely peaceful protests on Saturday, the latest in a series of youth-led protests that began in late September demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially schools.
Following previous clashes and looting, thousands of police officers were deployed across the country over the weekend, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities.
There were more than 770 arrests on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said.
But police said no one had been arrested for the attack caught on camera that set a police officer on fire, AFP reported.
The officer - part of the National Gendarmerie, a national law enforcement force that is technically part of the military but under the control of the interior ministry - said his unit "suddenly found ourselves facing several hundred hostile, well equipped adversaries".
Speaking to French newspaper Le Figaro, he said police were yet to identify the liquid used but that the incendiary device "had a far greater burning capacity than a standard Molotov cocktail".
"We faced hostile individuals who are not protesters," he said. "These adversaries are there with the intent to harm those who represent the state."
Fourteen other officers sustained wounds ranging from minor to serious, he said, adding some were struck by paving stones. The unit was supposed to be on leave but had been urgently recalled to police the weekend protests, he said.
French protest organisers, the Gilets Jaunes, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".
France suspended the use of one type of stun grenade while policing student protests in early October after a 15-year-old's hand was blown off, but French newspaper Le Monde has reported that police have continued to use a different model in subsequent protests.
Protests also took place in Germany and Italy over the weekend, as mainly youth-led protests continue across parts of Europe, with varying demands but broadly linked to a focus on cost-of-living issues and public services.

bbc.com.title: Antonelli - the boy 'born in a garage' who became world champion
bbc.com.text:
This is an updated version of an article first published in August 2026
Kimi Antonelli was 10 when his father Marco first realised the boy sitting on his lap, operating the steering and gears, might have an exceptional talent as a racing driver.
The pair were at the Adria circuit in north-east Italy, Marco with his Lamborghini sports car team, Kimi competing in a karting race.
It was the end of the day and Marco, a former driver himself, asked his son: "Do you want to try the Lamborghini?"
Of course he did.
Marco strapped himself and Kimi into the car, belts extended around both. Dad was in charge of the throttle and brake, his son would control the rest.
"I couldn't see the track because he was in front of me with a helmet on," Marco tells BBC Sport. "I could only see beside me the marker panels before each corner - 100m, 50m.
"We started to drive, step by step, faster, faster, faster. In the end, I pushed like I was alone and I arrived at the braking point at the end of the straight, 320km/h, braked very hard and at the limit.
"The car had a lot of oversteer. Kimi controlled the oversteer perfectly, then I went on the throttle, Kimi finished the oversteer, changed gear, and went.
"I said: 'OK, stop, because it has now become dangerous.' But when I saw the video, 10 years old, on my leg, oversteer, everything perfect, I said: 'Maybe he has something special.'"
And now Kimi, who turned 20 only in August, has dominated F1 in only his second season, and become the youngest world champion in the sport's history.
This is the story of a boy his dad says was "born in a garage".
"Kimi from 15 days old was in the garage and heard the sound of the engine and the smell of the exhaust," says Marco, who worked with his wife Veronica on their racing team business.
It was the Christmas holidays when Kimi was about three, and Marco had brought home a simulator he had bought for his guests to try out at the Bologna Motor Show.
"Each evening, Kimi wanted to drive," Marco remembers.
Just like seven years later in the Lamborghini, Kimi would sit on Marco's leg, the controls divided in the same way.
"I remember one night I started to fall asleep because I had been at work very early and we had a crash because I didn't brake when we arrived at the end of the straight," Marco says.
"And Kimi said: 'Dad, dad, no sleep, no sleep. I have to drive.'"
Marco Antonelli did not originally want his son to become a racing driver, because of his own struggles during his career.
"Sometimes you are fast but not in the right position to become a professional driver," he says.
In the 1990s, Marco Antonelli was on the cusp of becoming a works driver in the DTM touring car series, then a huge hit with audiences across Europe.
He tested for Alfa Romeo, but then the team boss left and the opportunity evaporated. Another chance came up with BMW, alongside Roberto Ravaglia and Steve Soper - stars at the time. Again, the same thing happened.
"I suffered a lot for it," Marco says. "And, of course, I was scared that my son [would] relive the same situation. At the beginning, I was very stressed about the passion my son had for motorsport."
Kimi tried a go-kart for the first time when he was five, and immediately showed an awareness of racing lines, braking points and car control.
The Antonellis were what Marco describes as "a normal family". They could not possibly afford to pay for Kimi to take part in all the categories on the way to Formula 1.
Marco decided he could fund Kimi through karting and a year of the basic single-seater category, Formula 4. After that, he figured he might be able to put him in one of his GT cars and become professional that way.
But Kimi immediately started to impress. Whatever category he entered, he was quick, and won.
By the time Kimi was 11, his name was buzzing around motor racing circles. Mercedes heard about him, and their driver academy scout Gwen Lagrue flew to Italy to check him out.
It was a season in which Antonelli had ended up driving a kart with less power than those of his rivals. Marco had told Kimi this would be good for him - he should think not about the result, but about how to improve, always push hard.
"Gwen was impressed about this condition of power and driving in this category that Kimi did," Marco says. "And maybe they understood that Kimi was a different child."
Now Kimi was a member of the Mercedes driver academy, Marco could stop worrying about money, and start focusing on helping his son achieve his full potential.
Mercedes were not the only big names in F1 who had noticed Antonelli's promise.
"When he was in karting, you could already see he was one of the stand-out talents," says four-time world champion Max Verstappen, the only other teenager to win an F1 race.
At 15, Antonelli was ready to move up to cars, and, as a final preparation, did a couple of races in a karting category with gears. On his debut, with minimal pre-event testing, he took pole position. After that, he went to the world final, and stuck it on pole again.
This was the end of 2021, after which Antonelli moved full-time into cars. Through 2022, he swept the board in various championships in Formula 4, and the same happened in Formula Regional in 2023.
1 of 4
By now, Mercedes team boss Toto Wolff was already thinking that Antonelli would be his next F1 driver, potentially a replacement for Lewis Hamilton. With the seven-time champion approaching 40, Wolff was planning on taking control of that generational transition.
So when it came time to negotiate a new contract with Hamilton in 2023, Wolff played hardball. Hamilton wanted to sign for at least two firm years, Wolff only one. In the end, they compromised on a contract for 2024 with an option for 2025.
Hamilton, unimpressed, decided to look at his options, and signed to join Ferrari in 2025, telling Wolff in late January 2024, before the start of that season.
Wolff immediately phoned Marco Antonelli, to tell him the "very big news".
"'We put Kimi in Formula 1,'" Marco remembers Wolff saying. "'What do you think?'
"I said: 'Oh, [it] is a difficult question you ask me. Of course I'm happy that you think about Kimi but are you sure he's ready?'"
Mercedes were at a management away day. Wolff called his senior engineers together to tell them about Hamilton's decision.
"We were reviewing options and trying to come to a fairly rapid conclusion," says trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin.
"We were all keen to just go with Kimi, which we knew was a bit of a risk. But it was quite exciting and we thought, based on his career to date, he had a good chance of being very good. It seemed like a good challenge."
Antonelli had not even driven an F1 car when Wolff made the call. Mercedes put together a testing programme for him, 20-odd days in cars a couple of years old at tracks all over the world to prepare him for his F1 debut in 2025.
Shovlin and the engineers were immediately impressed.
"It was how rapidly he would get up to speed," Shovlin says. "What you normally see with drivers is they're just incrementally going a little bit quicker, braking a bit later.
"If you compare with other drivers we've seen in an F1 car for the first time, the best I'd ever seen until then was George [Russell]. You suddenly saw someone who was quite similar.
"With Kimi, he took a couple of runs to work out how the car behaved and then he'd be more or less on the limit.
"The other thing you can see is the fidelity of the car control, how they can sit with it right on the edge of breaking away from them on entry to a corner, but they can just control it in that condition.
"Equally, when you looked at the mistakes he was making, they were often errors of judgement or lack of experience. They weren't run-out-of-talent mistakes."
Antonelli made one of these at the 2024 Italian Grand Prix. Wolff decided to give him his first experience of an F1 weekend in first practice at his home race at Monza.
It was a spectacular debut - for both good and bad reasons.
Antonelli set the fastest time on his first lap. Then he went for another. He was flying, miles quicker than anyone up to that point, but then he crashed heavily at the final corner, Parabolica.
"No-one on earth could have got the car around the corner at the speed he was attempting," Shovlin says. "He clearly got into his head that he would try and do something special and it was an error of judgment."
Wolff took Antonelli aside, told him it was OK, and not to worry about it. But the crash had a significant impact on Antonelli.
Wolff was very clear in public about managing expectations of Antonelli going into his debut season.
"I conditioned myself so strong that I said: 'There's going to be moments of brilliance and moments where you want to tear your hair out'," Wolff says.
There were stand-out moments, including pole for the sprint in Miami.
But the middle part of the season, through Europe, was a disappointment. A change to the rear suspension design made the car nervous and rocked his confidence. His pace was not impressive, and he made too many mistakes.
"We expected more highlights from him," Shovlin says.
Marco Antonelli explains: "Mercedes needed to have a good result after a period that was not like the Hamilton era. And, of course, needed two cars that always take points.
"Kimi felt this necessity. The crash in Monza was very tough for him to forget. It created on him a big pressure."
Wolff said the "moments of brilliance were there" but then there was "a spell of nine races that was really not good".
"Me, personally, I never doubted," says Wolff. "Other people doubted. In the team and externally."
A year on from his practice debut, Antonelli crashed again in Monza practice.
"This was the point where I said: 'Kimi, you've got to turn this around. This is just not good enough'," says Wolff. "He said: 'I know.'"
Marco Antonelli says he and his son talked a lot during this period and that Kimi "understood that everything can change".
"The period was bad but you can see light at the end of the tunnel," he says. "And step by step he started to take confidence."
Once F1 had left Europe in the autumn of last year, there was a shift.
"Suddenly, we felt like we were making really good progress," says Shovlin.
"There were signs towards the end of the year. I'm not saying any of us thought we'd see what we've seen so far this year, but that we had a decent F1 driver."
Antonelli has been rather more than that this year. He took the season by storm, and established a consistent supremacy over Russell.
In the best car in the field, Antonelli took six poles and six wins in the first 11 races, establishing a 50-point lead in the championship.
Mercedes lost their dominant form in the second half of the season in the face of challenges from first McLaren and then Red Bull.
But Antonelli remained a consistent threat at the front, and he killed off his Monza ghosts in the Italian Grand Prix with a stunning victory after an engine penalty led to him starting 19th on the grid.
He put in a drive of clinical excellence and, with help from a safety car, chased down and caught Russell in the final laps to take a win that will go down in folklore.
The extent of his turnaround in form has shocked almost everyone.
"We were all surprised," Wolff says. "My thoughts were always that he needed to make the experience of knowing all the tracks, the pressure of performing on such a high level under the spotlight of the media, the constant public feedback, whether you're doing well or not, the situations everyone wanted to be close to him.
"There wasn't one single defining factor where I would have said that made it difficult for him, but this year, he knew exactly what to expect. What was really nice to see is that the self-confidence, without feeling any entitlement, has shone."
Marco points to his son's "very strong" mentality.
"In F4 and Freca, he started with not good results, and he was able to remake everything and, at the end, work hard and win the championship," he says.
"We talk about F1. I don't know what the spark is in his brain, but Kimi in the past did the same."
Verstappen says: "For me, there was never any doubt that he would make the jump the year after and already be a lot more consistently competitive.
"It's normal in the progression of a driver. In your rookie season, it can be quite tough, but at the moment, of course, he's doing an amazing job."
Kimi pays tribute to his father, describing him as his "rock", while Wolff also praises the driver's "typical Italian family".
"They are caring, they are loving," Wolff says. "Kimi's character, he's gentle, he has empathy, he has charisma, he has the right amount of intelligence for being a racing driver."
Mercedes have been talking to Antonelli about managing his emotions, which have flared at times this season, such as in the sprint in Canada, when the racing between the two Mercedes drivers came close to boiling over.
Shovlin says: "He just says: 'I'm young, I'm Italian, what do you expect?'"
The remark reveals Antonelli's sense of humour, but also a maturity and self-awareness that might not always be expected in someone so young.
Wolff says: "He has all that. He's actually not [fitting the stereotype of] a typical emotional Italian. He's so clear [in] what he needs to do in a car. I don't see lots of emotion. I see full focus, full concentration. I see, 'OK, this is a problem, let's analyse it, and move on.'
"You see him in a debrief afterwards. You couldn't really say whether there was a bad or a good session. It's all very balanced and stable."
Antonelli took advice on this when he met tennis legend Roger Federer at Wimbledon this summer.
"We chatted about my races," Antonelli says. "About when he used to play, and about life in general.
