npr.org.title: UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
npr.org.text:
UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
CASABLANCA, Morocco — The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory's future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa's northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
"This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period," Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. "A smaller team reporting to the United Nations' Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.
Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force's mandate.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute.''
The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision.'' The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the ''excessive bias'' of the U.S. draft resolution.
Western Sahara is Africa's longest territorial dispute
The U.N. classifies Western Sahara as a "non-self-governing territory," while critics of Morocco's control describe it as Africa's last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the "free zone" that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.
After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.
Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco's foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco's diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.
The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.
The expired mission was established to monitor a referendum
A U.N.-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.
The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain's colonial census to determine voter eligibility.
Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.
As the mission ends, the U.N. secretary-general ''calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara,'' Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."
The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the U.N. said last month.
Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.

npr.org.title: 9 dead as jet nosedives and erupts into fireball near busy roadway in South Florida
npr.org.text:
9 dead as jet nosedives and erupts into fireball near busy roadway in South Florida
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation's transportation secretary said.
Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach County roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a "horrific tragedy." The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation, he said.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."
Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.
A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.
"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.
But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.
"We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.
"We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground."
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, said icing and turbulence could have been factors in the crash and may have caused the plane to stall while it was cruising at 34,000 feet (10,363 meters).
There are many potential factors and the NTSB will consider all of them, including how the pilot responded to the icing and turbulence reported over the radio. But investigators won't rule anything out at this early stage, he said.
The NTSB said investigators were expected to arrive at the crash site on Sunday and Monday. A media briefing is scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.
The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff's officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

npr.org.title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
npr.org.text:
Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.
The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."
Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.
Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:
B – BALANCE loss
Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.
E – EYE changes
Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.
F – FACE drooping
Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.
A – ARM weakness
Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?
S – SPEECH difficulty
Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?
T – TIME to call 911
If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.
A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.
Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.
Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

npr.org.title: Gulf region on edge as Qatar leads talks with Iran to stave off new U.S. attacks
npr.org.text:
Gulf region on edge as Qatar leads talks with Iran to stave off new U.S. attacks
Qatar has been leading intense mediation efforts over the past 72 hours to prevent a new round of possible U.S. attacks on Iran after Tuesday's midterm elections. The uncertainty has the entire Gulf region on edge.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:
Meanwhile, the U.S. and Israel are planning for possible strikes on Iran after Tuesday's midterms, and Qatar has been leading intense mediation efforts over the past 72 hours to try to prevent that from happening. The uncertainty of what comes next has the entire Gulf region on edge. NPR's international correspondent Aya Batrawy is in Bahrain, and she's with us to talk about all this. Hi, Aya.
AYA BATRAWY, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.
PFEIFFER: To start us off, a two-part question - what do these mediation efforts look like, and what has President Trump said, if anything, about how likely another attack on Iran is?
BATRAWY: All right. So Qatar has been really tight-lipped about what's been going on. They did have some mediators visiting Tehran, and also Iran had a delegation in Doha, Qatar - all of this over the past 72 hours. But Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, today, was quoted in Iranian state media saying there's still no definitive conclusion to these mediation efforts. But he said there is talk of a two-day plan. That would include basically the Iranians not attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz to allow for direct talks to begin again between Washington and Tehran.
And Trump was asked about the possibility of restarting the war with Iran. He was at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago, and he said, we're not in that much of a hurry. Have a listen.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We've knocked out almost every piece of military equipment there. We've knocked out a lot of their manufacturing capabilities. We've knocked out the nuclear. We've knocked out their nuclear. We still have to take care of, I would say, one or two sites, but we can do that in 10 minutes.
BATRAWY: So as you heard there, President Trump isn't really saying what he might do after Tuesday's elections. Now, everyone I have been speaking to in the Gulf - from senior European diplomats to Arab military generals - no one has any idea what Trump will do, but the lives of tens of millions of people in the Gulf hinge on his decision.
PFEIFFER: And we have heard President Trump say many times that Iran is essentially finished. We heard him say that again in the cut you just played for us. Based on your reporting, how true is that?
BATRAWY: Yeah. I mean, Iran was hit hard after the U.S. and Israel launched this war eight months ago, killing the country's supreme leader, top military commanders, taking out many of its ships, missile production sites. But even after eight months of war and crippling U.S. economic sanctions, the war has not toppled Iran's regime as Israel said it was its stated goal. And Iran's Revolutionary Guard force is still very capable of inflicting pain on Gulf Arab countries. These are some of the world's most important oil and gas producers, and this war and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz has caused oil and gas prices to rise globally. Brent crude oil is 60% higher today than it was before the war.
PFEIFFER: Aya, you said that Iran could inflict pain on other Gulf Arab countries. Is Iran saying what it would do if it's attacked again?
BATRAWY: Yes. The message from Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, to senior commanders of Iran's armed forces this weekend is that any threat to the country must be met with an immediate response that is, quote, "without geographical limitations." Now, Iran's state media says this means that any new Israeli or U.S. attacks on Iran will inflict even greater damage than we have already seen.
PFEIFFER: We mentioned that you are in Bahrain. Are you seeing signs of damage? Is it evident where you are?
BATRAWY: Yeah. So Bahrain is an island nation. It's a tiny country in the Persian Gulf, with Iran as its much larger neighbor to the East, and it's home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet. But on the first day of this war on February 28, Iran hit back at U.S. military sites across the region, and they hit here on the 5th Fleet's logistics hub and warehouses. So you can't take photos of facilities like this here in Bahrain that have been hit, but you can see the damage to the 5th Fleet's hub right there from the highway. I could see radar equipment that had been hit, and I could see charred and blackened warehouses where the 5th Fleet logistics hub is. And there used to be 8,000 military personnel on this base before the war, and now it's down to less than a hundred.
Now, I have been at the Manama Dialogue - it's a security forum here in Bahrain. And today, Bahrain's foreign minister, Abdullatif Al Zayani, spoke of the many missiles and drones fired at his country by Iran, not just at U.S. military sites but also civilian infrastructure. And he noted that Iran's Revolutionary Guard this month has made new threats to hit undersea internet cables that carry data through the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf States if a war resumes. Have a listen.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
ABDULLATIF AL ZAYANI: This follows the same pattern we have seen at sea - a shared artery is being used as a tool of pressure and threat.
BATRAWY: And Iran did hit Amazon data centers at the peak of this war in the United Arab Emirates in Bahrain.
PFEIFFER: Aya, you mentioned that you're at a security forum. Given that security is top of mind for the whole region now, what kind of emotions, sort of emotional tenor, conversations are you hearing at that event?
BATRAWY: Yeah. I mean, Gulf Arab states - they view Iran as a top threat to their security, but it is still their neighbor. And so while they welcome U.S. pressure on Iran, they did not and do not want war with Iran. Even the United Arab Emirates, which has strong ties with both the U.S. and Israel and has the most hawkish policy in the Gulf on Iran, does not want more war. Senior Emerati diplomat, Anwar Gargash, said it clearly today at the summit.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
ANWAR GARGASH: We really have to deal with this crisis with a lot of wisdom, with political tools being our main tools and with the understanding that military solutions will only complicate the current, very complicated scene that we have and will not actually bring any quick off-ramp to the solution.
BATRAWY: Yeah. So as you heard him say there, military solutions will not bring a quick off-ramp here. And, you know, places like Dubai known as safe havens to invest in and spend your vacations in - that's all been shaken by this war. Economies across the Gulf are suffering. And don't forget Saudi Arabia is struggling now to protect its airports and oil facilities from attacks by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. So the united message here from the Gulf is that more attacks on Iran will be devastating.
PFEIFFER: And the ripple effects of the war are rippling all across the region, for sure. That is NPR's international correspondent Aya Batrawy. Aya, thank you.
BATRAWY: Thank you, Sacha.
(SOUNDBITE OF BADBADNOTGOOD AND GHOSTFACE KILLAH'S "EXPERIENCE")

theguardian.com.title: Democrats condemn Haley Stevens’ ‘betrayal’ following endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers – US politics live
theguardian.com.text:
Democrats condemn Haley Stevens' 'betrayal' following Republican endorsement
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Democratic politicians have condemned congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, over her endorsement of his Republican rival just days before the midterm vote.
Stevens’ extraordinary endorsement of Mike Rogers was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.
As one might expect, top Democrats have been quick to express their outrage at the congresswoman’s “betrayal”.
California governor Gavin Newsom said on the political talkshow 2WAY that Stevens “went another 180 degrees overnight, so something was going on there”. “She’s been successful at taking our eye off the ball and that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it ... This may be curiously the October surprise of sorts,” he added.
Senate majority leader Chuck Schumer also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats. He said:
Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans.
These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.
Meanwhile, Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said:
Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us.
Bernie Sanders joined the controversy, attacking Stevens for what Democrats view as an extraordinary betrayal after Stevens accepted El-Sayed’s narrow victory over her in Michigan’s Democrat senate primaries.
“Rep. Haley Stevens’ staff is right to resign in disgust,” Sanders posted on X. “They understand that the election in Michigan is far more important than Haley’s fragile ego and that all of us must stand together to elect Abdul, defeat Rogers and end the Republican rubber-stamp control of the Senate.”
Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said Stevens had “betrayed” working class people “by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against”.
Read our full report here:
In other developments:
Donald Trump railed against Democratic US senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed at a campaign event in Iowa Sunday, repeatedly referring to the Michigan progressive as a “jihadist”. The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. “If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy,” Trump said.
A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses. Trump said on 23 October that he had ordered the justice department to file the lawsuit in a move that voting rights experts called an “unprecedented intervention” by the federal government with control of Congress in the balance.
Democratic US Senator Chris Murphy has been hospitalized after suffering a stroke. Murphy, 53, started feeling numbness in his arm while attending his son’s hockey game on Saturday, according to the Connecticut senator’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt. A hospital visit confirmed that Murphy had experienced a stroke.
Some of the people who worked for Stevens’s campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers endorsement.
Her long-time chief of staff, Justin German, and her communications director, Logan Basch, were among those who left, according to CNN correspondent Manu Raju.
German later released a statement on behalf of Stevens’ campaign team endorsing El-Sayed:
As Haley Stevens’ Chief of staff for eight years, I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate. This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines.
We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.

theguardian.com.title: Europe could face colder weather as polar vortex weakens
theguardian.com.text:
The stratospheric polar vortex over the northern hemisphere is facing the prospect of an unusually early weakening. Forecast models suggest it could weaken significantly over the next 10 days, when it would typically be strengthening.
A major sudden stratospheric warming (SSW) event is possible. This could influence weather patterns in the following weeks, increasing the likelihood of persistent areas of high pressure across the mid-latitudes and colder conditions weeks later.
The polar vortex is a large area of low pressure and cold air high above the Arctic. It weakens during the summer before strengthening during autumn and into winter. Its strong anticlockwise circulation helps contain the coldest air near the pole, although disturbances can allow colder air to spill southwards into the mid-latitudes.
An SSW event occurs when temperatures high in the stratosphere rise rapidly, often by as much as 50C in just a few days. This is associated with a dramatic weakening, or even reversal, of the strong westerly winds surrounding the polar vortex, disrupting its circulation. The earliest recorded major SSW, occurred on 28 November 1968, after records began 1958. Current forecast models strongly favour a significant weakening of the vortex, but a complete reversal of the winds required for a major SSW remains uncertain.
Such a development would mark a notable early-season disruption, with potential implications for weather patterns into early winter. The likelihood of colder, more settled conditions across northern Europe could increase, although a spell of severe cold appears unlikely over the next two to three weeks.
Meanwhile, an area of low pressure that deepened in the Mediterranean Sea last week is expected to bring heavy rain and strong winds to central and southern Italy on Monday, prompting warnings being issued for these areas. More than 100mm of rain is forecast to fall in just 24 hours across higher ground in southern Italy.
The system is expected to move eastwards across the Ionian Sea, before making its way to Greece, which is still recovering from exceptionally wet and unsettled weather last week.

theguardian.com.title: ‘A despicable betrayal’: Democrats incensed by Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Mike Rogers
theguardian.com.text:
Michigan Democrat Haley Stevens’ shocking last-minute endorsement of Mike Rogers, a Republican Senate candidate, has sparked fierce backlash from members of her party.
Stevens, who narrowly lost in the Democratic primary for Senate to Abdul El-Sayed, announced her support for Rogers after a feud with the El-Sayed campaign over an outside group’s campaign ad that blamed the high cost of living on US support for Israel.
Stevens had said she would appear at a campaign event if he denounced the advertisement, El-Sayed’s campaign disinvited her.
Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, a Democrat from New York, described the move as “a despicable betrayal”.
“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors,” Schumer posted on social media.
Nancy Pelosi, a California representative, posted that Stevens had “chosen to dangerously betray Michigan families’ healthcare, freedoms and future with her horrific endorsement”.
Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor, also said that “working class people’s lives are on the ballot on Tuesday”.
“Haley Stevens just betrayed them by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against,” Mamdani posted.
Curtis Hertel, the chair the Michigan Democratic party, said in a post that Stevens was not a member of the party “nor will she be in the future”.
A Detroit journalist, Sam Robinson, shared a video in which Hertel was asked why he thought Stevens made the endorsement.
“Obviously there are sour grapes from the election, but there is no reasonable explanation for this. I have known Haley Stevens for a long time, and I know what she has fought for her in her career, and this is the antithesis of all of that,” Hertel said.
Debbie Dingell, a Democratic representative from Michigan, said the state’s residents were focused on the cost of living, healthcare and housing.
“That’s what they’re talking about, not Congresswoman Stevens’ continued efforts to get attention,” she said in a statement.
While some Democrats and Jewish leaders also condemned the advertisement for El-Sayed, congressional nominees Brad Lander and Daniel Bliss, both of whom are Jewish and Democrats, issued a statement Sunday encouraging voters to support El-Sayed. They did not mention Stevens.
“In the closing days of this election, we must remember the true choice of this race,” the statement read. “One candidate represents a party that has stoked hatred, gutted anti-discrimination efforts and remained silent in the face of President Trump’s corruption and authoritarianism. The other represents the promise of accountability, affordability, and the fight for a more equitable, just, and democratic future.”
Meanwhile, Trump praised Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers on his platform Truth Social and described her as a “highly respected Democrat”. He continued to support Stevens during a campaign rally Sunday in Dubuque, Iowa, even going so far as to welcome her to join the Republican party.
“I’d love her to join the Republican party, actually, I think that could happen maybe. But she showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the great people of Michigan,” Trump said.

theguardian.com.title: Ukraine and Russia say emergency air-raid warning systems hit by cyber-hacks – Europe live
theguardian.com.text:
In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Russian emergency ministry app hacked hours after Ukraine attack
In Russia, authorities said this morning that hackers had gained access to the Emergency Ministry’s mobile app and sent out “fake information”.
The Emergency Ministry said it had to take the app offline temporarily but reassured residents that the wider alert system – SMS texts, broadcasts, street sirens and loudspeakers – was still in operation.
The Russian ministry didn’t say who was to blame for the attack. But Ukrainian media reported claims from Ukrainian cyber group Atesh that they were responsible for sending messages, which also contained nuclear threats.
One of the messages reportedly told residents, there was “a risk of getting lively” and warned them to “stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide”.
Belgian king 'considering' PM's resignation offer, criticises budget stall
An update in now on the Belgian PM, who’s just left the royal palace where he had a 90minute meeting with the king to offer his resignation.
The palace says that the King is “considering his decision and will consult with the party leaders of the various coalition partners starting tomorrow.”
Prime Minister Bart De Wever had offered his resignation to the king this morning after failing to pass a budget and coalition party talks breaking down last night.
The king admonished the lack of accord between politicians in the current environment of “great geopolitical uncertainty”. His statement reads:
The king regrets that no agreement has been reached on a credible budget aligned with current challenges.
In a context of great geopolitical uncertainty and significant economic challenges, the country cannot afford a prolonged political crisis.
'Disinformation as much a part of war as bombs and bullets'
Frances Mao
Back to the cyber warfare we saw last night in the app hacking in Ukraine, and then Russia.
As I noted earlier, this was direct attack on a core channel of communications between Ukrainian authorities and citizens; this app is embedded in everyday life in a war zone.
And while the full impact of the hack is still unclear – how many Ukrainians were deceived and believed the warnings for example - residents nonetheless have described how alarming it was getting a message on their phone warning of potential nuclear warfare.
Cyber-warfare expert Don Smith, from IT security firm Sophos, says these sorts of attacks are aimed at grounding down people’s mental toughness.
Disinformation is as much a part of war as bombs and bullets. Targeted information attacks could aim to impact the mental resilience of the people of Ukraine.
Their resilience is a key part of their ability to defend against the Russian military.
However he noted the ameaturish nature of this attack. One of the message sent out, in Russian, was almost jokey and casual in tone, reading: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying”, a reference to Russia’s hypersonic missiles which can pretzel and outpace most interceptors.
Usually the best information warfare is not obvious or explicit, where this very clearly is. It could indicate desperation from Russia.
Belgian PM meeting with King to tender resignation
Belgium’s prime minister Bart De Wever is handing in his resignation this morning following failed attempts to pass a budget, local media are reporting.
De Wever has been trying to get budget cuts through, and failed in late-night coalition talks yesterday to secure a compromise.
He arrived at the Royal Palace in Brussels this morning to meet with King Philippe, Belgian media say.
However they report he may be instructed to try and secure a deal again, by a certain deadline.
In Kyiv, residents received a succession of unusual alerts late on Sunday night over the period of roughly an hour.
Typically, people can receive several alerts a day warning of incoming Russian drones or missiles; locals after four years of living in a warzone are used to their phones going off, often followed by sirens in the street.
But these messages warned of radically different threats- a nuclear radiation warning, a chemical attack and even an incident of street fighting in Kyiv.
One of the messages was also transmitted in Russian, a clear tell that something was potentially off.
The messages sent out were:
22:47: “Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv.”
22:48: “Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don’t worry, it’s Oreshnik flying” [This message was written in Russia]
22:49: “Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
22:49: “Street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don’t go outside.”
23:53: An all clear is sent out
Ukrainian authorities within the hour had publicised messages on Telegram saying they believed the app system had been compromised.
The air raid alert channel said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with the system, which had been temporarily taken off line. It urged users to not click on links in “suspicious notifications”.
The Air Force wrote on Telegram: “The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.
Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.
These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).
This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.
In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.
Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.
Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.

theguardian.com.title: Tories accuse Shabana Mahmood of ‘u-turn’ on indefinite leave to remain policy – UK politics live
theguardian.com.text:
Andy Burnham is now on his way to the Commonwealth summit in Antigua. The government plane that is taking him left from Stansted early this morning, but it went to Manchester first, where it stopped to pick up the PM. He is now en route to the Caribbean, where he will arrive this evening after a refuelling stop in Canada.
Tories and Reform UK accuse Mahmood of surrendering to 'open-borders Labour left'
Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, is already ridiculing the indefinite leave to remain (ILR) announcement coming this afternoon. In a post on social media, he claimed that she was surrendering to “the open-borders Labour left”.
Later today the government will announce their u-turn on ILR, or Indefinite Leave to Remain.
It’s clear Shabana Mahmood has been forced to surrender to Angela Rayner and the open-borders Labour left. She will now allow hundreds of thousands of low-wage and no-wage migrants to stay in the UK forever and claim benefits.
By Mahmood’s own admission in a speech this March, letting low wage care workers alone stay forever will cost taxpayers £10 billion and be an “affront”. Now it looks like she’s about to do exactly that. After talking tough all year, Mahmood appears to have capitulated control of immigration policy to Angela Rayner - and Mahmood’s position is looking increasingly untenable
The Conservative plan is a ten year route to ILR, only for high wage workers. No more low wage workers should be allowed in, and those already here should be required to leave when their temporary work visa expires
Nigel Farage, whose Reform UK party wants to get rid of ILR completely, has made a similar argument in his own social media post.
The Labour Party is at war with itself over Indefinite Leave to Remain (ILR), with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood losing a fight to the far left of her own party. Tomorrow, she’s expected to cave on plans to even tinker with the ILR numbers. Angela Rayner emerges victorious, with her defence of the Tory-era policies hinging on “fair play” towards foreign nationals.
But what about fair play towards the British public? Doesn’t that count for anything anymore? Villages, towns, suburbs, and cities have to deal with the weight and strain of all this. Not only are ordinary Brits never consulted, but this current cabinet doesn’t even have an electoral mandate. It is rightly infuriating to most people who increasingly want net negative migration into Britain.
‘Was I not enough?’: care worker barred from meeting home secretary tells his story
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is due to meet some union leaders today to discuss with them her plans for indefinite leave to remain. Andrea Egan, who as Unison general secretary has many members working in the care sector, has been particularly critical of the original proposal to make foreign care workers wait 15 years for ILR. Recently she condemned Mahmood for refusing to let her bring a care worker to a meeting they were due to have about the plans.
That care worker was a Nigerian called Kolade. Aamna Mohdin has interviewed him, and he explained what he wanted to tell Mahmood.
For Kolade, the row encapsulates what he believes is missing from the immigration debate: the voices of those whose lives could be upended by its policies. He has watched politicians dismiss care work as low-skilled and portray migrant workers as a burden on the British economy.
“I was just going to tell her that is not correct,” he said. “We are not a burden to the British state. We are also contributing as much as we can, supporting British families.
“She talked about fairness to the British people. I was going to tell her that caring for British families is our own little way to show that we are contributing, and that we have earned our rights to stay in this country, a place we’re currently calling home.”
Burnham declines to say net migration still too high as Mahmood prepares to unveil tougher settlement rules
Good morning. Often these days, when the government has a big announcement and just before the relevant minister starts to give the details in a statement to MPs, Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, erupts with fury and rants and raves at the Treasury bench about how all the main points have already been leaked to the media, in contravention of the ministerial code.
Not today. Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will this afternoon unveil the final version of her plans to make foreign workers wait longer before they can apply for indefinite leave to remain, and we know relatively little about what she will say. The original plans were unveiled last November and they would require most workers to wait 10 years, not five, for ILR, with care workers having to wait 15 years. They would also apply to foreign workers already here, not just new arrivals. These proposals were hugely controversial, and Andy Burnham himself was among the ministers arguing that care workers should be treated more kindly.
As Jessica Elgot and Chris Osuh report in our overnight story, there has been some sort of climbdown in relation to care workers.
But it also seems to be the case that the broad thrust of the plan is being retained and that ILR rules are being toughened in a way that will affect hundreds of thousands of people.
The detail, which is coming after 3.30pm, will be crucial; so will the reaction of Labour MPs. When Mahmood announced these plans last autumn, some government backbenchers were horrified. But mostly public condemnation was muted. At the time Reform UK had a lead of more than 10 points over Labour in the polls and Mahmood – who was arguing that net migration was too high and that low-skilled foreign workers ended up being a burden on the taxpayer (a key Reform UK claim, although one contested by experts) – was pushing at an open door.
Now the situation is very different. The electoral threat from Nigel Farage has receded quite a lot. And net migration is falling like a stone. Here are the figures from last week’s OBR report.
To implement the ILR changes, Mahmood does not need primary legislation and that means there will be no chance for potential Labour rebels to amend the plans in the Commons. But it has been reported that more than 100 MPs are queasy about what is being planned.
And Andy Burnham himself has accepted that the context has changed. We won’t hear from him until much later, because he is spending most of the day on a flight to the Commonwealth summit. But, in an interview for an ITV documentary being broadcast tomorrow, he declined to say that net migration was too high. When Keir Starmer was PM, he regularly did say this, and that he wanted immigration to fall “significantly”. Burnham told ITV small boat crossing numbers were “too high, for certain”. However, asked about legal migration, he replied:
It’s come right down. And I think when you have planned migration, it’s difficult to say is it too high or too low, because it’s got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy.
Burnham said legal migration had “come right down”. He declined to be drawn on whether it had to come down further.
This means that Mahmood will today be defending plans drawn up in response to a problem that some might argue no longer exists. However, speaking in the Commons last November, Mahmood argued she had to do something about the “so-called Boriswave, specifically the cohort of lower-qualified workers who – along with their dependants – entered the country through the health and care visa” because some of them were “never expected to be net economic contributors”, making “more stringent” controls needed.
Here is the agenda for the day.
11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
12.30pm: Danny Kruger, Reform UK’s head of government preparations, gives a speech to the Policy Exchange thinktank.
2.30pm: Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
After 3.30pm:Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, gives her statement on the changes to indefinite leave to remain rules.
Evening: Andy Burnham arrives in Antigua for the Commonwealth summit.
Also, at some point today Labour will give an update on how many power-sharing agreements at council level with Greens will continue, in the light of Labour HQ saying recently Labour councillors should only continue to work with local Green parties willing to disown the “Zionism is racism” motion passed at the Green conference.
I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

theguardian.com.title: Palantir AI tech unused or little used by 29 NHS trusts said to be benefiting from it
theguardian.com.text:
More than two dozen hospital trusts the NHS claims have benefited from Palantir’s medical data platform are not using all or most of the AI-powered technology, the Guardian can reveal.
The 29 hospital trusts that NHS England publicly lists as “realising benefits” from the controversial £330m federated data platform (FDP) have said the system is not live or they are not using any of its applications. The apparent gap between the NHS claim and the trusts’ understanding was described as “very misleading” by one senior health official.
It comes as the health secretary, Yvette Cooper, faces calls from MPs and campaigners to axe the US tech firm’s contract to deliver the flagship government AI system, which aims to connect scattered medical files, speed up hospital discharges and improve surgery scheduling among other potentially life-saving improvements.
Palantir’s UK and Europe chief executive, Louis Mosley, said ending its contract would be “putting politics above patients” and accused critics of “Palantir Derangement Syndrome”. The company has contracts to supply AI to the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security crackdown, while its billionaire founder, Peter Thiel, has questioned democracy, said tech companies can “unilaterally change the world” and called technology an “incredible alternative to politics”.
NHS England has previously faced scrutiny over how it has used data to defend the Palantir contract, which began in 2024. It claims 117,539 more operations were carried out by trusts using the FDP in a year, but this summer it conceded it could not prove cause and effect, and the Office for Statistics Regulation (OSR) watchdog ran an investigation. Asked about the claim of NHS Trusts “realising benefits”, the OSR said it will now be “taking this forward under our casework function”.
The contrast between the number of hospitals the NHS claims realise benefits from Palantir’s technology and the statements of the hospitals themselves emerged from more than 100 freedom of information requests. NHS England states on its website that 137 trusts are “live” with the FDP, but of those described as “realising benefits”, 29 responded that they were either not using the system or its apps.
Epsom and St Helier said it was “not using FDP at the moment”, Kent and Medway said the trust “has been focused on other priorities … the FDP is not currently live”, Mersey Care said they had “not yet gone live with the FDP”, Nottingham University Hospitals said “no implementation timeline has been agreed”, and University Hospitals of North Midlands said: “FDP is not live. We do not intend to roll it out in the future.”
Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons science and technology committee, said: “If many NHS trusts don’t see the value of the FDP, serious questions need to be asked about whether the hype surrounding Palantir’s products matches reality.”
She called on the government to activate the 2027 break clause in Palantir’s contract and launch an open competition for a UK-owned and based supplier to handle patient records. The Commons health select committee is also calling for ministers to pull Palantir’s deal.
The FOIs were obtained by Medact, a medical charity campaigning for Palantir to be ejected from the NHS, and shared with the Guardian. Medact spokesperson Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne said: “Our NHS institutions are meant to work in the interests of public trust and evidence-based healthcare, not use creative accounting to justify a deeply controversial contract. There is no good reason for the government to continue this failing project. We now have to ask, if ministers are using these flawed claims to make their decision, are they being misled?”
Asked to respond, NHS England insisted nearly 140 trusts “have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform, helping staff join up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”
It has previously said that its list of hospital trusts reporting benefits includes those using the tools for back office data analysis and submission rather than to support patient care. It is understood trusts that say they do not use the FDP may use a small part of its functionality to help calculate treatment costs. For example, Torbay and South Devon NHS Foundation Trust said it is “not currently operationally using the FDP” but NHS England records it as “live” because infrastructure is in place “to support data submission, rather than active operational use of FDP apps.”
Palantir has been hitting back against criticism of its deal and last month hired Labour’s former deputy leader and member of the House of Lords Tom Watson as a full-time senior lobbyist. Watson this week has been posting videos on X aiming to debunk “myths” about Palantir, including concerns that public services will become “locked in” to its systems. He rebutted criticism from the Green party leader Zack Polanski, who said it was “beyond ridiculous” that Lord Watson was a life peer.
Watson and Mosley have also been writing directly to critical MPs in letters that have counted the times they have spoken out against the company, which one recipient, Labour’s Clive Lewis, described as “very Big Brother”.
Marc Farr, chair of the NHS Chief Data and Analytics Officers Network, said: “I am concerned to hear that there are 29 trusts reported as receiving benefits but when asked are not actually using the tool. It is great that a number of trusts that have adopted the FDP are benefiting from this nationally funded programme, but it is crucial for public support … that benefits are reported accurately, transparently and in a way that can be properly verified.”
A Palantir spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”

theguardian.com.title: Family of murdered student Henry Nowak say police misled and manipulated them
theguardian.com.text:
The family of the murdered teenager Henry Nowak, who was arrested as he pleaded for medical help after being stabbed, have said they were failed by the authorities and fear they were manipulated in their darkest hour.
His parents described how police wrongly told them Nowak, 18, had been the aggressor, and that officers had immediately administered first aid. They said the police watchdog had initially said there was no evidence of misconduct by officers.
“The story was evolving every time we had an interaction,” Henry’s father, Mark Nowak, told ITV News. “What started off as: ‘When the police arrived, we administered first aid,’ moved through a stage where: ‘When the police arrived, they detained everyone’ … to: ‘We actually only detained Henry,’ to then: ‘We handcuffed Henry,’ and then: ‘We placed Henry under arrest.’
“That evolution of what actually happened that night really shocked us, and we felt we were being hoodwinked. We felt we were being not told the truth.”
Novak’s stepmother, Katie Nowak, said: “I do feel that we have been failed multiple times. I fear that we may have been manipulated in our darkest hours. And I fear that some decisions were made to try and protect the police and their reputation rather than help us as a family.”
The student was murdered by Vickrum Digwa, who stabbed him as he walked home from a night out in Southampton in December 2025. Nowak was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa, who was eventually jailed for life, had falsely accused him of racial abuse.
In police bodyworn camera footage that prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.”
The police watchdog, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), is investigating and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder.
Speaking to ITV News, the student’s mother, Lucy Ross, said: “Henry told the police nine times that he can’t breathe, he can’t breathe and he’s been stabbed. What more do you want? Why, why’ve you just … ‘Don’t think you have mate’. What the hell is that all about? And then handcuff him. Why was Henry so dismissed and treated so badly?
“It’s bad enough losing a child. To know that then he was treated in his last moments like that. My poor little boy needed help and he didn’t get it.”
Hampshire and Isle of Wight chief constable, Alexis Boon, told ITV News: “I am incredibly sorry that in his final moments, when he needed us most, we failed him. I recognise that, for Henry’s family, this has been about more than the circumstances of one night. They have rightly raised serious concerns about the police response and their treatment throughout the investigation and since. No family should ever find themselves in this position.”
Novak’s family revealed that the IOPC had said in April: “No [Hampshire police] officers would be subject to conduct or criminal investigation. This was because there were no concerns identified in relation to officer actions.” Less than two months later, Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary was forced to apologise for its actions.
The police watchdog’s director of engagement, Derrick Campbell, told ITV News: “The IOPC is committed to establishing the full circumstances of this case, including whether any of the officers involved should face disciplinary proceedings, and providing Henry’s family with answers to the questions they rightly have about how the police treated Henry in the way they did on that terrible night, and why.”

theguardian.com.title: John Leeson, voice behind Doctor Who’s K9, dies at 83
theguardian.com.text:
John Leeson, the actor best known as the voice of K9, the robot dog in Doctor Who, has died at 83.
Leeson’s son, Guy Ducker, shared the news on Facebook. He wrote: “I regret to announce the death of my father … after a summer of illness. The end was peaceful.”
In a separate post on social media, Ducker said: “Many thanks to the Whovian community for the love they showed to my father over the decades, it meant a lot to him and me.”
Born John Ducker in 1943, he trained at Rada before embarking on a successful career on stage and screen. He was known for his character work across a range of TV shows such as Dad’s Army, Sorry!, Crown Court and Longitude, while other credits included The Bill, Vanity Fair, Doctors and Blake’s 7. He was also a continuity announcer on Channel 4.
But Leeson was best known for K9, created by Bob Baker and Dave Martin, who was introduced to Doctor Who in 1977 in a Tom Baker-led story called The Invisible Enemy.
Originally only intended to appear in that single script, the production team believed the character would be popular with younger viewers, and decided to have the metallic mutt join the Tardis team. He stayed until 1981 – although K9 was also voiced for a period by David Brierly – establishing the catchphrase “Affirmative, Master” when addressing the Doctor.
Leeson reprised the role in the 20th anniversary special of Doctor Who and in a spin-off K-9 and Company, which featured Elisabeth Sladen as popular companion Sarah Jane Smith. Sladen and Leeson were reunited in Doctor Who in 2006 in a David Tennant episode called School Reunion, before featuring in the CBBC spin-off Sarah Jane Adventures, which aired from 2007 until Sladen’s death in 2011.
In an Instagram post after Leeson’s death, the former Doctor Who showrunner Russell T Davies said: “There was no question that we’d ask John to provide the voice” when the robot returned. “A posh dog, uppity, haughty, wry, but somehow innocent too, and so funny. Pitched perfectly so that kids could impersonate him. That’s not easy. A true gent, and a great loss.”
Keith Barnfather, who first worked with Leeson in the 1980s and who produces behind-the-scenes documentaries about Doctor Who, described the actor as “kind, considerate, professional, charming, talented, unassuming”. Lisa Bowerman, who has credits for work across the Doctor Who universe, remembered him as “an utterly lovely man, excellent company and – and I don’t hesitate to use this word for once – a truly iconic voice”.
After leaving school, Leeson worked as a hospital porter before auditioning for Rada. Talking about his career in interviews, Leeson described it as being in two parts: “Half of my career has been pretty much as a stage actor and the television half of my career arose pretty much by accident.”
Leeson had a stint playing Bungle on the children’s show Rainbow, a job in which he described being “poured out of this costume every evening into a taxi”, because a day’s work in a small studio under the hot lights left him “really ill inside this bear suit”.
He also once lamented the haircut he was given when appearing on Dad’s Army, saying: “I was livid because they gave me an army haircut, a real basin job, and then of course put me in a balaclava and a tin hat, so nobody could see the hair anyway.”
He was still working as K9, providing voices for Big Finish audio dramas last year. This was despite, he once said, being told by producers at the BBC after his debut that “under no circumstances would there be anything after the first episode has been shot and is in the can. So don’t expect too much. And here I am in 2025 still attached to Doctor Who … I got to meet a tremendous number of knees doing K9.”

theguardian.com.title: Ryanair considers pay freezes and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar
theguardian.com.text:
Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including pay freezes, reducing crew numbers on flights and increasing the use of AI to offset soaring fuel costs driven by the Middle East conflict.
Europe’s largest low-cost carrier said it expected European airlines to raise ticket prices by up to 20%, with its own jet fuel costs forecast to rise by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.
“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”
Oil prices hit a six-month high on Friday before falling to about $110 a barrel on Monday.
Ryanair expects European short-haul fares to “increase materially” next year, as fuel hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs expire.
“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
The company said its increased use of AI would focus on improving productivity in operations and back-office and support functions.
Ryanair said 80% of its fuel requirements until the end of March were hedged at $67 a barrel. The company’s fuel requirements for the subsequent 12 months are 25% hedged at $95 a barrel.
The Irish airline, Europe’s largest by passenger numbers, said average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter ending in September. Ryanair added that fares in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.
“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said.“[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”
The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter ending inSeptember, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million during the quarter.

theguardian.com.title: Award‑winning Australian children’s author Craig Silvey jailed over child exploitation material
theguardian.com.text:
The award‑winning author Craig Silvey sent multiple messages about his sexual desire for young boys and was caught with explicit images of children and adults.
The young adult novelist was jailed on Monday for seven months after pleading guilty to distributing and possessing child exploitation material earlier this year.
The 44-year-old was found with numerous category one photos and videos on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his Fremantle home, the Western Australian district court heard.
Silvey, a father of three, also engaged in an online conversation with another user on a pornography website, where his handle was Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy.
In the chat, Silvey described himself as a “Fremantle guy” before telling the user: “You sound amazing … we have very similar interests, would love to chat more; do you have Signal or Session?”
The pair moved to an encrypted messaging app, where he said he was “extremely open-minded and obsessed with taboos” and preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the International Dublin Literary Award, also wrote he was “drooling” over a sexually explicit photo of a naked man and boy together.
Judge Hayley Cormann said it was very serious and very disturbing offending.
“This offending involves children and it is destructive and it is devastating,” she said.
The popular author is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, considered a modern Australian classic and adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.
Publishers Allen & Unwin and Fremantle Press, which released Rhubarb, stopped promoting his books after Silvey was charged and most of his titles were removed from reading lists across the country.
Two charges of producing and possessing further child exploitation material were dropped in May.

theguardian.com.title: Meeting Elvis was ‘my biggest day with the Beatles’, says road manager’s book
theguardian.com.text:
Meeting Elvis Presley was “the biggest day of all the years I have spent with the famous Beatles”, the band’s loyal road manager wrote.
It is among recollections in a memoir that Mal Evans had planned to publish, with the band’s permission, before his death in 1976, aged 40, in a shooting by the Los Angeles police. Distraught over the breakup of his marriage, it is believed to have been “suicide by cop” after he repeatedly pointed an air rifle at police.
Now, 50 years later, that memoir is to be published for the first time, having been made available by Evans’s family to Kenneth Womack, one of the world’s foremost Beatles experts and author of numerous books on them.
Evans became the Beatles’ roadie from their early days at Liverpool’s Cavern Club, where he had been a bouncer.
He wrote of working with John Lennon, Paul McCartney, George Harrison and Ringo Starr in diaries and notebooks, while taking thousands of photographs and scooping up discarded lyric sheets, receipts and other ephemera when they were on the road and in the recording studio.
For his memoir, he had hired a stenographer. Womack has all the recordings that Evans dictated into a portable cassette recorder in 1975. The memoir manuscript spans about 95,000 words. Although Womack drew on it for his Evans biography in 2023, the text itself will finally be published in December, titled With the Beatles.
Describing Evans as the Beatles’ first archivist, Womack told the Guardian: “It’s the book Mal was going to publish, taking us into the heart of Beatlemania, reminding us how electrifying it was. He pulls no punches. He shows us the Beatles. It’s very powerful. It’s a treasure trove of new material.”
Its passages include Evans’s first-hand account of the fabled meeting between the Beatles and Elvis – “rock’s greatest heavyweights of all time”, Womack said.
He added: “Mal loved Elvis more than he loved the Beatles, in terms of music. So, for that reason, when they meet Elvis in Bel Air in August 1965, Mal writes page upon page about the experience and what happened.
“There’s been so much debate among writers about that meeting – and now we have this complete record of Mal saying: ‘Here’s exactly what happened.’”
Evans idolised Elvis, writing in one passage: “If there is one day in my life I shall never forget, it is the day when the two biggest phenomena in showbiz met for the one and only time.
“The day the Beatles met Elvis Presley. I was there that day in El’s palatial Hollywood home. And that will always be the biggest day of all the years I have spent with the famous Beatles.”
He recalled that Elvis played them Beatles LPs before finding guitars for each of them. Evans listened in awe as “they began to make the place rock with … improvised beat music”.
Evans’s memoir follows the group from the Help! album through the Magical Mystery Tour EP to the Get Back single sessions and the final studio years.
In one chapter, he wrote of the band’s perilous tour of the Philippines, after they caused unintentional insult in turning down an invitation to an official event with the first lady, Imelda Marcos.
“A large number of the promoter’s staff were wearing automatic pistols in their back pockets … this was brought home to me personally the morning of our departure,” he wrote.
“I had just finished packing when one of the gentlemen entered my room asking for autographed pictures.
“I was in the middle of explaining that I had given away most of the photographs, keeping a few for the plane crew on the way home, when I was cut short by the same gentleman brandishing a gun in my face and repeating the demand. I couldn’t give them to him fast enough.
“This was the prelude to a morning of terror … I waited for the Beatles to arrive, then we proceeded to immigration. We were climbing a stairway inside the airport when suddenly … a dozen men appeared to impede our progress, and started to jostle us.
“It was obvious that they were looking to cause trouble … because of the fiasco the previous evening with the first lady.
“They were standing on our toes, jabbing us with elbows, generally giving us a bad time … I would give my right arm for any of those boys but, under these circumstances, it was most inadvisable to retaliate in any way whatsoever. To stand there and see my beloved Beatles treated so roughly was heartbreaking.”
Womack has pieced together the memoir from material that Evans had stored in “six massive boxes”. It will feature about 400 photographs, including some that have never been seen before.

theguardian.com.title: ‘Traitors in every family’: Hungary to unmask communist-era informants and confront past
theguardian.com.text:
Hungary’s new government will on Wednesday reveal the names of tens of thousands of state informants from the communist era in an attempt to confront the past and rebuild public trust.
From 1945 to 1989, Hungary’s communist state-security services relied on an extensive network of informants to monitor society and suppress dissent. Some were blackmailed or coerced into reporting on neighbours, friends, colleagues and even family members; others were recruited through promises of various advantages.
For decades, the extent of this network was hidden from public view. The “agent files”, held in the basement of the Historical Archives of the State Security services, remained largely inaccessible to the public, despite repeated calls and partial leaks.
During his campaign leading up to Hungary’s April parliamentary elections, Péter Magyar promised to make the state-security files public, a promise he seems intent on fulfilling now he is in power.
In September, his government passed a law paving the way for the files to be made public, a move more than two-thirds of the country supported according to polls. The release was initially scheduled for the anniversary of the 1956 anti-Soviet revolution but was pushed back to 4 November.
“A democratic society has the right to know its past,” Zoltán Tarr, the minister of social relations and culture, wrote on Facebook.
Previously, access to the reports on informants was restricted to researchers and relatives of victims. With the new, searchable online database, Hungary’s former state-service will become the most transparent in the former eastern bloc, researchers say.
“We are opening wide a door that was left ajar,” said István Papp, a historian and head of the academic department of the archives.
“As a historian, I agree with the release of the files. But on a personal level, I feel for those who will face their family’s history for the first time,” Papp said. Of the 50,000 to 60,000 people whose names appear in the files, historians estimate 10% are alive today.
For three decades, the former eastern bloc has been divided on how to publish agent files, and when. In East Germany, the Bundestag opened state security Stasi files in 1992. In the Czech Republic, they became open to the public in 2003. Most recently, Latvia published files on informants in 2018.
Miklós Kiss, a survivor of a Hungarian forced labour camp and president of an association for victims, would have preferred if Hungary had followed Germany’s example and released the files earlier. “If that would have happened, everything would be done and dusted by now.
“People will learn that there were traitors in every family, in every neighbourhood and street,” he added. “But what are we supposed to do with that now?”
Placed side by side, the documents would stretch for three miles, enough to trace the perimeter of London’s Hyde Park. Even so, the collection is small compared with that of the Polish or Romanian secret services, Papp said. In Hungary, many files were destroyed during the 1956 anti-Soviet uprising; others disappeared during the transition of 1989, a gradual, largely peaceful process that gave the authorities time to get rid of incriminating material.
Many of the records will be incomplete, as the agent’s motivation, or extent of reporting, will remain unknown. Of the 60,000 people mentioned in the files, the archives include detailed files, background checks and statements for only 9,000 people. These will be released in February, after personal information, including details of health, addictions and sexuality, as well as information about victims, has been redacted in accordance with privacy laws.
Alexander Faludy, a freelance journalist and Anglican priest, read the files on his family almost two decades ago. His grandfather, György Faludy, spent more than three years in a Hungarian labour camp on fabricated accusations, and later while in exile wrote his book, My Happy Days in Hell.
One report in the files, by a Hungarian woman living in London who befriended Faludy’s grandmother as she was dying of cancer, made him particularly angry. “But then, I looked at the details of the informant. There was a really ominous part in her file, with names of relatives living in Hungary, including details of her elderly parents. Suddenly, my anger evaporated. I just felt very sorry for her,” Faludy said.
“Exile was very painful for my family, but it also conferred certain moral luxuries. And that makes me hesitant in terms of passing judgment on people for what they did if they had to stay in Hungary,” he added.
The identities of secret-service agents have long fascinated Hungarians. Since the 2000s, several partial lists have emerged, naming politicians and prominent artists. Many of them denied involvement, but the allegations alone were enough to plunge governments into political crises.
To date, not many former agents have spoken publicly about their experiences, and the subject remains taboo.
In July, Szemlélek, an independent, religious online journal, published a call for former agents to come forward. Religious figures were a known target of the state services and they were often blackmailed into reporting on their congregation. According to some estimates, 7-10% of them cooperated with the state.
So far, no one has volunteered to tell their story. “I think many people feel that there isn’t really much to speak about,” the paper’s editor-in-chief, Szilárd Szşnyi, told the Guardian. “Or they think that their story is so complex that they cannot, do not want to, or are not ready to tell it.”
Domokos Szokolay, a historian, said he was hopeful that this time “the release won’t turn into a public shaming, but that people will understand that these are complex issues”. His father, Zoltán Szokolay, a poet and politician, was outed as an informant in an unofficial list published in 2005.
Szokolay has yet to read all the reports on his father, who died in 2020. By speaking openly about transgenerational trauma, he hopes to reassure others who discover their loved ones were agents that they are not alone, and to encourage them to start conversations about what they find.
“There are so many family secrets or traumas that we can already talk about: if someone’s parent is an alcoholic, or a gambling addict. But people worry that they will be judged based on the agent files,” he said. “I know confronting one’s family history can be scary or even painful. But learning about it is always better.”

theguardian.com.title: ‘Sharper, longer slowdown’ predicted for economy as fifth interest rate hike looms
theguardian.com.text:
Australia’s economy is set for a “sharper, longer slowdown”, major bank economists say, as the Reserve Bank is forced to keep interest rates higher to rid the nation of persistent inflationary pressures.
The RBA is widely expected to hit mortgage holders with a fifth rate hike on Tuesday, in a move that will push the cash rate to its highest since 2008 amid rising worries the economy could even be tipped into recession.
Belinda Allen, the head of Australian economics at CBA, said the extended Middle East conflict, collapsing house prices and a more aggressive central bank would drive real GDP down to just 1% by the middle of next year, nearly half the previous estimate of 1.8%.
Growth through 2027 would be barely stronger at an estimated 1.1%, according to the updated projections.
Allen said she had expected to see “signs of economic recovery” by the New Year, but now sees the economy “bottoming deeper and later”.
This more pessimistic outlook was “mainly given oil has been a lot higher than we had been expecting,” she said.
“Most people thought we would see a resolution to the Middle East conflict by now and oil [prices] looking more normal. Alas, that has not been the case.”
Instead, Brent crude, the global oil price benchmark, has surged from about $US72 a barrel in early July, to back above $US110 in recent days as the conflict broadens and hopes for a peace deal in the near future have all but disappeared.
After Jim Chalmers last month warned the December mid-year budget update would show a more pessimistic economic outlook, analysts at NAB also revealed a major downgrade to their forecasts.
Gareth Spence, the bank’s head of Australian economics, said “unemployment might need to rise higher than we thought” in order to get inflation back under control – a view he said reflected recent comments by top RBA officials.
The economy would grow below trend over 2027 and 2028, Spence said, echoing the forecast of just 1% growth next year.
Spence forecast the key jobless measure would need to rise from 4.7% to as high as 5.4% by the end of next year, as the RBA doubles down on its battle to regain control of inflation.
The CBA forecast was more optimistic, seeing unemployment peak at 5.1% over the same timeframe.
Either way, the RBA’s multi-year strategy of bringing inflation to heel without sacrificing post-Covid employment gains now looks unlikely to be achieved.
As union leaders protested against the anticipated rate hike in front of the RBA’s offices in Sydney on Monday morning, Spence said the risk was that the central bank would have to hike again.
The deteriorating economic outlook comes as new data showed Australia’s property slump remained on track to be one of the deepest on record.
Shane Oliver, AMP’s chief economist, said home prices could fall by as much as 15% before levelling off late next year, with Sydney property values already down by 10% from their recent peak.
